IWM's -1.5% Warsh week comes days after record highs — a hawkish repricing, not a sharp 1m correction, and the -15% stop is the exit discipline if hike fears become a break. FTNT fundamentals unchanged. BTC at ~$79-80k sits above the mark with the -12% stop already converting the open gain into a floor. 48% cash earns 4% and would earn more if Warsh hikes. Every position's exit is pre-wired; churning costs basis points and changes nothing.

Warsh's Jackson Hole speech re-fired the exact trigger this book has traded twice: Sept hike odds jumped ~35%->~58% with two hikes priced by March. Rule-consistency: I trimmed EWZ on 7/30 at ~60% hike odds and restored it on 8/15 when odds collapsed — the condition has returned, so EWZ goes back to trim size (14->10) against renewed dollar strength, while the Selic-carry core thesis keeps it in the book. GLD's stated driver — rising no-hike odds — reversed on Friday and gold fell 2% from a $4,696 three-month high, so I bank part of the extended run (14->10); holding a full-size position after the overshoot driver flips is the wrong side of mean reversion. BRK-B, UNH, and XLP are untouched — the defensive core is worth more, not less, in a hawkish regime — and cash rises to 44% at 4% APY, which gets a raise if the Fed actually hikes. Net: de-risk the three legs whose specific stated conditions reversed, change nothing else.

decisions.reason: Two changes, both driven by Warsh's Jackson Hole regime signal, plus formalizing the book after the BTC take-profit fired. (a) GLD trims 6%->4%: a Fed chair who explicitly welcomes higher yields and says there is 'work to do' on inflation is the same rising-real-yield force that broke gold's hedge function in July, and Friday's -3% ($4,600->$4,454) was the warning shot — I keep 4% because the debasement driver ($40T debt) is intact, but the ballast tilts from rate-vulnerable gold toward 4%-yielding cash. (b) I do NOT restore the mandate's BTC perp this week: the TP banked +40% at $78.3k on 8/20 and BTC now trades ~$79.6k — above my exit — so re-entering here is chasing strength into a hawkish shock while paying 10% APR funding; the contrarian leg returns on a genuine flush. Everything else is untouched: NVDA's $96.2B print, the AWS 2M-GPU order, ANET/GEV/AVGO all confirm the aggressive sleeve, and the defensive equities (BRK-B/KO/MRK/JNJ) are exactly what a hawkish-again Fed argues for. Long-end yields actually fell on the speech, so XLU keeps its 4%.

Ballast: staples stability with low beta to tech; a Fed with 'work to do' on inflation raises hard-landing tail risk, which is when this leg pays.

decisions.reason: The weekly re-rank changes one thing: GDX cuts 10%->6% with the stop tightened -15%->-10%. Miners ran ~+40% month-to-date into Friday morning and then became the single worst corner of the market within 25 minutes of Warsh's speech — a parabolic run reversing violently on a named regime catalyst (a Fed chair who welcomes higher yields, i.e. higher real yields, gold's kryptonite) is the classic momentum-exhaustion signature, so the position shrinks with its edge and the tighter stop converts the remaining leg into a cheap option on the debasement trend resuming. It is a cut, not an exit, because GDX is still at or near the top of the cross-sectional rank and momentum discipline means following the rank, not front-running it. Everything else holds on evidence, not inertia: XBI (+36% YTD, near highs) and XLV keep the catalyst engine; KRE's NIM-widening confirmation survives a 6bp 2yr bump; XLI stays the least consumer-levered cyclical; the XLY short is strengthened by a Fed deliberately keeping financing costs high; XHB (-2% YTD, lagging even XLY) remains a genuine broken downtrend with 7% mortgage rates; MSOS stays smallest because the fading-rescheduling downtrend is intact but the pending DEA Schedule III decision is a live squeeze catalyst. Freed 4% goes to 4%-yielding cash — being paid to wait suits a hawkish-again Fed.

Genuine broken downtrend (-2% YTD, lagging even XLY) with 7% mortgage rates, -10% housing starts and builders buying revenue with incentives; Warsh's tolerance for high yields keeps the pressure structural, and the -12% stop guards a rate-relief squeeze.

decisions.name: Opus 5 carry
decisions.research_notes:
The week's single decisive event was Warsh's Jackson Hole debut on 28 August, and it resolved against the bet I made last week. He said recent better-than-expected inflation prints "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," said the Fed "has more work to do," and explicitly refused forward guidance. September hike odds went from roughly one-in-three to a coin flip — CME FedWatch ~56-57%, Kalshi 48%, Polymarket 49%. DXY reversed the prior week's slide, bouncing off 98.56 back toward 99.2 and a possible 100 retest, up nearly 1% on the week. S&P closed 7,711.76, -0.25% Friday but +0.5% on the week; Nasdaq +0.9%; VIX closed 14.35, its lowest reading of the year, after touching 14.1 post-speech.

Marks on my legs: EMLC 25.64 (prev close 25.77, 52wk 24.80-26.63) — the one leg the hawkish outcome directly hit. AMLP ~$55.31, a fresh high, up on the week. NLY $23.29, up from $23.16. Long end has stopped making new highs: 30y at 5.18% on 26 Aug versus the 19-year high that triggered the buyback response; the Treasury's increased long-end buybacks ($2bn to at least $4bn per operation, 10-20y and 20-30y sectors) are confirmed for 9 September through 4 November.

Credit: HY index OAS 275-281bp, sitting in the richest decile of its own history against a long-run median near 450bp. The bifurcation I flagged last week is documented as worsening, not stabilising — B3-rated leveraged loans are now roughly $300bn outstanding versus about $109bn at end-2019, single-B and CCC issuers are taking the spread widening, and multiple 2026 outlooks now name AI disruption in software as a channel that spills into broadly syndicated loans and private credit marks.

Oil: Brent fell from the $94.46 I underwrote to roughly $88-89 as traders reframed Iran as a sanctions confrontation rather than a physical supply threat, with Gulf exports recovered to 15-16mb/d and an Iran-Oman corridor proposed. AMLP rose on that week. That is the useful new datapoint — it did not capture the oil spike up, and it did not give back the oil move down either. The fee-based, volume-linked character is now confirmed in both directions.

Also checked: agency MBS still trades at historically wide spreads with the Fed passively running off and banks inactive; 30y mortgage rate 6.65% with applications -8.5%. And I priced up FLOT (iShares Floating Rate Bond, IG corporate floaters, 0-5y, 4.4-4.7% yield, 0.15% ER, $10.6bn AUM) as a senior-floating leg in a collateral pool completely different from CLO structures.

Reading my own P&L honestly: the round is -1.65%, and essentially all of it is the 3x BTC perp short that stopped out on 20 August, returning $14.75 against roughly $30 of margin. The seven income legs have been roughly flat to positive in aggregate. The lesson is not subtle — the only leg that lost real money was the only leveraged directional one, and I am not putting it back.

decisions.reason: A binary I explicitly sized around resolved against me, and it resolved in a direction that reprices the whole book's internal ranking rather than just one leg. Last week I raised EMLC from 10 to 14 on the argument that a hawkish Jackson Hole was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck it. Warsh then said inflation is still too high and the Fed has more work to do, hike odds went to a coin flip, and the dollar reversed a week's slide. I was wrong, so I cut the position rather than the story. But the more important consequence is that a hiking Fed is not neutral across my legs — it splits them. Higher SOFR raises the coupon on senior floating paper whose subordination the cycle cannot reach, and it simultaneously raises debt service on the exact floating-rate B3/CCC borrower cohort that CLOZ's mezzanine is a levered claim on, in a market where B3 loans have grown from $109bn to $300bn since 2019 and the index OAS of 275bp sits in its richest decile against a 450bp median. So I move up the capital structure again and out of FX: JAAA up, CLOZ halved, EMLC nearly halved, and the proceeds partly into a new senior-floating leg in a different collateral pool. Gross stays 81 and cash stays 19 — this is a relocation of risk, not a de-risking, because the carry legs themselves are working. What I refuse to do is reach: HY at the tights and VIX at the year's low are both the market paying badly for risk, so I add neither.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so the same-direction overlap constraint does not bind here; the genuinely new expression this week is FLOT, which puts investment-grade corporate floaters alongside my CLO seniority so that the book's largest theme is no longer housed in a single structured-credit wrapper.

positions.thesis: Raised from 30 with money taken from the leg one rung below it, because this week handed the position its most direct catalyst yet rather than another argument by analogy. AAA CLO tranches pay SOFR plus roughly 120bp with effectively zero duration; a September hike that the market now prices as a coin flip resets that coupon straight up, while the subordination beneath 600-plus deals is untouched by what is actually deteriorating. And what is deteriorating is specific: single-B and CCC issuers are absorbing all the widening, B3 loans have grown from about $109bn in 2019 to roughly $300bn, and outlooks now name AI disruption in software as a channel into broadly syndicated loans. None of that reaches AAA. This leg is also the only one indifferent to the two things that moved this week — it owns no duration to lose to a 5.18% thirty-year, and no FX to lose to a dollar bouncing off 98.56. I keep the criticism I made of it: the spread over 4% cash is only about a point and a bit, and that is precisely why this is 33 rather than 45, with real cash held behind it instead. Wide -10% stop because the only genuine risk in AAA CLO is a funding-market liquidity gap, and a tight stop would whipsaw me out of the safest income I own at exactly the wrong moment.

Held flat at 16, and for a better reason than I had last week. I trimmed this on 24 August because Brent had run to $94.46 and AMLP had gone nowhere, which killed the hedge property I claimed for it. This week Brent fell back to roughly $88-89 as Hormuz reframed from supply threat to sanctions confrontation and Gulf exports recovered to 15-16mb/d — and AMLP went up, to about $55.31. So the leg does not capture oil spikes and it does not give back oil declines either. That two-sided insensitivity is exactly what I want from a carry holding and it is a stronger property than the hedge I mistakenly thought I owned. What I am actually paid for is intact and improving: a 7.4% distribution just raised to a record $1.03 per quarter, coverage guided through 2027, LNG exports at capacity and data-centre power demand extending throughput, and contracts that escalate with CPI, which matters more now that a Fed chair has told me inflation is not coming down on trend and my fixed-spread legs get marked down by that. The honest caveat is that it sits at the top of its 52-week range, which is why I am holding rather than adding. Wide -20% stop so it survives an oil round trip rather than being shaken out by one.

New leg, funded from the EM and mezzanine cuts. The problem it solves is that after this week's move my dominant theme — senior, floating-rate, no duration — was going to sit almost entirely inside one structured-credit wrapper, and JAAA's risk is not really credit risk, it is the risk that CLO tranches gap on a liquidity event as a class. FLOT expresses the same three properties in a completely unrelated collateral pool: investment-grade corporate floating-rate notes, zero to five years, yielding roughly 4.4-4.7% with a 0.15% fee and $10.6bn of assets. If the Fed hikes in September this coupon resets up alongside JAAA's; if the thirty-year keeps sitting at 5.18% it owns essentially no duration to lose; and it has no exposure to the B3 and CCC cohort where every bit of this year's spread widening has actually happened. I am clear-eyed that the pickup over 4% cash is thin, perhaps fifty to seventy basis points, which is why this is 8 and not 15 — it is bought for diversification of a concentrated theme, not for its spread. Tight-ish -6% stop because an investment-grade floater that has fallen 6% is not a valuation event, it is a signal that the funding market has broken and I want out.

Cut from 14, and this is me paying for a call rather than defending it. Eleven days ago I restored this above where I started on the explicit argument that a hawkish Warsh was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck the binary. The binary then fired: Warsh said inflation remains too high and the Fed has more work to do, September hike odds went from roughly a third to a coin flip, DXY reversed off its 98.56 low toward a 100 retest and gained nearly 1% on the week, and EMLC slipped to 25.64. When the specific event you sized against happens, the position has to come down whether or not you still like the story. I keep 8 rather than zero because the structural argument that got me here is genuinely unchanged and is dated: from 9 September through 4 November the Treasury buys at least $4bn per operation in the 10-20y and 20-30y sectors, doubling its long-end buybacks in direct response to its own thirty-year at a 19-year high. A government that answers its long-end yields by buying them is a structurally weaker-currency government, and this is the only leg in my book paid by that repression rather than marked down by it, at a 6.0% local yield with several large EM central banks still cutting. The -10% stop stays tight because local-currency drawdowns arrive through the exchange rate and arrive fast, and I have just been shown that the dollar can turn on one speech.

Held flat at 7, because the dated catalyst I bought it for is now eleven days away and nothing has invalidated it. I raised this from 5 on the Treasury's announced buyback expansion, and that is confirmed and calendared: at least $4bn per operation in the long-end sectors from 9 September to 4 November, aimed squarely at the long-end volatility that Annaly's own disclosure names as the source of its spread pain. The long end has stopped making new highs, sitting at 5.18% rather than pressing higher, and the stock is up on the week at $23.29. The fundamentals continue to deliver — dividend raised to $0.75 on $0.79 of earnings available for distribution, $20.15 book value, 5.5% economic return in Q2 and 6.9% for the half, net interest spread up 8bp to 1.50%. I am not adding despite that, because a September hike with a stable thirty-year is a bear flattener, which is the curve shape that most directly compresses the spread on a 5.6x-levered agency book by raising repo cost against static asset yields, and because agency MBS still trades at historically wide spreads with the Fed running off passively and banks inactive. Holding is the honest answer when the catalyst is intact but the rate path has turned less friendly. -15% stop.

Halved from 10, one rung below JAAA and for the mirror image of JAAA's reason. BBB and BB CLO mezzanine at roughly 7.2% is a levered claim on the single-B and CCC loan cohort, and this week gave me two independent reasons to want less of it. First, a September hike now priced as a coin flip raises the debt service of floating-rate leveraged borrowers, which is a direct solvency pressure on exactly this collateral rather than a mark-to-market one. Second, the distribution keeps getting uglier in ways that are now documented rather than inferred: the HY index OAS of 275-281bp sits in the richest decile of its own history against a long-run median near 450bp, B3 loans have grown from about $109bn at end-2019 to roughly $300bn, and 2026 outlooks now explicitly route AI disruption in software into broadly syndicated loans and private credit marks. The fund's own numbers already show me paying for this — a 5.05% total return against a 7.22% distribution means principal is funding the coupon. I hold 5 rather than zero because top-of-collateral performance is genuinely fine, payment defaults remain below long-run averages, and floating-rate coupons are still the right place to sit while the long end is the volatile part of the curve. What I will no longer do is take that subordination in size for three and a half points over cash. -15% stop respects how mezzanine gaps.

Held flat at 4 for the second week, and once again I decline to add — this time with the cleanest version of the argument I have had. My standing objection is that writing index calls deserves size when volatility is expensive and not when it is cheap. VIX closed at 14.35 on Friday, touched 14.1 after the Warsh speech, and that is the lowest print of the entire year; the market absorbed a Fed chair signalling hikes by selling volatility. Selling premium into the cheapest insurance price of 2026 is the definition of getting paid badly for a real risk, so this stays a token sleeve that satisfies the mandate's equity-premium requirement and clears monthly cash, nothing more. The two caveats I have stated before still hold and still cap the size: the 11.85% distribution carries a 331% payout ratio, so much of what I collect is return of capital rather than harvested premium, and the fund is roughly 8% NVIDIA, 7% Apple and 6% Microsoft, which is concentrated single-name beta wearing an income label. For identical reasons I again decline to open SVXY — with VIX at the year's low, short variance is the single worst-compensated carry available to me. -15% stop.

decisions.research_notes:
Macro: Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech (8/28) was the week's dominant new information — PCE 3.7% y/y and 4.1% annualised over six months, a "firm, fixed" 2% target, explicit refusal to give forward guidance, and "hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive." September hike odds repriced from 35% to ~59% into the 9/16 FOMC (Kalshi 48%, Polymarket 2026-hike 69%). Gold lost $70 in ten minutes and ~2.75% on the day to ~$4,472 spot. Indices: S&P -0.25% Friday to 7,711.76 and Nasdaq -0.52% to 26,402.42, but +0.5% / +0.9% on the week — so my 47% index short cost roughly 0.3% of NAV over the week, which is what a hedge does in an up week.

Leg-by-leg checks. DLTR — the one dated binary I deliberately held through — printed pre-open 8/27: EPS $2.70 vs $1.15 consensus (including $1.31/share from $383m of tariff refunds), net sales +7% to $4.9bn, comps +3.5-3.7%, gross margin +850bps, traffic positive earlier than expected, stores-below-standard cut from ~half to a third of the fleet, and FY adjusted EPS guided up from $6.70-7.10 to $7.70-8.05. The stock still fell ~3% to $128.76 on a soft Q3 guide while Dollar General rose 5% on share-take. That is a company-specific outcome in both directions with no index content — the leg did its job even though the sign went against me. MRNA priced a $2bn convertible and slid ~3.5-6% to ~$141 (day range 137.72-148.59 on 8/27); dilutive, but it substantially retires the cash-burn half of the bear case, and FDA cleared the updated 2026-27 COVID vaccines. NEM made an all-time high of $135.29 on 8/25 and closed 8/28 at $132.29 against a $131.60 prior close — i.e. up on the session gold fell 2.75%, which is the direct evidence against cutting the leg on Warsh; +44.5% on the month, record $2.2bn Q2 FCF, realised gold $4,414/oz. GM: Trump threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, parts and steel effective 1 Jan 2027 with a deal deadline (8/24); GM closed $86.98 -1.1%, Ford -3.3%; Q2 filing quantifies ~$900m/quarter gross tariff impact in H2 — a fresh dated binary layered on the DRAM-cost thesis. OXY $60.11 (8/24) to ~$59.17 (8/27) as Brent fell over 5% on the week to ~$88 on Hormuz reopening progress and regional exports back to 15-16 mb/d — the symmetric risk I flagged, doing exactly what I said it would while RCL gets the offsetting fuel relief. CHTR completed Cox and Liberty Broadband, ~$150.70, all 6m Cox customers on Spectrum by mid-September, debt/equity 5.71 and Altman Z 0.6 — the leg most exposed to a hiking Fed, and the one I will watch first. QCOM ~$165 after Deutsche Bank tech conference (8/26) detail on High Bandwidth Compute and the Dragonfly C1000, first-gen HPC shipping 2027. HUM: 2027 star ratings land in early October — the next dated, purely regulatory catalyst in the book. BA 777-9 in ETOPS on the seventh test aircraft past 4,800 flight hours, deliveries still 2027, FAA Administrator Bedford still saying certification slips to 2027 — debate unchanged and two-sided. CF: no news in the window.

Drift check: with entry on 8/24 and the largest single-leg move about +5% (NEM) against -3% (MRNA, OXY, DLTR), every leg sits within roughly 0.2pp of its 4.25% target. Nothing resembles the ~10% MRNA drift that forced last week's rebalance, so there is no equal-weight discipline to enforce and no trade that clears 2bps of cost.

decisions.reason: Five trading sessions after the 8/24 rebalance, every leg is within roughly 0.2 percentage points of its 4.25% target — the largest move in the basket was NEM at about +5% against MRNA, OXY and DLTR at about -3%. Equal-weight dispersion books harvest by rebalancing drift, and there is no drift here to harvest; last week I acted because one leg had run to ~10% of NAV, and applying the same rule honestly this week means doing nothing. No thesis broke. The single dated binary I deliberately held through — DLTR's Q2 — resolved on 8/27 with a large beat, a 15% FY guidance raise and a 3% decline on a soft Q3 guide while Dollar General rallied on share-take: the sign went against me but the move was entirely company-specific, which is what I am paid to own, and the reinvestment of the $383m tariff refund plus the banner-restructuring debate keeps the name two-sided into the November print. MRNA's $2bn convertible is dilution that buys away the burn case; NEM closed up on the day gold fell 2.75%, which is the evidence I need that the gold-miner leg is not simply a levered bullion position; GM picked up a new 1 Jan 2027 Canadian-tariff deadline that adds two-sidedness rather than removing it. The one genuinely new macro fact — Warsh taking September hike odds from 35% to ~59% with PCE at 3.7% into the 9/16 FOMC — is an argument for carrying the full 28% SPY / 19% QQQ hedge untouched rather than for resizing it. I have already made the mistake once of re-cutting that split on a week of observed data and had to reverse it; guessing at hedge size ahead of a macro binary is the same error wearing a different hat, and a book whose net index beta straddles zero is precisely the thing that does not need a view on the FOMC. CHTR is the leg a hiking cycle actually threatens on a rates factor rather than an idiosyncratic one, given 5.71x debt/equity and a 0.6 Altman Z, and it is the first thing I will cut if the September meeting delivers; it is not something to pre-trade on 59% odds at 4.25% of NAV behind a 22% stop.

decisions.name: Opus 5 mean reversion
decisions.research_notes:
Week of 2026-08-24 to 08-28. Tape: S&P 500 +0.5% on the week to 7,711.76, Nasdaq +0.9%, Dow +0.5%; NVDA +8.7% Thursday on a Q2 beat ($2.22 EPS, $96.22B revenue, +4.8% vs est) drove the rally; Friday -0.25% after Fed Chair Warsh flagged inflation worries at Jackson Hole. So this was an UP week — an important denominator for judging my laggards.

Marks vs last week (all 2026-08-28 closes): AXP $333.20 (+0.4%), APP $321.40 (+5.1%, +3.37% Friday alone), TSLA $348.75 (-3.9%), CSCO $109.93 (-0.6%), WMT $103.09 (+0.7%), HONA $162.37 (-1.9%), SNPS $442.61 (+11.2%), PEG $73.19 (-3.2%). Weighted ~+0.5%, roughly in line with the index.

SNPS — the event I deliberately sized 7% for, resolved. Q3 FY26 (8/26 after close): non-GAAP EPS $3.91 vs $3.67 consensus (+6.5% beat), revenue $2.477B vs $2.44B est and $1.740B a year ago (+42%). Revenue, margin AND EPS all exceeded the high end of guidance. Full-year raised across every metric: revenue to $9.715B midpoint (from $9.625-9.705B) and non-GAAP EPS to $15.07 midpoint (from $14.72-14.80). Critically, the two things that caused the 39% drawdown — Design IP softness and Ansys integration — were both called out as strong contributors, so the drawdown's cause is refuted, not just outgrown. Baird upgraded to Outperform, PT $560; consensus PT ~$565-575 vs $442.61 spot. BofA cut its target to $500 from $600 but kept Buy — still 13% above spot. Price path: $410.00 on 8/26, gapped +13.39% to $464.89 on 8/27, gave back 4.79% to $442.61 on 8/28. It retained roughly two-thirds of the gap, which is a hold, not a fade.

PEG — failed the test I set for it. Last week I argued that failing to fall on bad news (treasury selloff, down equity week) partly answered the concern that it had failed to rise on a dovish CPI/PPI print. This week ran the third and cleanest test: an up week for equities with no adverse rate shock, and PEG fell 3.2% to a fresh range low. It now has no response function in either direction. Fundamentals confirm the drift: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance merely maintained at $4.28-4.40, midpoint $4.34 BELOW $4.38 consensus; Morgan Stanley cut to $91 from $93, Truist to $84 from $90. Q2 did beat ($0.86 vs $0.80 on $2.55B). Ex-dividend 9/9, 3.66% yield.

TSLA — information improved while price fell. Nevada raised Tesla's Las Vegas robotaxi cap from 10 vehicles to 5,000, a 500x expansion of the exact regulatory catalyst I added on last week. The 3.9% decline came from a China voluntary recall of ~3mn vehicles for electronic door-handle function, plus profit-taking after the Nevada rally.

WMT — stabilized. $103.09, first up week since the 8/20 guide-down, no further breakdown. News flow immaterial: $50M DOJ/DEA pharmacy settlement, tap-to-pay rollout, a sub-$25 women's apparel brand.

CSCO — genuinely nothing. Third straight flat week ($109.93 vs $111.55 entry). Week's news was an internal AI-agent rollout and a Secure AI Factory partnership with NVIDIA/Supermicro — neither touches the gross-margin-mix question that caused the 8.4% drop.

HONA — $162.37, still holding well above the $150.03 capitulation low, 52-week range $150.03-$297.50. No new casting-shortage news.

APP — rebounding off the Q2 revenue-miss gap, +5.1% on the week, but Friday's range was $315.05-$335.45 (~6% intraday), so the volatility that justified capping it has not gone away. Average analyst PT ~$526.

decisions.reason: One position earned a change and one earned an exit; everything else genuinely did not move, so I am making exactly two trades rather than redecorating the book. SNPS was held at 7% for one stated reason — a binary print I wanted to survive without needing to be right. That print resolved, and it resolved on the specific axes that caused the drawdown: EDA, Ansys and IP were all called out as strong, revenue/margin/EPS all beat the high end of guidance, and full-year guidance was raised on every metric to $9.715B and $15.07. When the reason for holding a position small stops existing, the correct response is to stop holding it small; keeping 7% now would be treating a resolved uncertainty as if it were still unresolved. It gapped 13.4% and then held two-thirds of that on a red Friday, which is what distinguishes a repriced stock from a squeeze, and at $442.61 it remains ~28% below its 52-week high with a ~$565 consensus target, so the reversion this mandate exists to capture is only partly paid. PEG funds it one-for-one. I set PEG an explicit test over three weeks: it failed to rise on a dovish CPI/PPI print, it held flat through a treasury selloff, and this week — an UP week for the index with no rate shock — it fell 3.2% to a fresh range low. A name that will not rise on good news and will not hold on no news has no response function, and the fundamentals now agree: full-year EPS guidance merely maintained with a $4.34 midpoint below $4.38 consensus, plus target cuts from Morgan Stanley and Truist. That is the same genuinely-negative earnings trend that cost WMT four points, and PEG's only remaining argument was portfolio construction rather than reversion. A 3.66% yield is not a thesis. I am NOT adding to TSLA despite Nevada lifting the robotaxi cap from 10 vehicles to 5,000, which is the strongest single piece of news in the book — I have already sized it up once on this same turn, the 3.9% decline came alongside a real ~3mn-vehicle China recall, and pressing a high-beta name a third time would be sizing to the story rather than to what I can survive. Cash stays at 17% against a 13% mandate: I am deliberately keeping the buffer above spec after Friday's reversal on Warsh's inflation remarks, and I would rather hold the excess than manufacture an eighth conviction I do not have.

positions.thesis: Held at 14%, no trade. It closed $333.20 against ~$332 last week — dead flat through an up week with an 8.7% NVDA melt-up in it. That is precisely the job I hired it for when I moved the ballast mandate here from WMT: it does not participate in AI-capex weeks, which is the same reason it should not participate when that complex unwinds. Its zero AI exposure is a feature, not a drag. The original dislocation is unchanged and still unresolved: a beat-and-raise sold on a $50mn revenue shortfall and 12% expense growth, while the stated bear case of consumer credit deterioration is contradicted by provisions improving to $1.1B from $1.4B, against 2026 EPS guidance of $17.30-17.90. It sits roughly 14% below the $387 high. It earns no addition because it did not decline — I add to this name on price weakness without information change, and there was neither this week.

Doubled from 7% to 14%, now tied for my largest weight. I held this at half-size into the 8/26 print explicitly so I could own it without needing to be right, and the print came in beating on every line: non-GAAP EPS $3.91 against $3.67 consensus, revenue $2.477B against $2.44B and up 42% from $1.740B, with revenue, margin and EPS all above the high end of guidance. Full-year guidance was raised across the board to $9.715B revenue and $15.07 EPS. What matters more than the beat is its composition — Design IP softness and the Ansys integration were the two named causes of the 39% drawdown, and both were cited as strength. That refutes the drawdown's premise rather than merely outgrowing it, which is the strongest form of confirmation a reversion thesis can get. The tape corroborated: +13.39% on 8/27 to $464.89, then a 4.79% give-back to $442.61 on a red Friday, retaining two-thirds of the gap. Baird upgraded to Outperform at $560, consensus sits near $565-575, and even BofA's cut target of $500 is 13% above spot. At $442.61 it is still ~28% below the $615.79 high, so I am paid for maybe a third of the move. I go to 14% and not higher because a 30% stop here is 4.2% of NAV and because the remaining risk is multiple compression in a crowded AI-adjacent name, which no earnings report can insure against.

Held at 12%, no trade, for the third straight week. It closed $321.40, up 5.1% on the week and 3.37% on Friday alone — the first genuinely green week since the Q2 gap, and the beginning of the reclaim I have been waiting for. But one week is a bounce, not a turn, and Friday's range of $315.05 to $335.45 is a 6% intraday swing that says the name is still being traded rather than owned. My rule is that I add to turns after they establish, and this one has not. The fundamentals never justified the gap: Q2 net income grew 54.5% to $1.27B on an 84% adjusted EBITDA margin, Q3 is guided to $2.055-2.085B or +46-48% year over year, and the 1% revenue shortfall traces to the next model step-up landing just after quarter end. Average analyst target near $526 against $321 spot. This is the deepest laggard on both my lookbacks and therefore the truest expression of the mandate, which is exactly why it stays capped rather than sized to the screen rank.

Held at 12%, and this is the hardest hold in the book because the news got materially better while the price got worse. Nevada raised the Las Vegas robotaxi cap from 10 vehicles to 5,000 — a 500x expansion of the identical regulatory catalyst I sized up on last week, and regulatory throughput is the variable that converts robotaxi from narrative to revenue. Against that, it fell 3.9% to $348.75 on a China voluntary recall of roughly 3mn vehicles for electronic door-handle function plus profit-taking. A door-handle recall is a one-time warranty cost, not a demand or franchise impairment, so on my own stated rule — size up on price weakness when information has not deteriorated — this qualifies as an add. I am declining it anyway. I have already sized this leg up once on this same turn, it is the highest-beta name I own, and a third press on a 500x headline is how a position stops being sized to what I can survive and starts being sized to how good the story sounds. The $297.38 low still holds and the reversion toward the $498.83 high is unfinished; 12% is enough exposure to be paid for that.

Held at 11%, no trade. Closed $109.93 against $111.55 at entry — a third consecutive week of doing nothing, this one against a rising index. That is frustrating but it is not information: the week's news was an internal AI-agent deployment and a Secure AI Factory partnership with NVIDIA and Supermicro, neither of which speaks to the gross-margin mix question that caused the 8.4% drop. The setup is fully intact: FY26 Q4 revenue $17.25B against $16.82B expected, adjusted EPS $1.22 against $1.17, next quarter guided $18.0-18.2B versus $16.8B consensus, and FY27 guided to $72.2-73.4B, up 15% at the midpoint. The market repriced mix inside a revenue guide 7% above the Street. I neither add nor cut: adding to something that has refused to move for three weeks would be buying my own patience, and cutting a thesis that nothing has contradicted would be paying costs for boredom. Stops stay at the tighter -15%/+18% because this entered as a one-week dislocation from near a 52-week high, not a deep-drawdown buy, so both the recovery and the tolerable loss are proportionally smaller.

Held at 10%, no trade. It closed $103.09, up 0.45% Friday and up 0.7% on the week — the first week since the 8/20 guide-down in which it did not make a new low. Stabilization is what I needed to see and it is why I do not cut further, but it is not a reclaim and it is not a reason to restore weight. The reason I took this from 14% to 10% still holds exactly: FY adjusted EPS guided $2.80-2.87 against ~$2.90 consensus and US comps decelerating to +2.6% against +3.8% expected is an earnings trend that turned genuinely rather than optically negative, and that is the one condition under which I refuse to add regardless of how attractive the price looks. And the price does look attractive — roughly 23% below the May high, unambiguously bottom-decile, with eCommerce hitting double-digit incremental margins for the first time, Marketplace +52%, ads +38%, and every major broker holding its rating at targets of $120-131, all above spot. The week's news was immaterial: a $50M DOJ pharmacy settlement, tap-to-pay finally arriving, a new sub-$25 apparel line. 10% is the size at which I am paid if the reversion comes without having rewarded a guide-down.

Held at 10%, no trade. Closed $162.37, down 1.9%, which gives back part of the reclaim but leaves it comfortably above the $150.03 capitulation low that anchors the position — the low is still holding two weeks on, which is the specific thing I said I needed. No new information on the casting shortage this week. The cause of this drawdown remains what separates it from the guide-downs that have actually cost me money: a precision-casting shortage steering scarce components toward Boeing and Airbus production lines and away from higher-margin aftermarket, which defers revenue against end demand nobody disputes, rather than destroying it. Against a 52-week range of $150.03 to $297.50 the reversion is barely begun. It stays capped at 10% for the two reasons that have not changed: a casting shortage can plausibly run several more quarters, and a freshly spun-off holder base can still produce mechanical supply that has nothing to do with the business.

decisions.name: Opus 5 event driven
decisions.research_notes:
MARKS THROUGH 08-28. TEAM 190.42 (fill 155.24, +22.7%; +11.1% since the 08-24 book date, incl. +10.18% on 08-27 and +2.58% on 08-28 to an all-time high on analyst upgrades citing Rovo/AI attach). SMCI 37.08 (fill 37.24, -0.4%; -3.59% on 08-28). HRB 52.48 (~-2%). ACA 145.28, gross spread to $150 now 3.25%, special meeting still fixed 09-04. SPY 763.47 on 08-24 -> 769.35, so the short is ~-0.8%. No stop is within reach of any leg.

MACRO: Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote on 08-28 read mildly hawkish - inflation "still too high," possible hikes - and September hike odds jumped to ~57%. S&P -0.3%, Nasdaq -0.5% Friday, but all three indexes closed the week up. I note this as context for hedge sizing, not as a directional view; I have retired hedge increments before for justifying them on macro that then reversed.

GAP SCREEN, 08-25 to 08-28 (my filters: up-gap >6%, volume >2x base, prior 20 sessions >+10%; entry 1-2 sessions after the gap). Six large up-gappers, five fail:
- NVDA: +8.74% gap 08-27 on 2.4x volume, but prior 20 sessions only +6.4% (it went in on a 7-session skid) and it gave back 4.57% on 08-28. FAILS trend.
- OKTA: +28.6% on 6.5x, prior 20 sessions -1.3%. FAILS trend badly; -3.9% on 08-28.
- CRWD: +20.5% on 3.1x, prior 20 sessions +4.1%. FAILS trend; -4.2% on 08-28.
- ADSK: +6.2% on 2.2x, prior 20 sessions +7.3%. FAILS trend; -3.7% on 08-28.
- CRM: +22.6% gap on 5x volume, and uniquely it ADDED 1.57% on 08-28 while the tape fell. But prior 20 sessions +9.15%, just under my threshold, and the headline $5.90 vs $3.27 EPS beat is mostly a $2.6bn mark-to-market gain on its Anthropic stake - revenue beat was 0.3% ($11.35bn vs $11.32bn). PEAD works through analysts revising OPERATING estimates; a one-time investment gain does not generate that. SKIPPED despite the day-2 follow-through.
- VEEV: PASSES every filter on measured data. Closed 244.91 on 08-26 and 282.13 on 08-27 = +15.20% gap, on 6.39m shares against a ~1.6m July-August base (4.0x), with the prior 20 sessions running 207.91 (07-29) to 244.91 = +17.80%. Q2 FY27 revenue $928m +18%, subscription $766.8m +16%, operating margin above 44%, FY27 guidance raised, "best CRM quarter ever," Lilly/Biogen/Regeneron added to Vault CRM taking it to 12 of the top 20 biopharma. Held the gap on 08-28 (-1.93% against Nasdaq -0.5%). Monday fill is a 2-session lag, inside the rule.
- MRVL: -10.3% on 08-28 on Google-ASIC monetisation timing, but prior 20 sessions were up, so it fails the capitulation trend filter too. Skipped.

DOWN-GAP / CAPITULATION SCREEN (down-gap >6%, already down >10% over 20 sessions):
- DKS: PASSES cleanly and is the most extreme capitulation print this book has seen. 179.33 (08-24) to 124.31 (08-25) = -30.68%, on 38.4m shares against a ~1.3m base (~30x), with the prior 20 sessions running 205.60 (07-27) to 179.33 = -12.78%. Cause: Q2 adj EPS $3.53 vs $3.78, FY guidance slashed to $11.00-12.00 against $14.20 consensus (-19% at the midpoint), driven by Foot Locker proforma comps -3.6% and heavy footwear discounting - the legacy Dick's business still comped +4.9%. Three straight up sessions since (124.31 -> 129.66 -> 131.77 -> 135.09, +8.7% off the gap close) on collapsing volume, which is what stabilisation looks like. ~11.7x the midpoint of the freshly cut guide.
- AAP: -24.6% on 08-20, but prior 20 sessions were roughly flat (55.80 on 07-24 vs 56.55 pre-gap), so it fails the trend filter, and it is now six sessions past the gap anyway. Skipped.

CALENDAR: TEAM's 20-session window from the 08-07 gap ends ~09-04, so this is its last full week and it comes off at next weekend's desk, the same one-session-after-window cadence I ran on ISRG, NFLX and the six legs I rolled on 08-22. SMCI and HRB gapped 08-12, windows to ~09-09. HRB's fiscal year ended 06-30 and Q1 FY27 does not report until November, so no earnings lands inside its window. VEEV's window runs to ~09-25, DKS's to ~09-22, neither with an earnings date inside. ACA votes 09-04 with a Q1 2027 outside date.

decisions.reason: Two clean qualifiers finally appeared after three weeks of an empty screen, and 56% cash earning 4% is not what I am paid for when the tape hands me signals that pass every filter on measured data. VEEV is the cleanest post-earnings-drift setup available anywhere in the market this week - +15.2% gap on 4x volume with the prior 20 sessions at +17.8%, and it held the gap on Friday while every other big gapper (NVDA -4.6%, OKTA -3.9%, CRWD -4.2%, ADSK -3.7%) gave back a chunk - and a Monday fill is a 2-session lag, dead centre of the window my testing says is strongest. DKS gives me the capitulation leg my mandate specifies and I have had zero of: -30.7% on 30x volume into a name already -12.8% over 20 sessions, with the guidance now reset 19% below the Street and three sessions of stabilisation since. I skipped CRM despite a +22.6% gap on 5x volume and the only day-2 follow-through in the group, because its prior 20 sessions were +9.15% rather than the +10% my rule requires and because the 80% EPS beat is largely a $2.6bn mark on its Anthropic stake rather than an operating surprise - the drift mechanism runs on analysts revising operating estimates, and a one-off investment gain does not produce those revisions. I also skipped NVDA, OKTA, CRWD and ADSK for a shared reason worth stating: all four gapped hard, none had the pre-gap uptrend, and all four gave ground the next session, which is precisely the failure mode the trend filter exists to screen out. The other reason to restate the book rather than hold is TEAM: it has drifted to ~14.3% on a +22.7% gain, and rebalancing re-marks its 14% stop from 155.24 to 190.42, moving the exit up to ~163.76. That is not a take-profit - my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37% and I am not taking one - it is the same stop width re-referenced, which protects roughly +5.5% on the leg while still leaving room for a full round-trip of Thursday's move during its final week. Gross goes 44% to 65% into a Fed chair who just put September hike odds at 57%, so the SPY offset goes 3% to 4% - the honest ratio on a beta-bearing long base that grows from 33% to 53%, not a macro bet; cash stays at 35% and earns more if he is right.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book in this experiment, so the cross-round overlap constraint does not bind; within Round 3 the new work this week is genuinely new exposure - VEEV brings life-sciences vertical software with no AI-capex, semiconductor or consumer sensitivity, and DKS is the book's first capitulation leg and its first short-consumer-cycle long, neither of which overlaps anything I have held.

positions.thesis: PEAD, final week. Signal unchanged and now largely paid: reported after the close 08-06, gapped +35.31% on 08-07 from 110.16 to 149.07 on 20m+ shares against a ~4m base with the prior 20 sessions roughly +20%, filled 08-10 at 155.24 at a one-session lag. It closed 190.42 on 08-28, +22.7% from my fill, and the two-session run that got it there (+10.18% on 08-27, +2.58% on 08-28 to an all-time high) came on analyst upgrades citing Rovo attach rates - a second wave of estimate revision inside the same window, which is exactly the mechanism the drift is supposed to exploit rather than a separate story. Fundamentals unchanged: revenue +28% to $1.8bn, cloud +31%, RPO +44% to $4.8bn, ARR $6.6bn, GAAP EPS +$0.55 from -$0.09, guide $1.705-1.715bn against $1.665bn consensus. The 20-session window from the 08-07 gap closes ~09-04, so this leg comes off at next weekend's desk - the same one-session-after-window discipline I applied to ISRG, NFLX and the six legs I rolled on 08-22, and I apply it because LMT showed me what happens when I let a window-expired position keep working. Restating at 14% is its drifted weight, not an add; what the restatement buys me is the stop re-marked from 155.24 to 190.42, so 14% now exits at ~163.76 and locks in roughly +5.5% while still allowing a full retrace of Thursday's pop. No take-profit.

New PEAD and the only name in the entire week's tape that passed every filter. Measured: closed 244.91 on 08-26 and 282.13 on 08-27 for a +15.20% gap, on 6,392,733 shares against a ~1.6m July-August base (4.0x), with the prior 20 sessions running 207.91 on 07-29 to 244.91 for +17.80% - the trend component my testing says carries most of the edge, and it is the strongest reading I have had on any leg since HRB. The fundamental surprise is operating rather than accounting, which is the distinction that made me pass on CRM: Q2 FY27 revenue $928m +18%, subscription revenue $766.8m +16%, operating margin held above 44% while growing, FY27 guidance raised to roughly $1,640m non-GAAP operating income, and management called it their best CRM quarter ever with Lilly, Biogen and Regeneron committing to Vault CRM to take it to 12 of the top 20 biopharma. That last item is the real analyst problem - the Veeva/Salesforce CRM displacement is a multi-year revenue reallocation the Street models slowly, and slow model updates are precisely what a 20-session drift monetises. The confirming detail is the second session: on 08-28 VEEV gave back only 1.93% against Nasdaq -0.5% while NVDA, OKTA, CRWD and ADSK all shed 3.7-4.6% of their gaps. Filling Monday 08-31 is a 2-session lag, inside the rule, unlike the seven-session lags I had to accept on SMCI and HRB. Sized at 12% - just under TEAM because I am entering at 276.69 rather than at the gap, and because a name that gaps 15% carries post-gap realised vol that argues against a bigger unit. Stop 12%, wider than standard 10% for that vol reason but tighter than SMCI's 15% because the gap was smaller. No take-profit. Life-sciences vertical software is also orthogonal to everything else here - no AI capex cycle, no semiconductor cycle, no consumer, no duration.

PEAD, held unchanged at 11% and roughly flat since my 08-24 fill at 37.24 (37.08 on 08-28, including -3.59% on Friday as the whole AI complex faded post-Warsh). Signal unchanged: closed 31.60 on 08-11 and 37.61 on 08-12 for a +19.02% gap on 165.7m shares against a ~35m base (>4x), prior 20 sessions 28.31 on 07-10 to 31.60 for +11.6%, ~$1.3bn dollar ADV. The estimate dislocation behind it is the largest in the book and has not been worked through: FY26 revenue $39.1bn against $22.0bn, Q4 gross margin 17.5% against 9.5% a year ago and above the 15-17% preliminary range management signalled in July, Q1 FY27 guided $14.5-15.5bn against $11.68bn consensus - roughly 26% above the Street. The independent investigation completing retires the governance discount. Nothing in this week's tape touched the thesis: NVDA's print was a beat with fiscal 2028 revenue growth guided to 70%, which is confirmation for the server supply chain, and the 08-28 weakness was a hawkish-Fed multiple move, not a demand datapoint. Its window from the 08-12 gap runs to ~09-09, so it stays. I remain honest that a seven-session entry lag cost me about a third of the available drift, which is why this is 11% and not the 20%+ the raw signal strength implies. Stop 15% for post-19%-gap volatility. No take-profit.

PEAD, held unchanged at 9% and down about 2% from my 08-24 fill to 52.48 - inside normal noise for a name whose gap-day range was five points wide. Signal unchanged: fiscal 2026 results 08-11 after the close, closed 46.67 on 08-11 and 54.18 on 08-12 for a +16.09% gap on 8.38m shares against a 1.5-2.5m base (3-5x), with the prior 20 sessions running 39.12 on 07-08 to 46.67 for +19.3%, the strongest pre-gap trend in the book. Window from the 08-12 gap runs to ~09-09, so it has two more weeks. I checked the calendar risk specifically: the fiscal year ended 06-30, so Q1 FY27 does not report until November and nothing lands inside the window. The reason this leg earns its slot beyond the statistics is stronger this week than last, not weaker - a counter-cyclical, subscription-like tax-preparation business with no AI capex exposure, no semiconductor cycle and no duration is exactly what I want sitting next to two software drift trades in a week when the Fed chair put September hike odds at 57% and the bond market started pricing tightening. Sized at 9% for the seven-session entry lag and ~$95m dollar ADV, which is the thinnest thing I own; stop 12% for that same liquidity reason. No take-profit.

Merger arb, held unchanged at 8% and effectively flat at 145.28. The catalyst is now six days out and still fixed: CRH signed 06-22 to acquire Arcosa at $150 per share in cash, $8.5bn enterprise value at 11.5x 2026E adjusted EBITDA, all cash with no stock and no CVR, definitive proxy filed 08-03 and mailed 08-04, special stockholder meeting 09-04, approval needing a majority of outstanding shares. Regulatory posture unchanged and clean - HSR filed 07-06 with the thirty-day period lapsed and no second request reported, Australia 07-21, Mexico 07-23. Gross spread at Friday's close is 3.25%, tighter than the 3.52% I underwrote a week ago, which is the spread doing exactly what an unopposed deal's spread should do into a vote. I underwrite it the same honest way: parties guide to a Q1 2027 close, so this is roughly five months for 3.25%, maybe 12-15% downside to the pre-deal $127 area on a break, call it 6-7% annualised against 4% on cash. Thin, which is why it is 8% and not larger. What it buys me is a leg with essentially no equity beta and collapsed realised volatility in a book that is now four high-beta event longs, and that ballast is worth more this week than last given the Jackson Hole repricing. The 12% stop is a circuit breaker against slow widening - a second request, a divestiture demand - not protection against a break, which would gap through it.

New capitulation long, the first this book has had and the most extreme down-gap signal my screen has produced. Every filter passes on measured data: closed 179.33 on 08-24 and 124.31 on 08-25 for a -30.68% gap - a record one-day decline for the name - on 38,387,205 shares against a ~1.3m base (roughly 30x), with the prior 20 sessions running 205.60 on 07-27 to 179.33 for -12.78%, so it was already broken before the print rather than falling from a high. The news is real and I am not pretending otherwise: Q2 adjusted EPS $3.53 against $3.78, and full-year adjusted EPS guidance cut to $11.00-12.00 against $14.20 consensus, a 19% reduction at the midpoint, driven by Foot Locker proforma comps -3.6%, bloated legacy footwear inventory and heavy discounting. What makes it a capitulation candidate rather than a falling knife is the composition of that miss and what has happened since. The legacy Dick's business still comped +4.9%; the damage is concentrated in an acquisition whose problems are inventory and promotion, not demand collapse, and inventory problems clear on a known clock. The guide is now reset low enough that the bar for the November print is a bar management set themselves after seeing the quarter. And the tape has stabilised: 124.31, 129.66, 131.77, 135.09 across three sessions, +8.7% off the gap close on steadily falling volume, which is what forced selling exhausting looks like. At 135.09 that is about 11.7x the midpoint of the freshly cut guide. Sized at 7%, not more - my measured capitulation edge is +1.23% market-hedged against +2.44% raw, genuinely thin, and a hawkish Fed chair is a real headwind for a levered discretionary retailer, so a 20% stop puts only 1.4% of NAV at risk. Stop 20%, the middle of the 18-22% band my mandate specifies for these, because a name with 30% gap-day volatility would be stopped out on noise at normal width. No take-profit, so the mean-reversion can run its 20 sessions to ~09-22.

Partial beta offset, resized 3% to 4% on arithmetic, not on a view. The justification is unchanged and mechanical: my measured edge is materially larger market-hedged than raw - PEAD +2.06% hedged against +2.81% raw, capitulation +1.23% against +2.44% - so an index short shifts realised return toward the event component I actually have evidence for. The base being hedged grew this week: beta-bearing event longs go from 33% (TEAM, SMCI, HRB) to 53% (adding VEEV and DKS; ACA is deal-driven and carries no beta worth hedging). At last week's ratio of roughly 9% that would argue for 4.8%; at the ratio I ran before the roll, closer to 4.0%. I take the lower end, so 4%. I want to be explicit about what this is NOT, because I have made this mistake before and retired an increment of this leg for it: it is not a bet on Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks, not a bet on 57% September hike odds, and not a bet on the bond market repricing tightening. If I wanted to express that I would cut gross, and I have not - gross went up. My own backtests showed the index short was a drag on raw return in all three windows; it exists to shape the edge, and 35% cash earning 4% is where the actual defensiveness lives. 4% borrow at 3% APR is immaterial and shorts pay no funding. 9% stop.

decisions.name: Opus 5 seasonality
decisions.research_notes: Checked: (1) Warsh's Jackson Hole debut, 2026-08-28 — he said inflation remains above 2%, that summer's better-than-expected PCE/CPI "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," and that rates may need to be RAISED. September hike odds jumped from ~30% to 48% on Kalshi / 55.7% on CME FedWatch, ~+20pts in a day; economists near 60%. (2) Curve reaction: 2Y +6bps to 4.298%; long end EDGED LOWER. That is a bear FLATTENER — the exact inverse of the bear steepener (30Y 5.34%, 10Y 4.75%, short end anchored) that I built this book around three weeks ago. Prior week's marks: 10Y 4.68%, 30Y 5.20%. (3) NVDA reported 2026-08-26: beat and raised, stock +8.7% Thursday; SMH/semis rallied. Tech +1.3% and Comm Services +1.4% led the week; S&P +0.5%, Nasdaq +0.9%, but only 3 of 11 sectors finished higher and fewer than half of stocks advanced — leadership narrowed back into my named core-overweight sleeve rather than rotating away from it. (4) Gold: hit a 3-month high near $4,700 midweek on fiscal/Treasury-buyback concerns, then fell 0.5% to $4,576.30 spot into and after the speech, ~-2.2% off last week's $4,680.60 mark. September is historically gold's worst month. (5) Iran: exports collapsed to ~260kbpd, -80% y/y; blockade reimposed July 14, Hormuz declared closed by Tehran, Bessent's "economic D-Day" sanctions still pending — the geopolitical tail is live and escalating, unlike the monetary bid. (6) Regionals: 2026 NIM expansion at >half of banks in Q2 was driven specifically by DEPOSIT COSTS ROLLING OVER, and the cited outlook is explicitly conditioned on the Fed holding rather than hiking; 2s10s +0.52% and now flattening. (7) Industrials: XLI +15-17% YTD, UBS says the recovery is broadening across capex/pricing/demand, $156.2bn defense bill signed July 4 feeds GE Aerospace/Eaton/Caterpillar — but the sector carries a ~30 P/E. (8) EquityClock 8/28: bull flag intact, elevated exposure near-term, but flags September volatility and rising rates as the top macro threat with greater caution from mid-September. Conclusion: one force in this book reversed — Fed reaction function — and I repriced only the legs that were actually bought off it.

decisions.reason: One mechanism in this book reversed this week and I am repricing only the legs that were actually bought off it, not rebuilding. For three weeks every leg here has leaned on the same claim I wrote down explicitly: Warsh will not hike against inflation, so the long end rises on deficit supply and term premium while the short end stays anchored — a bear steepener. On Friday he said the opposite, September hike odds went from ~30% to 50-60% in a day, the 2Y jumped 6bps to 4.298% and the long end edged LOWER. That is a bear flattener. I am not entitled to keep the positions I sized off a forecast that just inverted. Gold takes the largest cut because I am the one who wrote last week that its bid was a 'debasement and Fed-credibility bid' from that exact mechanism — with credibility being restored by a hiking chair, that reason is gone, and separately my own calendar says the Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54% average) is roughly 4x spent at ~+12.5%. I do not need price to reach my $4,798 exit to admit the reason I was holding has expired. XLF gives back precisely the increment I added for the steepener and keeps the core the calendar justifies. KRE goes to a token because the specific engine of 2026 regional NIM expansion is deposit costs rolling over, and a hike re-inflates them at the exact institutions with no fee-income cushion. Against that, two legs got confirming evidence: NVDA's beat-and-raise and an 8.7% session is the cleanest available refutation of the AI-capex-and-financing bear case I named as QQQ's risk last week, in a week where only 3 of 11 sectors rose and leadership narrowed back into my sleeve; and on IEF I stated the precise condition for adding — that I would not size into a dated catalyst I could not handicap — which has now passed and resolved in my favour, with the belly the part of the curve a hiking cycle bites hardest. XLI and XLU stay untouched because nothing changed for them and a one-point nudge is churn, not a decision. Cash rises 7% to 14% as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 utilities rotation and the Nov-1 regional/financials rotation, which is where the overwhelming mass of my measured window return actually sits, earning 4% through the one month of my window that measures negative.

positions.thesis: Raised 17% to 22% and now my largest leg. Last week I listed this position's bear case honestly and declined to act on it: semis more than 20% below their June high, NDX down ~9.7% from its record, AVGO's cautious AI-chip guide stacked on the $370bn financing-vehicle story and a memory-chip crisis. On 2026-08-26 the company at the dead centre of that case answered it — NVDA beat and raised, the stock added 8.7% Thursday, and semis rallied with it. That is not sentiment improving, it is the specific falsifiable claim being falsified by the primary source. The tape corroborates in the way that matters most: in a week when only 3 of 11 sectors finished higher and fewer than half of stocks advanced, Technology (+1.3%) and Communication Services (+1.4%) were the two that led. Narrowing leadership INTO the sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight is the opposite of the late-August rotation into healthcare and energy I was told to fear. The seasonal was never the problem and is intact: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%), with the mass in November and December. I am adding four points rather than eight for one real reason: a September hike is a duration de-rating for exactly this sleeve, and paying up the week after an 8.7% pop is chasing at the margin. The -15% stop stays unchanged and untightened — a financing-driven de-rating is what it is for, and tightening it into the single most volatile month of the calendar is how you get ejected at the low of a drawdown you correctly sat through.

Held flat at 18%, and holding is the decision. This is still the strongest statistic in my window set and nothing this week touched it: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone +4.68% at 81%, t=+3.78, and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. The fundamental stack I added on last week is also unchanged or better: UBS now describes the industrial recovery as broadening across capex, pricing and demand rather than concentrating; the $156.2bn defence bill signed in July feeds XLI's largest holdings directly through GE Aerospace, Eaton and Caterpillar's power business; and the Iran situation escalated rather than resolved, with exports down 80% year on year and sanctions still pending. Why I do not add despite that: the sector carries roughly a 30 P/E on a +15-17% YTD move, which is a lot of expectation already paid for, and a hiking Fed is a valuation headwind to a cyclical trading at a premium. Adding into that on a week where my conviction did not actually change would be buying the story rather than the number. A one-point nudge would be noise costing 2bps, so I take none. Still no stop — a stop mechanically ejects me during exactly the soft late-summer patch this window is built to sit through, which is a cost I pre-agreed to pay a month ago.

Cut from 20% to 17% — I am handing back exactly the increment I bought for a reason that expired, and keeping the core the calendar pays for. Last week I raised this to 20% because 'short-end anchored, long-end rising is the steepener that widens net interest margin' and said that mechanism had stopped being a forecast and become the regime. On Friday it stopped being the regime: Warsh signalled hikes, the 2Y jumped 6bps to 4.298% and the long end edged lower. Short end up with long end down is NIM compression, not expansion, and I will not pretend a flattener is a steepener because I liked the position. What survives is substantial and is why 17% rather than 10%. The seasonal is among my best and is untouched: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone +3.64% in 19/26. Credit is genuinely clean — Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals. The money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams do not care about the shape of the curve, and financial ETFs actually took August inflows ON rate-hike bets, so the flows are not reading this the way a pure NIM model would. What is new is the stop. I have run this leg unstopped on the stated logic that its drawdown case is a growth scare my gold position is held to pay for; I just cut gold from 18% to 8%, so that hedge is materially thinner and I should say so rather than quietly carry the same naked risk. A -15% stop is wide enough not to fire on September chop and is there for a genuine credit event, which is the one outcome my remaining hedge no longer covers.

Raised 8% to 10%, and this is the one add where I named the condition in advance and it was met. Last week I wrote that I was stopping at 8% for one honest reason: IEF is the 7-10 year belly, the part of the curve a dovish Warsh at his first Jackson Hole would rally hardest, and I would not size into a dated catalyst I could not handicap. That catalyst has now happened and resolved against the dovish case — he said inflation's underlying trend has not meaningfully improved and that rates may need to rise, and the market repriced September from roughly 30% to 50-60% odds of a HIKE with the 2Y up 6bps. The belly is precisely where a policy repricing bites, because it discounts the path of the funds rate rather than term premium. So the two mechanisms now push the same way: the original deficit-supply, AI-corporate-issuance and term-premium story that has been paying since July, and a live hiking cycle on top of it. The seasonal remains the most extreme statistic in my entire study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. I add two points and not six because I have been whipsawed twice sizing this leg off a hike call, and one speech without forward guidance from a chair who explicitly refuses to give it is not a committed cycle. The -8% stop stays: a rally in the belly big enough to hit it means recession is being priced, and that is the state of the world where this leg's loss correlates with losses in QQQ, XLI and XLF at the same time.

Cut from 18% to 8% — the largest change in this book and the main source of funds. I am cutting because the reason I gave for holding is the reason that died. Last week I upgraded this from a spent seasonal to a core hold on a specific claim: that gold was rising WHILE long-end Treasuries sold off, which made it 'a debasement and Fed-credibility bid... the same Warsh-will-not-hike-against-inflation mechanism' driving my XLF and IEF legs. On Friday Warsh announced he will fight inflation and the market put 50-60% odds on a September hike. A chair restoring credibility by hiking is the direct negation of a Fed-credibility bid, and rising real short rates are the textbook headwind for a non-yielding asset. Price agreed immediately: after touching a 3-month high near $4,700 midweek, spot fell to $4,576.30, about -2.2% from last week's mark. Separately, my own calendar has been telling me to leave for two weeks — Jul-27 to Oct-27 averaged +3.54% at 14/21 years and t=+1.69, and I am sitting on roughly +12.5% from $4,066, some 3-4x the entire average window return, with September historically gold's worst month. I have removed the $4,798 take-profit rather than waiting for it: that level was set to harvest a mechanism that no longer exists, and refusing to sell until an arbitrary number prints is not discipline, it is an excuse. I keep 8% rather than zero for the reason that is genuinely still live and got stronger, not weaker, this week — Iranian exports are down 80% year on year at ~260kbpd, the naval blockade is reimposed, Tehran says Hormuz stays closed, and Bessent's sanctions package is still pending. That is a real tail, and 8% is the size at which I am compensated for owning it while carrying 57% in cyclical and growth longs. The -10% stop is new and caps the give-back if the hike repricing extends.

Held flat at 4%. I cut this from 9% to 4% last week for the correct reason and I am not going to reverse myself on one session of price action. There is a real argument to nudge it up: the long end edged LOWER on Friday, which relieves the precise mechanical pressure I cited — a bond proxy yielding 2.5-3% could not compete with a 4.7% 10Y and a 5.28% 30Y — and the window where this sleeve actually earns, Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24% positive in 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade, is now a month away rather than two. I decline it anyway on two grounds. First, one point on a 4% leg is a rounding error that costs 2bps to execute and changes nothing about my outcome; doing it would be motion mistaken for judgment. Second, and more to the point, I already said what I would do with this capital: the rest of this position belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I earmarked, to be bought when my calendar says the sleeve works rather than three weeks early on a narrative, which is the exact error I corrected here last week. The measured Jul-27 to Sep-30 leg is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY, so the sleeve is still not earning its keep for another month. 4% keeps the mandate sleeve occupied and keeps me exposed to the structural AI power-demand bid without paying for a window that has not opened. No stop at this size.

Raised 3% to 4% — a small add, but the first genuinely favourable news this leg has had all quarter. I have been candid for weeks that both halves of the original mechanism were impaired: EAFE kept outperforming US equity in USD on cheaper European and Japanese valuations, and a Fed that would not hike while foreign central banks held was the wrong rate differential for the dollar side. Friday repaired the second half. A chair signalling hikes against foreign central banks that are not tightening is precisely the policy divergence a dollar leg needs, and the 2Y moving 6bps to 4.298% is where that divergence first shows up. The valuation half remains against me and I am not pretending otherwise, which is why this is one point and not five. The seasonal is unchanged and among my better relative measures: EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade, averaging -2.65%. At 4% the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.05% of NAV across the remaining window, so being wrong is immaterial and being right is modest carry that is now backed by a live mechanism rather than only a calendar. The -10% stop stays and caps the tail if European outperformance accelerates on a US growth scare.

Cut from 5% to 3%, because this week's news is specifically bad for this sleeve in a way it is not for the money-centres. The single most useful thing I learned about regionals this week is the source of their 2026 recovery: net interest margin expanded at more than half of them in Q2 because DEPOSIT COSTS ARE ROLLING OVER, and every forward outlook I read conditions further gains on the Fed holding rather than hiking. A September hike re-inflates deposit costs directly at the institutions that fund themselves with rate-sensitive deposits and have no investment-banking or wealth fee streams to cushion the hit, while 2s10s at +0.52% flattens rather than steepens. That is a cleaner reason to be small than the one I gave last week, which stands anyway: the Russell 2000 keeps making records on AI-linked small caps while KRE sits well below its 2022 peak, and a group that will not rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something a seasonal cannot see. I hold 3% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24% at 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14% — but that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91%. Being small in September and rebuilding with the Nov-1 rotation cash is the cheapest way to own a Q4 window, and it costs me almost nothing to keep the sleeve occupied while I wait. The -18% stop is unchanged.

decisions.name: Opus 5 pairs
decisions.research_notes:
Marks through 2026-08-28 close, all verified against stockanalysis.com/quote pages rather than memory.

WFC/BAC (my working pair): WFC $83.84 -> $86.69 (+3.40%), BAC ~$61.68 -> $62.32 (+1.04%). Relative +2.3% in my direction in one week. The measure I actually underwrote moved a lot: WFC's implied upside to a $100.24 target fell from 19.6% to 15.63% while BAC's to $68.77 fell from 11.5% to 10.35%, so the convergence gap closed from 8.1 points to 5.28 - roughly 35% of the gap captured in a week. WFC still 11% below its $97.76 52-week high at 12.6x on $6.88 EPS; BAC at 14.4x, $62.32 against a $65.23 52-week high. Neither reports until 13 Oct (confirmed), so nothing sits inside my horizon.

Macro, and it matters: Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech was the week's event. He said the better summer PCE/CPI prints "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved"; futures moved September rate-HIKE odds from ~35% to ~55%, the 2-year to 4.35% and the 10-year to 4.72%. S&P 500 +0.5% on the week to 7,711.76, -0.25% Friday. This is a live regime item for two of my pairs and I treat it as such below rather than as noise.

LOW/HD (my losing pair): LOW $216.09 -> $208.05 (-3.72%), HD $335.61 -> $330.19 (-1.61%); ratio 0.6439 -> 0.6301, about 2.1% against me. LOW touched a six-week low. The mechanism is the rate shock, not a new fundamental: hike odds are directly hostile to housing turnover, and LOW's DIY-discretionary mix carries more of that than HD's Pro mix, so the common shock did not cancel cleanly. But the valuation evidence moved further my way, not against: LOW now 17.59x with 22.26% upside to $254.36, HD 23.10x with 14.33% upside to $377.50 - a 7.9-point gap versus 5.3 last week and a 5.5-turn discount. Sell-side framing has if anything hardened in my favour since the prints: Zacks #3 on LOW against #5 Strong Sell on HD, consensus earnings growth ~9% for LOW versus ~5% for HD. LOW declared its $1.25 quarterly dividend 08-28. Both are a full quarter from the next print.

TSM/KLAC: TSM $417.52 (-2.29% Friday, ~-0.34% on the week), KLAC $183.77 (~-0.12%). Ratio 2.277 -> 2.272 - flat. TSM 28.44x, Strong Buy, $554.45 target implying 32.8% upside; KLAC unchanged. The spread simply paused after last week's 40% capture.

New work - MA/V, which I screened at entry and never put on. MA $595.30, V $381.60, ratio 1.560. A year ago that ratio was ~1.69: MA has trailed V by 8.3 points over twelve months (-2.5% vs +5.8%). The reason is real and I want to be honest about it - MA's revenue growth decelerated to 15.8% then 14.1% in Q1-Q2 2026 while V's accelerated to 17.1% then 14.4%, so the growth premium that justified MA's multiple did invert. But the multiple has now fully repriced for it: 30.2x vs 29.5x, against a traditional 3-5 turn MA premium, and stockanalysis puts them at 32.74 vs 32.49. Meanwhile MA still beat Q2 with revenue $9.28bn +14% and adjusted EPS $5.04 +21%, guided FY net revenue to the high end of low-double-digit growth, and Bernstein has MA's EPS momentum at 22.1% versus V's 10.2% with fair-value upside +6.8% MA against -1.4% V. Target upside 12.46% MA vs 9.83% V. Litigation asymmetry favours the short leg too: V took $707m of interchange MDL provisions in Q1 FY26 and $899m in Q4 FY25 against MA's $82m in Q2 2026, and the $200bn swipe-fee settlement got only preliminary approval on 09 Jun before NRF, RILA and Walmart said they would rather go to trial. Hedge quality fits the mandate screen: betas 0.82 vs 0.76, both near 52-week highs so neither leg is a falling knife, and both report in late October within days of each other so the event is close to common. I checked XLU/D and the factor pair as alternatives and rejected both - shorting utilities into a hike scare would just stack the same rate bet I already carry through WFC/BAC.

decisions.reason: Two things force my hand and they point the same way. First, my own audited rule: convergence gets taken rather than admired. WFC/BAC closed 35% of its target-gap in a single week, 8.1 points to 5.28 - that is the same trigger, at the same magnitude, that made me cut TSM/KLAC last week at 40% captured. If I book profit on a pair that works and hold full size on the one that works better, the rule is decoration. So WFC comes 23.0 to 19.0 and BAC 22.7 to 18.7, trimmed in beta-proportion so the cut does not quietly leave a directional bank bet. Second, concentration: WFC/BAC was 69% of gross, which meant I owned one spread wearing a diversified book's clothing. The trim plus a fourth pair takes it to 52% of gross and my largest single leg from 23% to 19%. I am not doing this to be smaller - gross rises 66.4% to 72.9% - I am doing it to be less singular. Where the money goes is long MA / short V, a pair from my original screen that I sized at zero because the spread was not stretched then and now is: MA has trailed V by 8.3 points over a year and the traditional 3-5 turn Mastercard multiple premium has gone to zero, while MA still compounds EPS at 22% against V's 10% and carries an order of magnitude less interchange-litigation provision. LOW/HD and TSM/KLAC hold. On LOW/HD specifically I am neither adding nor cutting, and I want the reason on the record: the spread widened against me on a rate shock, not on news, and everything I underwrote got cheaper - 7.9 points of target gap versus 5.3, a 5.5-turn discount, 9% versus 5% consensus growth. A mean-reversion mandate would normally add there. I do not, because I halved this pair a week ago on a fundamental point that has not been retracted - LOW guided to the bottom end while HD reaffirmed - and adding into a stretch I myself argued was fundamentally deserved would be doubling down against my own stated read. Holding is the honest position between those two facts. I carry no stops anywhere, unchanged and deliberate: a stop on one leg of a beta-matched pair does not reduce risk, it converts a spread into a naked directional position at the worst possible moment. Net SPY beta lands at about +0.06% of NAV rather than the mandate's +3.2%; with September hike odds at 55% I would rather run flatter than my brief than tilt long into it, and I state the deviation rather than bury it.
decisions.novelty: I manage only the Round-3 book this round, so the cross-round overlap rule does not bind me, but the new work is genuine: MA/V is a pair I screened at entry and deliberately sized at zero, brought on now for a specific reason - the Mastercard multiple premium has fully collapsed to Visa's while its EPS growth runs double Visa's - and it is the only leg in the book with no rate or housing sensitivity, which is precisely what a book carrying a bank pair and a home-improvement pair into a hawkish Fed needs.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, cut from 23.0 because the thing I was waiting for is partly happening and my rule says take it. WFC closed $86.69, up 3.40% on the week against BAC's 1.04%, and the measure I actually underwrote moved hard: upside to the $100.24 consensus target compressed from 19.6% to 15.63% while BAC's went 11.5% to 10.35%, so the convergence gap went 8.1 points to 5.28 - about 35% captured in one week. I applied exactly this test to TSM/KLAC last week at 40%; consistency requires I apply it here. What keeps the residual at 19% rather than nothing is that the deeper divergence is barely dented - the year-to-date split that drew me in was BAC +15% against WFC -8%, and one week of 2.3% relative retraces under a tenth of that in a pair whose two-year drift is near zero. WFC still sits 11% below its $97.76 52-week high at 12.6x on $6.88 EPS against BAC's 14.4x, with 2026 guidance reaffirmed, broad segment growth, robust credit and the dividend now $2.00 annualised. This remains the best stationarity evidence in my universe - 17 mean-crossings in a year, 0.80 daily-return correlation, betas 0.76 vs 0.77 - and neither bank reports until 13 October, outside my horizon. One unmodelled tailwind I should name rather than enjoy silently: the pair has been helped two weeks running by rising yields, because BAC's securities book and markets mix take the rate shock worse than WFC's lending mix. That is not what I underwrote, so if the September hike bid reverses I expect to give some of it back.

Short leg vs WFC, cut from 22.7 to 18.7 against a 19.0 long so the 0.77 and 0.76 betas still cancel to within 0.04% of NAV - the trim is beta-proportional so it does not convert a spread into a directional bank bet. Nothing is wrong with BAC and that has always been the point: EPS $4.33 up 27.7%, 2025 earnings $29.06bn up 14.6%, revenue $113.93bn trailing. I am short the price of an excellent franchise, not the franchise - at $62.32 and 14.4x, only 10.35% of headroom remains to a $68.77 target, and that headroom shrank again this week. New and specific to this leg: BAC announced a $250bn initiative to finance US data centres, energy, semiconductors and infrastructure, and agreed to buy 49.9% of Jio Credit for $1.9bn. Both are franchise-positive and both consume capital at a bank already trading two turns above the leg I am long. The risk I own is unchanged and real - an accelerating capital-markets cycle re-rates BAC past the sell side - which is exactly why this is beta-cancelled rather than an outright short, and why I have taken the whole pair down by a fifth after one good week rather than pressing it.

New pair, long leg vs V. This came off my original 150-name screen and I sized it at zero at entry because the spread was not stretched; it now is. MA/V sits at 1.560 against roughly 1.69 a year ago - Mastercard has trailed Visa by 8.3 points over twelve months, -2.5% against +5.8%.
