The reason was real and I underwrite it explicitly: MA's revenue growth decelerated to 15.8% then 14.1% across Q1-Q2 2026 while Visa's accelerated to 17.1% then 14.4%, inverting the growth premium. What makes this a trade rather than a value trap is that the market has now finished paying for that inversion. The traditional 3-5 turn Mastercard multiple premium is gone - 30.2x against 29.5x, or 32.74 against 32.49 on trailing - and at parity I am no longer paying anything for the faster compounder. MA still beat Q2 with $9.28bn revenue up 14% and adjusted EPS $5.04 up 21%, guided full-year net revenue to the high end of low double digits, and carries 12.46% upside to a $669.46 Strong Buy target against Visa's 9.83%. Bernstein, the most detailed work I found on the pair, prefers MA on 22.1% EPS momentum versus 10.2% and puts fair-value upside at +6.8% against -1.4%. Hedge quality is why this is the diversifier the book needed: betas 0.82 and 0.76, one of the highest daily-return correlations in the market, negligible two-year drift, both names at record highs so neither leg is a falling knife, and both report in late October within days of each other so the earnings event is close to common. Sized at 7% rather than large because the edge is genuine but modest - a 2.6-point target gap - and because Bernstein's own caveat is mine: if MA's deceleration continues, parity is the correct price and this spread simply sits.

New pair, short leg vs MA, sized 7.5 against 7.0 so the 0.76 and 0.82 betas cancel to within 0.04% of NAV - beta-matched, not dollar-matched. Visa is a superb business having a superb year and that is the whole reason it is the short: $381.60 against a $385.57 52-week high after closing at record levels on resilient consumer spending, 32.49x trailing, and only 9.83% left to a $418.92 target - the narrowest headroom of any leg in my book. Trailing revenue is $44.49bn up 14.4% and fiscal 2025 earnings $19.85bn, so I am shorting price and expectations, not execution. The asymmetry that made me pick the direction rather than coin-flip it is litigation: Visa absorbed $707m of interchange MDL provisions in Q1 FY26 and $899m in Q4 FY25 against Mastercard's $82m in Q2 2026, and the $200bn swipe-fee settlement got only preliminary approval on 09 June before the NRF, RILA and Walmart told the court they would rather go to trial. Structural interchange risk sits on both names in this duopoly, but it demonstrably lands harder on this one, and a trial outcome is the single event most likely to reopen the multiple gap in my favour. The risk I own is that Visa's growth acceleration persists and parity turns out to be the new equilibrium rather than an overshoot, which is why the whole pair is 14.5% of gross rather than a statement.

Long leg vs HD, held at 6.0. This was my worst pair of the week and I am neither adding nor cutting, which needs a reason on both counts. LOW fell 3.72% to $208.05 against HD's 1.61% and touched a six-week low; the mechanism was the rate shock, not company news - September hike odds jumped from 35% to 55% on Warsh, and LOW's DIY-discretionary mix carries housing-rate sensitivity that HD's Pro mix does not, so the common shock I expected to cancel instead moved the legs apart. Everything I underwrote got cheaper rather than weaker: LOW now trades at 17.59x with 22.26% upside to a $254.36 target against HD's 23.10x and 14.33%, a 7.9-point convergence gap versus 5.3 a week ago and a 5.5-turn multiple discount, and it sits $8.65 above its $199.40 52-week low. Sell-side framing hardened my way after both prints - Zacks #3 on LOW against #5 Strong Sell on HD, consensus growth ~9% against ~5% - and the board declared its $1.25 quarterly dividend on 08-28. A pure mean-reversion mandate would add into a spread this stretched with 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings and -6% two-year drift. I do not add, because I halved this pair a week ago on a fundamental point that has not been retracted - LOW guided full-year sales and comps to the bottom end on persistent DIY softness while HD reaffirmed - and pressing into a stretch I myself argued was partly deserved would be doubling down against my own read. Holding is the honest middle between a widening spread and a fundamental I got wrong.

Short leg vs LOW, held at 5.7 against 6.0 so the 0.68 and 0.65 betas cancel to within 0.03% of NAV. I keep stating the evidence against this leg because it is still true: HD cleared the harder bar on 08-18 with $47.9bn of sales up 5.7%, comps +1.7% and adjusted EPS $4.92, and held full-year guidance through a housing slump with the CEO on medical leave. That is why the leg is half its original size rather than full. What keeps it on is price and the direction of the rate shock. At $330.19 HD is 23.10x with 14.33% upside to $377.50, five and a half turns richer than the leg I am long for four points less consensus growth, and it sits 23% below its $426.75 52-week high - this is not a stock the market is defending, it is one that has simply fallen less. If September brings the hike the futures now price at 55%, it hits housing turnover on both legs; the question my pair asks is whether five and a half turns of relative premium is the right compensation for HD's better Pro mix, and I think it is too much. No stop here, unchanged and deliberate: stopping out one side of a beta-matched pair leaves me naked long LOW into exactly the shock that triggered it, and with both companies a full quarter from their next print there is no dated event to stop against.

Long leg vs KLAC, held at 5.0 - nothing material changed. The ratio went 2.277 to 2.272 on the week, which after last week's 40% capture of the modelled convergence is exactly the pause a 34-day half-life implies; there is no new information to trade and churning a spread that is doing nothing just pays spread. TSM closed $417.52, down 2.29% on Friday's broad semis de-risking but only ~0.3% on the week, still at 28.44x - a large discount to the equipment names it supplies - with a $554.45 average target implying 32.8% upside and a Strong Buy consensus across 19 analysts, 2025 revenue up 31.6% and earnings up 46.6%, and the $100bn Arizona build extending the capacity story. The 15 mean-crossings and -12% two-year drift are unchanged, so last year's relative fall still reads as oscillation rather than decay. I keep this as the smallest pair in the book because it is the most violent, not because I doubt it.

Short leg vs TSM, held at 4.0 against a 5.0 long because KLAC's 2.70 beta still exceeds TSM's 2.15 - beta-matched, not dollar-matched. KLAC closed $183.77, essentially flat on the week after the prior week's 9.7% fall, so the spread neither extended nor retraced and there is nothing to act on. My position is unchanged and so is my discomfort with it: KLAC guided fiscal Q1 revenue and profit above consensus on AI infrastructure demand, so every dollar of the recent decline was multiple compression on improving fundamentals, and the cheap part of this short has already been paid. What holds the residual is that 50x trailing remains an extraordinary price for a cyclical whose 52-week range runs $83 to $307, and the target gap versus TSM has not closed to zero. This stays the smallest and most violent spread in the book on purpose - it is the leg most likely to be wrong fastest, which is why it is sized so being wrong costs the book almost nothing.

decisions.name: Opus 5 trend following
decisions.research_notes:
Verified every leg's mark and trend structure against the 2026-08-28 close, plus the macro drivers I sized on last week.

PRICES (last week -> 2026-08-28): SPY 769.35 (S&P 7,674.37 -> 7,711.76, +0.49% on the week, 52wk high 779.37). XLE 63.64 -> 62.68 (-1.5%, 52wk range 42.35-64.70). XLV 174.62 -> 171.16 (-2.0%, high 176.60). DBA 28.32 -> 29.19 (+3.1%, 52wk range 25.40-29.20 — a NEW 52-week high). XLF 57.48 -> 58.10 (+1.1%, high 58.41). CPER 39.99 -> 39.67 (-0.8%, high 40.97). BTC ~77,000 -> ~80,200.

MACRO. (1) Jackson Hole: Fed Chair Warsh called inflation "concerning," said this summer's better prints "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," and explicitly put rate INCREASES in play. Markets now price ~34% odds of a hike at the Sept 15-16 meeting; some houses pushed easing into 2027. Gold -3.7% on the week to $4,506 is the clean read-through. (2) Oil reversed hard: Brent 94.39 -> 88.29, WTI 87.06 -> 83.38 (-3.8% wk, ~-5% intra-week trough). The driver flipped — traders now frame Iran as a sanctions/economic confrontation rather than an imminent physical supply threat, Hormuz flows are improving, and Goldman puts Persian Gulf exports back at 15-16 mb/d versus the March low of 5-6 mb/d (pre-war 22-24). That is the exact "economic D-day" thesis I raised XLE on last week, running backwards. (3) Long end: 30yr ~5.20% on 8/27, off the 5.33% 19-year high of 8/18 — pressure eased slightly but the structure is unchanged. (4) Copper -0.71% on the week; I re-checked Section 232 and refined cathode is still exempt with no determination.

NEW CANDIDATE SCREENED: TLT. Below all moving averages (10dma crossed below the 50dma on 2026-07-14), printed a 22-year low this month, $82.88 close against a 52wk range of 81.17-92.19 and an all-time low of $80.67. 3-month momentum is only marginally negative (~$83.5 in late May -> $82.88), so this is a strong-MA / weak-momentum signal, and I size it accordingly rather than to full inverse-vol.

CONCLUSION: no leg failed its trend filter, so nothing gets closed. But the ranking inside the book changed materially — DBA and XLF accelerated, XLE's physical driver reversed, XLV gave back exactly the relative strength I paid up for, CPER stalled a third week, and BTC's flip is now confirmed. This is a re-sizing week, not a rebuild.

decisions.reason: Every leg still passes its trend filter, so I close nothing — but the internal ranking moved enough that holding last week's weights would mean holding theses the tape has already contradicted. Three specific things forced size to move. First, I raised XLE to 19 last week explicitly because Brent went to $94.39 and the Iran story was turning into a physical supply war; Brent is now $88.29, WTI $83.38, and the market has re-read Iran as a sanctions fight while Gulf exports recovered to 15-16 mb/d from the 5-6 mb/d March low. XLE itself is only -1.5% because the equity lags the barrel, which means the deterioration is not yet marked. I will not hold a 19% weight underwritten by a $94 Brent when Brent is $88, so it goes back to its inverse-vol baseline. Second, I added 2 points to XLV for outperforming a falling index; it then fell 2.0% while the index rose 0.5%, so I take those 2 points back — I add for relative strength and I remove for its absence, symmetrically. Third, DBA printed a new 52-week high and XLF pressed its own while gold, oil and copper all fell, and Warsh putting hikes in play is a higher-for-longer, steeper-curve setup that is the cleanest bank tailwind available; those are the two legs momentum is actually being added to, so they get the size. Separately, a time-series trend book carrying zero shorts while a qualifying short sits in plain view is a construction failure, not neutrality: TLT is below every moving average at a 22-year low with the Fed chair signalling hikes, and it is short precisely the risk I have flagged as my book's main pressure point for two weeks. Net long falls from 88 to 78 even as gross rises, which is the right direction into a Fed that has taken the put away.
decisions.novelty: The book gains its first short since I closed the BTC short — a 6% TLT leg that is short duration rather than short risk — and the weight centre of gravity moves out of the energy/healthcare pair that dominated it into agriculture and financials, the only two legs making new highs.

positions.thesis: Trimmed 20 to 19, which is a funding trim and not a signal change. The index closed 7,711.76, +0.49% on the week and within a percent of its 779.37 SPY high, so price is comfortably above both moving averages with 3m momentum still strongly positive — and at ~13% realised vol it remains the lowest-volatility trend I own and therefore still my largest weight under inverse-vol sizing. What changed is the character of the risk rather than the trend: Warsh explicitly put rate increases in play at Jackson Hole and the market now prices ~34% odds of a September hike, so the equity leg no longer has a Fed put underneath it. The disciplined response to that is not to sell a trend that is working but to stop paying for it with cash and start paying for it with a duration short, which is what the new TLT leg does. Wide -15% catastrophe stop; weekly reassessment stays the real exit.

Cut hard from 19 to 14 — the largest single move in the book — because I sized it up for a driver that has since reversed. Last week I raised it to 19 on Brent at $94.39 and a US move to cut Iran out of banking, shipping and settlement entirely. Brent is now $88.29 and WTI $83.38, the market has re-priced Iran as an economic and sanctions confrontation rather than an imminent threat to physical supply, and Goldman has Persian Gulf exports back at 15-16 mb/d against the 5-6 mb/d March low. XLE at $62.68 is only 1.5% lower, still above both moving averages and still inside striking distance of its $64.70 high, so the trend filter passes and I keep a real core position — the equity simply has not yet marked what the barrel did. But a 19% weight was the expression of a specific escalation thesis, and that thesis is running backwards; 14 is roughly the inverse-vol baseline for the highest-volatility equity sleeve I own (~24% realised). The stop stays wide at -25% for the same reason as always: a headline gap in either direction is the known failure mode and a tight stop guarantees being taken out on the first one.

Back to 15 from 17, reversing exactly the add I made last week and for exactly the mirror reason. I raised it to 17 because it gained 3.9% in a week the index fell 1.4% — five points of relative strength at a 0.56 beta. This week it fell 2.0% to $171.16 while the index rose 0.49%, which is two and a half points of relative weakness, and the outperformance I paid up for did not persist. The underlying trend is untouched: still above both moving averages with the golden cross intact, still within 3% of its $176.60 52-week high, still the strongest 3m momentum among my low-volatility sleeves, ~18% realised vol. So this is not a doubt about the leg, it is a refusal to let a one-week tactical add calcify into a permanent overweight. It stays a substantial core holding because a low-beta trend that works when the tape does not is worth more, not less, now that the Fed has stopped promising cuts.

Raised 11 to 13 because it did the one thing nothing else in my commodity complex did: it broke out. $29.19 against $28.32 a week ago, +3.1%, and that is a new 52-week high — the 12-month range now reads 25.40-29.20 and price is sitting on the top of it. Set that against the week it happened in: gold -3.7%, crude -3.8%, copper -0.7%. Agriculture made new highs while every other commodity I follow fell, which is the definition of a leg extending its own trend rather than riding a complex-wide beta. It also carries the two properties this book needs most right now — a ~0.12 beta makes it the least equity-correlated thing I own, and ~13% realised vol makes it the cheapest risk unit available under inverse-vol sizing, at a moment when I am cutting a high-vol energy leg and the Fed has turned hawkish. Two weeks ago I declined to trade this on a 0.1% move; I am adding now because the move is real, directional, and confirmed by a range breakout.

Raised 9 to 13, the largest add in the book, because the condition I cut it for has resolved in its favour. I took it to 9 and then held it flat two weeks running with an explicit reason: the trend passed but momentum was not being added to, and the rate picture cut both ways so it cut neither. That ambiguity is gone. $58.10 against $57.48, +1.1%, now pressing the $58.41 52-week high, and Warsh at Jackson Hole put rate increases in play with ~34% priced for September — higher-for-longer at the front end with a 30-year already near 19-year highs is a steeper curve and better net interest margin, which is the cleanest bank tailwind on offer. The systemic-stress side of the argument, a buyers' strike in the long end, has eased modestly with the 30-year back to ~5.20% from 5.33%. I said I would size this up when momentum resumed rather than anticipate it; it resumed, and I am paying for the add out of the energy leg whose driver went the other way.

Cut again, 8 to 5, for the third consecutive week and for the same compounding reason. The price path is $40.12, $39.99, $39.67 — three weeks of no progress at the top of a $27.37-$40.97 range, with copper itself down 0.71% on the week. The moving-average filters still pass, which is why this is a trim and not an exit, but a trend that has stopped trending is no longer paying me for the risk it carries. And the risk it carries is not ordinary volatility: Section 232 remains unresolved with refined cathode still exempt and no determination made, the 15% phase-in still only contemplated for 2027, and CPER holds exactly the COMEX futures that embed the US tariff premium. A stalled price and an unpriced gap risk in the same leg is worse than either alone precisely because inverse-vol sizing cannot see the second one. I keep taking size down by hand while the -25% stop stays wide enough that normal copper volatility does not hit it.

Raised 4 to 5 because the flip I made a week ago has been confirmed rather than faded. I sized this at the very bottom of the inverse-vol range specifically because every filter was marginal — a one-day-old 200dma reclaim on +4.8% 3m momentum, entered after a 22% squeeze week, which is the worst possible entry. A week later BTC closed near $80,200 against ~$77,000, the 200-day sits at $69-75k so the reclaim now has a real buffer instead of being a single print, and 3m momentum has strengthened to roughly +9% ($73,525 to $80,173). That is the marginal case becoming an ordinary one, which earns one point of size and nothing more — realised vol here is multiples of anything else I own and inverse-vol sizing keeps it the smallest leg in the book regardless of how good the signal looks. Still 1x with no liquidation-relevant leverage. Funding at 10% APR on this size is a rounding error and not a reason to change wrapper. The -20% stop sits near $64k, back inside the abandoned range, which would falsify the breakout outright.

New leg, and the first short since I closed the falsified BTC short. My mandate is symmetric — short where both filters are negative — and a time-series trend book running no shorts at all while a qualifying short sits in plain sight is a construction failure, not neutrality. TLT closed $82.88, below every moving average with the 10dma having crossed under the 50dma on 2026-07-14, after printing a 22-year low this month; the 52-week range is 81.17-92.19 and the all-time low is $80.67, so price is pinned at the bottom of its own distribution rather than mid-range. The fundamental driver is now pushing the same way: Warsh explicitly said rate increases are in play, ~34% of a September hike is priced, easing calls are being pushed into 2027, and the 30-year is near 19-year highs with debt approaching $40tn. I size this at 6% rather than the ~12% inverse-vol would suggest for a ~13% vol asset, deliberately, because the momentum leg is weak: late-May TLT was ~$83.5 against $82.88 now, so 3-month momentum is only marginally negative and the last three months are really a flat range at the lows, not a downtrend paying me to be in it. Strong MA structure plus weak momentum earns a half-size position, not a full one. The second reason to own it is portfolio construction: this is short precisely the long-end stress I have named as my book's main pressure point for two weeks running, so it cuts net long from 88 to 78 while diversifying an all-long risk book. Borrow at 3% APR on 6% of NAV is immaterial. The -15% stop would require the 30-year to collapse roughly a full point, which is a recession or QE regime change and should take me out.

decisions.name: Opus 5 unrestricted
decisions.research_notes:
Two regime breaks this week, both against my stated theses, and one confirmation.

1) CRUDE — my ERX thesis broke. Brent fell from $93.86 to ~$88.3-89.3, a >5% weekly loss and the first weekly decline in three. The mechanism matters more than the price: (a) the Bessent "economic D-Day" sanctions that I explicitly bought last week landed Monday 8/24 and were, per market analysts, LESS severe than anticipated — oil fell on the announcement; (b) Iran and Oman announced a phased framework on 8/26 for a temporary 7-mile-wide Hormuz transit corridor plus a joint mine-clearing initiative, with Oman "hopeful" of formalizing; (c) Goldman puts Persian Gulf exports back at ~15-16 mb/d versus a March low of 5-6 mb/d (pre-conflict 22-24). Traders have reclassified this from a physical-supply threat to a sanctions/economic confrontation. That is not a headline gap-down — it is the slow version of exactly the tail I named as my largest risk. XLE $63.58 -> $62.50. Offsetting: the interim peace deal has lapsed, Iran says the US is blocking the Hormuz deal, mines are still in the water, and ~8 mb/d is still missing. Re-escalation is live but no longer the base case.

2) THE FED — inverted. Kevin Warsh gave his first Jackson Hole speech on 8/28 and said inflation reports "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," that the Fed "has more work to do," and put rate INCREASES in play. Two-year yield 4.22% -> 4.30%; CME FedWatch September hike odds moved to roughly 50%; consensus commentary is no hike in September but one by October or December. My GLD and SLV theses were written verbatim around "Powell opening the door to a September cut with markets at 91% odds." That premise is gone. Notably, gold barely flinched — spot $4,608 on 8/28 after a $4,697 high on 8/25, with central banks buying a quarterly record 288.9 tonnes in Q2 — so the non-rate bid (fiscal, central banks, geopolitics) is real, but the specific reason I was 30% in metals is not. Silver $69.35, flat on the week after last week's 8.8% run.

3) REFINING — confirmed, and confirmed in the best possible way. The US diesel crack hit a record $102.20/bbl on 8/17 (first triple-digit print ever, ~15% above the Oct-2022 record) and sits near $93-94 in late August; NWE gasoil crack ~$78, Singapore ~$72; roughly 7-8 mb/d of global refining capacity is offline from Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and Gulf drone attacks; US distillate inventories entering late August are at their lowest since 1996, a 30-year trough. MPC printed an all-time high of $367.99 on 8/28 — an all-time high in the same week crude fell 5%. That is the divergence I bought MPC for, demonstrated in live fire rather than argued.

4) EQUITIES/AIRLINES — S&P 7,711.76, +0.49% on the week, Nasdaq +0.9%, index at records into a hawkish Fed. XLV ~$172.4, still the low-beta ballast, unremarkable week. On JETS: lower crude does NOT relieve airlines while the crack is at a record, because carriers buy the product, not the barrel — jet fuel is inside the same squeeze complex. IATA still has the industry's 2026 profit forecast roughly halved, US carrier fuel spend ran $6.66bn in May at +85% y/y, and ~20% of exported jet fuel is still stranded. A Fed threatening hikes into a soft labor market strengthens the demand-side leg independently.

Synthesis: the correct read is that I was long the wrong end of the energy complex. The crude bet depended on supply staying removed; supply is coming back. The crack bet depends on refining capacity staying destroyed and distillate inventories staying empty — and cheaper crude is a direct feedstock tailwind to it. I am rotating from the barrel to the barrel's bottleneck, and cutting the metals sizing that was justified by a rate cut that is now a coin-flip rate hike. Note: my web-research budget ran out before I could pull a fresh 8/28 quote on VLO, which is reflected in that position being sized at 10 rather than larger.

decisions.reason: Two of my three stated premises broke this week and I am not going to hold positions whose written reasons are now false. The ERX thesis was supply removal — blockade plus 'toughest sanctions in history.' The sanctions landed softer than billed, Iran and Oman announced a phased Hormuz corridor framework with joint mine-clearing, Gulf exports have recovered from 5-6 mb/d in March to 15-16 mb/d, and Brent fell 5%+ to ~$88.5. That is my named worst tail arriving in slow motion rather than as a gap, which is the version where I actually get to act on it. The GLD and SLV sizes were justified in writing by '91% odds of a September cut'; Warsh used his first Jackson Hole speech to put rate HIKES in play, the two-year moved to 4.30%, and September hike odds are near 50%. Meanwhile the one leg that does not depend on either premise got materially stronger: the diesel crack printed a record $102.20, sits near $93-94, distillate inventories are at a 30-year low, 7-8 mb/d of refining capacity is offline, and MPC made an all-time high in the same week crude fell 5%. Cheaper crude is a feedstock tailwind to the crack, not a headwind. So I am selling the barrel and buying the bottleneck: ERX 22 to 8, MPC 12 to 20, new VLO 10, and the book's center of gravity moves from 'crude goes up' to 'refined products stay scarce' — a thesis that survives the de-escalation that is killing the old one and is paired against a short in the product's captive consumer. Metals go 30 to 19 because their engine reversed, not to zero, because gold held $4,608 through an explicitly hawkish Jackson Hole on record central-bank buying. Cash to 13 because a Fed that may hike makes 4%+ a real competing asset, and because I just cut my highest-conviction directional bet and do not want to force the proceeds somewhere to avoid looking idle.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book, so there is no Round-2 book to overlap with; the novelty is structural rather than nominal — this is no longer a levered crude bet carried by hedges but a long-crack-spread book, expressed as long two refiners and short the refined product's largest captive consumer, with the crude leg demoted to a small option on re-escalation.

positions.thesis: Raised 12 to 20 and now my largest position, because this is the only leg in the book that got a live proof rather than an argument this week: MPC closed at an all-time high $367.99 on 8/28 during a week Brent fell more than 5%. That is the exact divergence I sized it for. Refining margin is a product-scarcity bet, not a crude-price bet, and the scarcity is at records with a physical basis I can point at — the US diesel crack hit $102.20/bbl on 8/17, the first triple-digit print in history and ~15% above the 2022 record, and still sits near $93-94; roughly 7-8 mb/d of global refining capacity is offline from Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and Gulf drone damage; and US distillate inventories are at their lowest since 1996. Against that, falling crude is a tailwind: the refiner buys the cheaper feedstock and sells into a market that is still physically short distillate. MPC's own refining and marketing margin has gone $17.58 to $36.33 per barrel — realized cash, not a forecast. I am buying more at an all-time high, which is the honest cost of a setup that is working; the real risk is that record cracks mean-revert as offline capacity returns or demand rectifies, and heading into winter with 30-year-low distillate stocks that reversion looks like a Q1 problem rather than a September one. Stop -18% caps the leg at 3.6% of NAV. Take-profit cut 40 to 35 because at that level the crack has to have held records for a full quarter, and I would rather be paid on a mean-reverting spread than greedy.

Held at 20, and its job just got more important. This was ballast for a 2x energy fund; it is now ballast for a book whose largest exposures are a single-factor bet on refined-product scarcity, held into a Fed chair who has openly put rate hikes back on the table with the S&P at 7,711 and records. Healthcare at ~18x forward with a 0.65-0.75 beta, carried by real Q2 earnings beats and the GLP-1 franchise rather than by defensive flows, is the cleanest thing I own for a multiple-compression regime — when the discount rate rises, the low-multiple low-beta sector gives back least. It stays unstopped for the same reason as last week, unchanged: this is the position I want to still be holding if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only fire in a market-wide flush, which is precisely the moment I need to be holding it. Its honest weakness is that it did nothing at all this week (~$172.4), and in a book that just cut both of its exciting theses, that is a feature.

Trimmed 20 to 14 because the reason I wrote for owning 20 is no longer true. I sized this on 'Powell opening the door to a September cut with markets at 91% odds'; Warsh told Jackson Hole that underlying inflation trends have not meaningfully improved and the Fed has more work to do, the two-year went 4.22 to 4.30, and September hike odds are near 50%. Rising real rates are the single cleanest headwind to a non-yielding asset and I will not pretend otherwise to protect a position. I trim rather than exit because the rest of the bid is intact and demonstrated itself under fire this week: gold made $4,697 on 8/25 and still closed 8/28 at $4,608 immediately after an explicitly hawkish speech, with central banks buying a quarterly record 288.9 tonnes in Q2 against $40 trillion of federal debt. And a Fed hiking into a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs is a stagflationary policy-error setup, which is the one regime where gold works with rates going the wrong way. Stop held at -12%, capping the leg at 1.7% of NAV; a 12% break from a record would mean the fiscal and central-bank bid failed too, and at that point I am wrong on all of it rather than early.

New 10%, and the reason it is a second name rather than simply a larger MPC is idiosyncratic risk. The dominant single-name event for a refiner is an unplanned outage — a fire, a unit trip, a turnaround overrun — and in a market this tight, one of those at one facility is company-specific pain while the sector thesis stays perfectly intact. Splitting 30% of crack exposure across two operators converts a plant-level accident from a 5-6% NAV event into roughly half that. Valero is the purest expression of the trade: the least diversified of the large US refiners away from refining itself, so the most levered to the distillate crack that is actually at records, with a Gulf Coast system positioned into cheapening feedstock as crude falls. Same thesis, same catalyst and the same failure mode as MPC — record cracks mean-reverting when the ~7-8 mb/d of offline global capacity returns — which is why the pair together is 30 and not 45. I could not pull a fresh 8/28 quote before my research budget ran out, so I am sizing this at 10 rather than 15 and putting the same -18% stop on it, capping the leg at 1.8% of NAV.

Held at 10, and I want to correct the lazy bear case against it: crude falling 5% does NOT relieve airlines, because carriers buy the refined product, not the barrel, and the jet-fuel crack sits inside the same record complex I just increased my long exposure to. That is the point of the pair — MPC and VLO are long the crack, JETS short is short the crack's largest captive consumer, and both legs pay off on the same physical fact of refined-product scarcity. The industry has already conceded the math: the global sector nearly halved its 2026 profit forecast on Middle East fuel costs, US carriers' fuel bill ran $6.66bn in May at +85% y/y, roughly 20% of exported jet fuel is still stranded, and managements are cutting unprofitable routes and grounding less fuel-efficient aircraft. The demand leg strengthened independently this week: a Fed chair signaling hikes into a soft labor market pressures discretionary leisure travel, which flinches first when fares rise to cover fuel. What improved is that this no longer double-counts with a large crude long — cutting ERX removed the shared Hormuz failure mode I flagged last week, so this is a cleaner hedge than it was. Squeeze risk stays specific: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a possible government equity stake. Borrow costs ~30bps a year on 10%. Stop -18% caps it at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25%.

Cut 22 to 8 — the largest single change in the book and an admission that I was long the wrong end of the energy complex. I bought this on supply removal. Supply is coming back: Persian Gulf exports have recovered from a March low of 5-6 mb/d to 15-16 mb/d, the 8/24 sanctions package landed softer than its 'toughest in history' billing and oil fell on the news, and on 8/26 Iran and Oman announced a phased framework for a temporary 7-mile Hormuz corridor with joint mine-clearing. Brent went $93.86 to ~$88.5 and XLE $63.58 to $62.50. The market has reclassified this from a physical-supply threat to an economic confrontation, and a 2x fund with daily-reset decay is an expensive way to be stubborn about a thesis that has moved from base case to tail. Layer on a Fed that may hike: a firmer dollar and slower demand are both crude-negative. Why 8 and not zero — the re-escalation tail is genuinely live, not rhetorical. The June interim deal has lapsed, Iran publicly says the US is blocking the Hormuz agreement, the corridor is explicitly temporary and conditional on US compliance, mines are still in the water, and roughly 8 mb/d is still missing from the market. If that unravels, crude gaps up hard and 2x is the cheapest way to have owned the option. At 8% with a stop tightened -22% to -20% the leg costs at most 1.6% of NAV, a price I will pay rather than be flat a live geopolitical binary. Take-profit held at +40%.

Cut 10 to 5, the sharpest proportional trim in the book, because this is the leg whose written thesis was most explicitly a rate-cut bet — I raised it from 7 to 10 only last week citing 'a September cut at 91% implied odds.' Those odds are now roughly a coin flip on a HIKE. Silver is the higher-beta expression of the debasement trade, which means it is the higher-beta expression of a driver that just inverted, and its industrial half is precisely what a Fed deliberately slowing the economy damages — so both legs I bought it for weakened at once. It went flat on the week ($69.87 to $69.35) after an 8.8% run, so the gold/silver catch-up I paid up for has stalled rather than continued. I keep 5 rather than none because the structural supply deficit is independent of the Fed, silver is still well below its February mid-$80s high while gold sits near a record, and if the policy-error stagflation path is what Warsh is actually engineering then silver leads gold on the way up. But it is now a tail position, not a thesis position. Stop stays wide at -18%, capping it at 0.9% of NAV; this metal traded mid-$80s to $64 to $70 inside a year and anything tighter is noise.

decisions.name: Opus Broadening
decisions.research_notes:
MACRO — the regime input changed this week and it is not my own chart inference this time. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole address stated that "inflation is running too high"; markets repriced toward rate HIKES rather than cuts. S&P 500 -1.4% on the week, snapping a three-week win streak; Friday S&P -0.25%, Nasdaq -0.52%, Dow flat. Gold -2.88% and Bitcoin -2.29% to ~$77.6k on Friday, i.e. the classic liquidity-tightening repricing. VIX only 14.43, so this is a repricing, not a panic. This matters because a hike-risk regime lands hardest on exactly the cohorts my Round-2 breadth mandate owns (small caps, regional banks, leveraged small-cap) and on the long-duration high-multiple software my Round-3 mandate owns, while it is a tailwind to both of my Round-3 shorts (ORCL: -$23.7B FCF, $97.6B net debt, ~$40B FY27 financing need; UPST: unsecured consumer lender funding costs).

ROUND-2 PRICE READINGS (52-wk range %, 08-28 close, prior week in brackets): RSP 93.3 [97.4], IWM 87.6 [93.7], XLE 91.0 [99.5], XBI 90.7 [95.3], XLB 91.7 [100.0], TNA 81.9 [90.0], KRE 80.5 [85.3], XLI 73.1 [84.3], QQQ 83.3 [83.0]. Every long deteriorated; nothing broke. Two readings stand out: XLI has now fallen for a second straight week and is the worst sector read I own, and TNA lost roughly 4.5% against IWM's 1.5% — the 3x daily-compounding drag I have flagged three weeks running, now in a tape with a fresh reason to chop. The RSP/QQQ concentration spread went slightly against me for the first time in three weeks (QQQ roughly flat, RSP -0.8%), which is what a hawkish repricing does: cash-rich mega-cap beats leveraged small-cap. ETH $2,434.86, sitting at the low end of a $2,409-$2,526 seven-day range — the CLARITY Act / melt-up bounce has stalled and BTC has rolled over, so the catalyst I refused to chase has now passed.

ROUND-3 — THE FINDING THAT DRIVES THIS WEEK. I checked every earnings date rather than trusting last week's notes, and one of them was wrong. Three of my nine positions print INSIDE the coming window: PANW Tue 09-01, SNOW Wed 09-02, and ORCL Fri 09-04. I wrote last week that ORCL reports "~09-10, outside the window"; that is factually incorrect. At current weights that is 18+15+6 = 39% of the book on binary events in four sessions, in an account already -2.62% with a -7.73% max drawdown. Setups: SNOW $328.00, 93.8% of range, consensus PT $327.85 — the stock is exactly at target, 156x forward, no valuation floor. PANW $371.59, 89.5% of range [85.0], -2.94% Friday, consensus PT $364.01 — trading ABOVE target, 95x forward, China security review still live. ORCL $150.85, 15.7% of range [15.0] — it stopped underperforming and ticked up ~1% in a -1.4% tape, so the non-participation confirmation I upsized on has weakened, and it goes into a print with 62% consensus upside and a Citi positive-catalyst-watch $330 target. Names with NO print in the window improved their readings while the cohort fell: FTNT 92.1 [84.1], TWLO 87.1 [80.3], NET 81.3 [77.9], XYZ 91.3 [93.0], and my best short UPST fell to 9.6% of range [12.3], -4.6% on the week, the lowest reading in my universe. MU $932.86 is 71.8% of range [77.5] with earnings 09-30 (outside window) and the supply-shortage story still contested by Samsung/SK Hynix additions.

THE GOVERNING POINT: a stop-loss does not work through an earnings gap. A -22% stop on SNOW is worthless if it opens -18%. For an event inside the window the only risk control that exists is position size, and my mandate is cross-sectional momentum, not event trading — I have no edge in a single-name print. So I cut event size and redeploy into the momentum names that carry no event.

decisions.reason: Warsh told the market inflation is too high and the market is now pricing hikes, and unlike my two previous rate-driven trades in this book I am not acting on that inference alone — I am acting where the price readings independently agree. XLI has deteriorated a second straight week to 73.1% of range, the worst sector read I own, so I finish the trim I started rather than restate the concern a third time; last week I said I was removing size justified by a record close that no longer existed, and that logic exits it now. TNA goes 6->3 because a 3x daily-rebalanced small-cap instrument in a chop with a fresh macro reason to chop bleeds regardless of direction, and I already own the directional view at 16% in IWM. ETH 3->2 because the CLARITY Act catalyst has passed, BTC has rolled over, and at 29% of its 52-week range it fails every screen this book uses. The proceeds go to the two best readings, not to the sidelines: RSP 19->23 (93.3% of range, held up best of anything I own and is the lower-vol breadth expression that survives a hawkish repricing) and XLB 5->6 (91.7%, still the leading cyclical). IWM 19->16 shifts a slice of breadth from the most rate-sensitive expression to the most durable one without abandoning it. Critically I am NOT touching XBI at 12: I committed in writing last week to stop trading it on a macro rate argument after being wrong twice on exactly that, its reading is still 90.7% of range, and honouring that commitment is worth more than this week's -2.2%. Cash to 13% at 4% is a buffer, not a view; gross 96->87 is a measured step back, still long-heavy as the mandate requires.

positions.thesis: Raised 19->23 and still the anchor. At 93.3% of its 52-week range it lost the least of anything I own in a -1.4% week, and it is the version of breadth that does not depend on the rate path: equal-weight large-cap has no leverage, no funding sensitivity and no size premium to give back if the Fed hikes. I am adding here rather than holding cash because the deterioration across my book was a consolidation from record levels, not a break, and this is the leg I would most want to own if I am wrong about the macro. It also remains the long half of the anti-concentration pair, which has carried that view far better than the short.

Trimmed 19->16 and given a stop for the first time. Small caps are the single most rate-sensitive cohort in my book and the Fed chair just made hikes a live scenario; IWM fell 1.5% and slipped from 93.7% to 87.6% of range. I am not exiting the size factor — 87.6% of range with the 12-1 trend intact is a consolidation and I have twice been punished for abandoning this on a rate argument. I am moving three points to RSP, which expresses the same anti-concentration idea with none of the funding sensitivity. The new -15% stop, roughly two monthly sigma at 20 vol, exists because the identified vulnerability of this book now has a name and I would rather define the loss in advance than argue about it later.

Held at 13 through a -3% week that took it from 99.5% to 91.0% of range. Energy is the one cyclical whose thesis a hawkish Fed does not damage — it is short-duration cash flow with a commodity behind it, and refiner margins are at records on Middle East supply risk and AI-driven power demand. Giving back part of a run from a 52-week high is what a leader does; 91% of range is still top-tier in my universe. I have been whipsawed twice on this sector by trading the weekly number instead of the reading, so the discipline is to leave a correctly-sized position alone. Stop stays -18%, capping the leg at 2.3% of NAV.

Untraded at 12, deliberately, and this is the position where my own audit trail binds me. I cut it a week earlier on a 30-year-yield argument, the argument was rejected by the tape, I restored it and committed in writing that only the -22% stop would take it out and that I would not trade it on a macro rate story again. A hawkish Jackson Hole is precisely that story in a new costume. The reading has not broken: 90.7% of its 52-week range after -2.2% on the week, with the sector M&A and FDA calendar underneath it unchanged. Cutting here would be running the same failed trade a third time with better prose. The -22% stop, about two monthly sigma at 38 vol, is the entire risk control and it is sufficient.

Untraded at 6. I cut this in half last week on the labour-market and CRE credit worry and it promptly outperformed the complex it sits in, -1.3% against IWM's -1.5% and XLI's -2.5%, holding 80.5% of range. That is the position now sized correctly rather than a position to keep cutting: the size that was justified by an old record close is already gone, and 6% is small enough that the credit scenario I am worried about costs me under a point of NAV. Rate hikes are genuinely two-sided here — better asset yields against deposit costs — which is another reason to hold rather than take a view I cannot support.

Raised 5->6 with money from the XLI exit. Materials came off a flat 100% of range to 91.7%, which now makes it the best cyclical read I own alongside energy, and it did that while industrials fell to 73%. That is the whole reason this position exists — it was added as the cyclical that was actually leading, and one week later it is still leading while the one it replaced keeps falling. The add is one point rather than five because 12-1 momentum here is a middling reading and the position earns its slot on confirmation and low vol, not conviction.

Cut 6->3. This is the third consecutive week I have written that 3x daily compounding punishes a chopping small-cap tape, and the third consecutive week it has: -4.5% against IWM's -1.5%. What changed is that the tape now has a specific reason to keep chopping — a Fed chair calling inflation too high, with small caps the cohort that pays for it. I am not exiting, because the mandate names TNA amplification and 81.9% of range with the underlying trend intact does not justify abandonment. I am removing the amplification I cannot defend paying decay for while the rate question is open, and I already hold the directional small-cap view at 16% in an unlevered wrapper. Stop stays -25%, now capping the leg at 0.75% of NAV.

Cut 3->2. I refused to chase this into the CLARITY Act melt-up and said it was a violent bounce off a deep hole rather than a leader; that call is now settled — Bitcoin fell to roughly $77.6k and ETH sits at $2,435, the low end of its $2,409-$2,526 weekly range, with the catalyst spent. Tightening liquidity expectations are the wrong backdrop for the asset, and at 29% of its 52-week range with deeply negative 12-1 momentum it fails every screen the rest of this book is built on. Cut to 2 rather than zero because the mandate asks for a speculative convexity tail and 2% at 100% realized vol still delivers real optionality; the -25% stop caps it at 0.5% of NAV.

Untraded at 6 and I am holding it through its first bad week in three. QQQ was roughly flat against RSP's -0.8%, which is exactly what a hike-risk repricing does: cash-rich mega-caps outperform leveraged small caps. That is a real headwind to this leg and I am stating it rather than hiding it. I am not cutting, because with 81% of the book in longs this is the structural offset that makes a long-heavy breadth basket survivable, and QQQ at 83.3% of its range against RSP at 93.3% means the spread I am short is still wide. I am equally not upsizing it into a macro story — pressing this leg on conviction is the mistake that cost me three weeks ago, and the mandate asks for a small anti-concentration short, which 6% against 81% of longs is.

decisions.reason: I re-checked every earnings date instead of trusting my own notes and found an error that changes the week: PANW prints 09-01, SNOW 09-02 and ORCL 09-04 — all three inside this window, not two of them. Last week I wrote that ORCL reported ~09-10 and was outside the window; that was wrong, and I am correcting it rather than carrying a short into a catalyst I told myself was not there. At last week's weights that is 39% of the book on binary events in four sessions, in an account already -2.62% with a -7.73% drawdown. The decisive argument is mechanical: my per-name stops, which are the stated risk control of this entire mandate, do not function through an overnight earnings gap — a -22% stop on SNOW is worthless if it opens -18%. For an event inside the window, size is the only control that exists. My edge is cross-sectional momentum, not predicting prints, so I halve the three event positions (SNOW 18->9, PANW 15->8, ORCL short 6->3) and keep every thesis intact. This is not a flinch on the screens: SNOW is still my best range read at 93.8% and PANW actually IMPROVED to 89.5% of range this week. The freed capital goes to the names that pass the same screen and have no print until late October and therefore express the mandate cleanly — FTNT 8->12 (92.1% of range, up from 84.1%, best pure-software 12-1 in my universe), TWLO 8->12 (87.1%, up from 80.3%), NET 7->10 (81.3%, up from 77.9%), XYZ 6->8 — and UPST goes 5->6 because it is the only leg where the macro news is unambiguously in my favour: a hike-risk repricing hits an unsecured consumer lender's funding costs directly, and it fell to 9.6% of its 52-week range, the lowest reading in my universe, with no event in the window. MU stays at 9 unchanged — no print until 09-30, but at 71.8% of range with the supply story contested it has not earned an add. Cash 18->23 is the residue of stepping out of event risk, not a market call.
decisions.novelty: This book shares no instrument and no factor with my Round-2 breadth basket — Round 2 is long equal-weight, small-cap, energy, biotech and materials index exposure against a QQQ index short, while Round 3 is single-name cross-sectional momentum in software, memory and fintech against two single-name laggard shorts, so same-direction gross-weight overlap is zero; the two books also now diverge in what drove this week's decision, since Round 2 was rebalanced on deteriorating sector range readings and Round 3 was rebalanced on an earnings-calendar correction that no index position in Round 2 is exposed to.

positions.thesis: Raised 8->12, now the largest long. Last week I sized it at 8 because it was one metric short of a clean sweep, closing 1.6% below its 50-day; that gap has closed. It moved from 84.1% to 92.1% of its 52-week range in a week when the whole software cohort fell and it kept the best pure-software 12-1 momentum in my universe at +94.9%, at 38 realized vol against CRWD's 52. It reported 07-29 and does not print again until late October, so it carries the mandate's momentum exposure with none of the event risk I am paying to remove elsewhere. I am aware the sell side rates it Hold with a target below spot and that it fell 3.92% Friday — this mandate is built on cross-sectional momentum, not analyst targets, and one down day in a down tape does not touch the ranking. Stop -20%, capping the leg at 2.4% of NAV.

Raised 8->12. I bought this last week precisely because it passed every leg while the cohort broke down around it, and it then did the thing that claim predicts: 80.3% -> 87.1% of range on the week, with 12-1 momentum of +83.3% and record Q2 revenue and profit behind it. It reported 08-06 with nothing until late October, and it is my only communications-infrastructure exposure, so adding here concentrates conviction without concentrating theme — this is not a third way to own security. Sized to 12 rather than higher because 52 realized vol is the highest among my longs; the -24% stop is about a week and a half of sigma, wide enough not to be triggered by ordinary movement, and caps the leg at 2.9% of NAV.

Raised 7->10. Last week I argued NET was a name pulling back inside an uptrend rather than one breaking, and distinguished it from CRWD on that basis; it has now recovered from 77.9% to 81.3% of range while the cohort fell further, which is the confirmation of that distinction. Reported 08-06 with FedRAMP High certification and analyst upgrades behind the print and no event until late October. The add is three points rather than five because its 12-1 momentum remains middling relative to FTNT and TWLO, so it still earns its slot on breadth within the mandate rather than on conviction. Stop -22% caps it at 2.2% of NAV.

Halved 18->9 for the print on 09-02, and only for the print. The screen still loves it — 93.8% of its 52-week range is the best reading among my longs and it was the only long that rose in last week's rout. What I cannot defend is 18% of NAV on a coin flip where the stop cannot protect me: a -22% stop is inert against an overnight gap, so size is the only control I have, and I have no edge in forecasting a quarter. The setup is uncomfortably balanced — consensus target $327.85 against a $328.00 close means the sell side sees exactly zero upside, on 156x forward with no valuation floor to land on, which is the same reason I refused to press this at 18 last week. Half the position keeps the momentum expression and the drift I would want to own if the print is good; the other half stops being a bet on something I cannot handicap.

Untraded at 9 for a second week, and the honest reason is that it is neither good enough to add to nor broken enough to cut. It has slipped to 71.8% of its 52-week range, the weakest reading among my longs and 26% below its June high, and the supply-shortage story I originally wrote is still being argued with by Samsung and SK Hynix capacity additions. Against that, its 12-1 momentum of +756% remains the top reading in my universe by a factor of three and Nvidia continues to name memory as the binding constraint. It reports 09-30, safely outside this window, so it is not part of the event problem I am solving this week and there is no calendar reason to touch it. The wide -30% stop stays because 59% vol makes anything tighter noise; a full stop-out costs 2.7% of NAV.

Halved 15->8 for the 09-01 print. Note that I am cutting a position whose screen reading got BETTER — 85.0% -> 89.5% of range on the week despite -2.94% Friday, with 12-1 of +77.6% — which is the point: this is a calendar decision, not a ranking decision. Two things make the print asymmetric against a large position. The stock closed at $371.59 against a $364.01 consensus target, so it is already trading through where the sell side thinks it should be, on 95x forward; and China's security review is an unresolved negative that a guidance call can crystallise. At 8% a 10% adverse gap costs 0.8% of NAV instead of 1.5%. I keep the position because I want to own the momentum after the event, and I would rather re-size it next week with the print in hand than pay to guess it now.

Raised 6->8. I opened this as the honest consequence of covering COIN — the right answer to being wrong on a factor's direction is to stop fighting it — and it has held that ground, 91.3% of its 52-week range after a 1.5% down day in a down week, above its 10-, 50- and 200-day, with record Q2 profitability and raised guidance behind it. It reported 08-05 and has no event in the window, which is exactly what I am buying more of this week. The add is two points rather than five because the weak part of the case has not changed: 12-1 momentum of +3.2% is thin, and thin 12-1 is the reason this is a moderate position and not a conviction one. It remains my only long expression of the fintech leg the mandate names.

Upsized 5->6, the only position in this book where the week's macro news is unambiguously in my favour. It fell 4.6% to 9.6% of its 52-week range — now the lowest reading in my universe, below both its 50- and 200-day, with 12-1 momentum of -56.6% — and it did that in the same week that the Fed chair put rate hikes back on the table, which lands directly on an unsecured consumer lender's funding costs and credit box. It reported 08-04, so unlike ORCL it carries no event in this window, which is why this is the short I am adding to rather than the one I am cutting. The add is one point, not three: I know the fundamentals are good — 50% origination growth, conditional OCC bank approval, a $4B Castlelake forward-flow — and that is precisely the squeeze risk, so 6% at 65 realized vol with a wide -30% stop caps the leg at 1.8% of NAV.

Halved 6->3, and this is a correction of my own error. I upsized this last week explicitly on the reasoning that earnings were around 09-10 and therefore outside the window; the print is 09-04, inside it. Two things follow. First, the confirmation I upsized on has weakened — ORCL rose about 1% in a week the S&P fell 1.4%, so it is no longer failing to participate. Second, the squeeze setup into the event is the worst in my book: consensus sees 62% upside, Citi has an open positive catalyst watch at $330, and a strong AI-backlog number could gap it violently through a -20% stop that cannot fill on an overnight move. The laggard case is still the best on my screen — 15.7% of range, 12-1 of -47.9%, -$23.7B free cash flow, $97.6B net debt, BBB- one notch off junk with roughly $40B of FY27 financing needed into a market that just repriced toward hikes — so I keep the short at a size where being wrong through the print costs well under a point of NAV, and I will re-size it once the number is public.

decisions.name: Opus 5 vol regime
decisions.research_notes:
DATA CAVEAT FIRST: my WebSearch budget was exhausted at the start of this session, so the only source I have for the 2026-08-28 session is the desk market summary in the shared scratchpad (round_assessment.txt). My own price series, pulled fresh from the Yahoo chart endpoint into /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-stockguessr/6bfae9dc-06bd-53f8-be1e-316de2554bac/scratchpad/mkt, runs through the 2026-08-27 close. Every statistic below is mine and reproducible from the scripts a1.py-a5.py in that directory; the Warsh/FOMC-odds facts are the desk's and I could not independently verify them.

WHAT THE DESK REPORTS FOR 08-28: Warsh's Jackson Hole debut was hawkish - PCE at 3.7% called "concerning" - and September hike probability repriced from 34% to 57%. SPY -0.3%, Nasdaq -0.5%. NVDA beat (+8.7%, FY28 guide to 70% revenue growth) yet the Nasdaq still fell.

WHAT I MEASURED MYSELF (through 08-27):

1. THE VOL REGIME COMPRESSED FURTHER, NOT LESS. VIX 15.13 -> 14.51. SPY rv20 fell 11.65 -> 10.54, rv10 7.81. My calm-index call is more true than a week ago, not less.

2. MY CENTRAL VOL ARGUMENT FROM LAST WEEK HALF-REVERSED, AND I AM RECORDING THAT. Last week I raised the flag that VIX minus rv20 was 1.98 points, 27th percentile against a 4.11 two-year mean, and concluded implied vol was cheap. It is now 3.97 points, 41st percentile, versus a 4.00 mean - dead average. Realized vol fell faster than implied, so the vol LEVEL is now fairly priced, not cheap. That specific argument for adding VIXY is gone.

3. BUT THE CONVEXITY ARGUMENT STRENGTHENED TO ITS SAMPLE FLOOR. VVIX printed 82.90, the 0th percentile of my entire two-year sample (86.27 and 2nd percentile last week). The price of a large move in VIX has never been lower in anything I can measure. Fairly-priced level with floor-priced convexity is exactly the structure to own into a dated binary.

4. VIXY MECHANICS, NEWLY MEASURED. Regressed on the 100 days VIX rose more than 5%, VIXY captures 0.43 of a VIX percentage move. So my standing +60% take-profit implies roughly VIX 35 from a 14.51 base - whereas at VIX 18.6 it implied ~44. The falling VIX base made that trigger nine VIX points more reachable without my touching it. Unconditional 25-day forward run-up probabilities: P(>=30%) 12.2%, P(>=40%) 5.2%, P(>=60%) 3.6%.

5. THE TERM-PREMIUM SHOCK PAUSED. 10y 4.74 -> 4.67, 3m bill pinned 3.71 -> 3.68, TLT +0.96% on the week. The long-end impulse I built the hedge around stalled. I note ^IRX has almost no variance in this sample, so front-end regression betas are noise and I refuse to lean on them.

6. THE COMMODITY HEDGE'S DRIVER ROLLED OVER. Brent peaked 94.39 on 08-21 and printed 89.70 on 08-27, -4.97% from the high; WTI 87.06 -> 83.53. XLE -2.29% on the week, COMT -1.17%. The two-consecutive-6%-week Brent rally I explicitly cited when raising XLE from 7% to 9% seven days ago has stalled and partially reversed. This is the de-escalation path I named as the risk to that leg.

7. THE HEDGE ARCHITECTURE ITSELF RE-VALIDATED. Trailing-year, on the 12 largest 10y yield-up days: XLE +1.08% avg, positive 11 of 12; COMT +1.03%, 9 of 12; VIXY +1.25%, 9 of 12 - against SPY -0.40, RSP -0.61, USMV -0.45, TLT -1.02, GLD -1.01, XLU -1.04. XLE and COMT are still the only long legs in my universe with positive rate sign. On SPY's ten worst trailing-year sessions: VIXY +7.69% (10 of 10 positive), COMT +0.04%, XLE -0.10%, USMV -0.70%, RSP -1.33%, SPY -1.87%. 60d beta to SPY: USMV 0.24, RSP 0.55, COMT -0.21, XLE -0.53, VIXY -2.80.

8. THE EQUAL-WEIGHT TILT GAVE BACK. RSP +0.53% versus SPY +1.11% this week - megacap tech led (XLK +3.01%, QQQ +1.43%), erasing most of last week's 88bp. RSP still realizes less at 20d (9.87 vs 10.54) and 60d (11.24 vs 14.02) and captures 71% of SPY's downside, but its 10y yield beta stays worse than SPY's (-0.85 vs -0.71 at 60d), the liability I flagged last week and did not act on.

9. USMV DID ITS JOB: +1.30%, beating SPY, with the lowest rv20 in the book at 7.66 and the smallest-magnitude yield beta of any equity sleeve at -0.44.

10. SIZING TESTED BEFORE TRADING. Trailing-year book backtest, current (XLE 9 / VIXY 7 / cash 16) versus proposed (XLE 6 / VIXY 9 / cash 17): return 13.56% -> 11.05%, volatility 5.00 -> 4.75, max drawdown -2.29 -> -2.27, ten-worst-day average -0.25 -> -0.10, twelve-yield-up-day average -0.07 -> -0.08. The proposal dominates on volatility, drawdown and crash payoff with rate protection unchanged, and costs 2.5pp of trailing-year return - roughly 15bp over a three-week horizon. I also tested VIXY at 10% and 12%: each marginal point past 9 kept costing about a point of annual return for diminishing protection, the same verdict my test returned last week, which is why I am adding two points and not five.

decisions.reason: Two facts moved in opposite directions and the correct response is to move risk between hedges rather than to add or shed any. First, the driver behind my commodity hedge reversed: Brent peaked at 94.39 on 08-21 and closed 89.70, -4.97% off the high, and I raised XLE from 7% to 9% exactly seven days ago citing that rally by name. Sizing to a driver means cutting when the driver decays, so XLE goes to 6%. Second, the event my volatility hedge exists for became substantially more likely while its price fell to a sample floor: the desk reports Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole repriced the 09-16 FOMC from 34% to 57% odds of a HIKE - twelve trading days inside my horizon, and a direction no equity leg I own is positioned for - while VVIX printed 82.90, the 0th percentile of my two-year sample. So VIXY goes from 7% to 9%. I am adding to the leg that lost the most since entry (-4.88%), and the reason is that it got cheaper while what it insures got more probable, which is the only good reason to add to a loser. I am deliberately honest that my headline argument for owning vol last week has weakened: VIX minus rv20 went from 1.98 points at the 27th percentile to 3.97 at the 41st, which is exactly average - the vol level is no longer cheap, only its convexity is, and that is why this is a two-point add rather than the five my enthusiasm wanted. My own backtest still says every marginal point of VIXY costs about a point of annual return. What makes the swap defensible rather than a hunch is that it improves the book on the measures I care about while leaving rate protection untouched: trailing-year volatility 5.00 -> 4.75, max drawdown -2.29 -> -2.27, ten-worst-day average -0.25 -> -0.10, twelve-yield-up-day average -0.07 -> -0.08. Everything else holds. I am not touching RSP after one week in which it lagged SPY by 58bp, because I wrote last week that I refuse to trade on a single window, and a week where megacap tech leads is precisely the state the equal-weight tilt is supposed to lag. Total turnover is 5% of gross, about a basis point of cost.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round 3 book in this experiment, so the overlap constraint does not bind; the distinguishing construction here is a vol-regime book that hedges a policy-rate shock with measured positive-rate-beta legs (XLE, COMT) plus a floor-priced convexity leg, rather than with duration or gold, both of which my own regressions show carry the wrong sign against yields.

positions.thesis: Unchanged at 30%, and this week it cost me. RSP returned +0.53% against SPY's +1.11%, giving back most of the 88bp it earned the week before, in a week when megacap tech led outright (XLK +3.01%, QQQ +1.43%). I am holding for the reason I gave when I made the move and would be a hypocrite to abandon after five sessions: a week in which megacap leads is the exact state the equal-weight wrapper is supposed to lag, and one such week is not evidence against a claim built on a year. The underlying statistics are intact on re-measurement: RSP realizes 9.87% at 20d and 11.24% at 60d against SPY's 10.54% and 14.02%, it averaged -1.33% across SPY's ten worst trailing-year sessions against SPY's -1.87% (71% downside capture), and it returned +19.64% over the year against +20.85% - roughly a fifth less volatility for a matched return. I owe the same caveat I owed last week and still refuse to hide: RSP's beta to 10y yield changes is worse than SPY's, -0.85 against -0.71 at 60d and -0.63 against -0.53 at one year, so if the hawkish repricing the desk reports out of Jackson Hole becomes the dominant driver, this tilt is a mild liability rather than a hedge. That is a real cost I am accepting knowingly, and it is bounded: the rate hedging in this book is done by XLE, COMT and VIXY, the only three legs in my universe with positive sign on yield-up days, not by the choice between cap-weight and equal-weight. The -14% stop stays a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same roughly 1.3-annual-sigma severity as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs stop at equivalent pain rather than at equivalent-looking numbers.

Unchanged at 14%, and this week supplied the counter-evidence I said I was keeping the position against. I trimmed from 20% to 14% on a duration-selective repricing argument - a term-premium shock hits the longest-dated cash flows hardest, so SPY's ~40% megacap block is the right place to fund a hedge. This week the mechanism paused and the trade went the other way: the 10y fell from 4.74 to 4.67, TLT gained 0.96%, and megacap duration led the tape with XLK +3.01% and SPY +1.11% against RSP's +0.53%. Holding 14% rather than cutting further is the position I designed for exactly this ambiguity - the argument was always relative and the counter-evidence was always real. What changed on 08-28 sharpens rather than settles it: if the desk is right that Warsh's hawkishness moved September hike odds to 57%, the discount-rate pressure returns through policy rather than through term premium, which still hits duration-extended equity, but a credible inflation-fighting Fed can equally compress the long end and hand leadership straight back to the names I just trimmed. I have a measured view on volatility and a measured view on rate beta; I do not have a leadership forecast, and 14% is the size that says so honestly. The -18% stop stays wide and deliberately loose: XLE, COMT and VIXY are the paid-for convexity in this book, and stacking a tight stop on top of purchased insurance double-buys the same protection and invites a whipsaw exit at the worst possible moment.

Unchanged at 18%, and it is again the leg I would defend hardest. It printed +1.30% this week, beating SPY's +1.11% while carrying a fraction of the risk, and every statistic that justifies owning it improved or held: it realizes 7.66% at 20d and 9.08% at 60d, the lowest of anything in the book; its 60d beta to SPY is 0.24, the lowest of my equity sleeves; its beta to 10y yield changes is -0.44 at 60d, the smallest magnitude of any equity leg I own against RSP's -0.85 and SPY's -0.71; and it averaged -0.70% across SPY's ten worst trailing-year sessions, roughly 37% downside capture. The composition worry that keeps recurring - min-vol books are structurally heavy in staples, utilities and healthcare, classic bond proxies - keeps failing to show up in the data, because MSCI's optimizer excludes high-volatility constituents outright, so its technology weight sits in low-beta software and payments rather than the semiconductor complex, and the same screen keeps it out of the most rate-levered utilities. The honest cost is unchanged and I will not stop restating it: USMV returned +10.54% over the trailing year against SPY's +20.85%, so this is a regime-conditional sleeve and a drag whenever beta is being paid. Its role is precise: it is the only thing I own that keeps working in a soft-landing rotation that punishes beta without producing a volatility event or an inflation shock - the single state in which the equity core, the commodity hedge and VIXY all fail together. If the Fed hikes credibly and inflation expectations fall without a market accident, that is the state, and this is the leg that survives it. Stop unchanged at -14%, capping the leg near -2.5% of NAV.

Cut from 9% to 6%, reversing more than the raise I made seven days ago, because the specific evidence I cited to justify that raise reversed. I went to 9% naming a second consecutive ~6% Brent week and a supply impulse from constrained Hormuz transits and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refining. Brent topped at 94.39 on 08-21 and closed 89.70, -4.97% from the high, with WTI down from 87.06 to 83.53; XLE lost 2.29% on the week and is the worst leg in the book after VIXY. This is precisely the de-escalation path I flagged as the binary risk when I sized it, and sizing to a driver means cutting when the driver decays rather than defending the number I wrote last week. I am cutting to 6% rather than exiting because the structural reason for owning it is undamaged and is not about the price of oil: regressed on daily 10y yield changes XLE's beta is +1.85%/10bp at 60d and +1.38 at one year, and across the twelve largest yield-up days of the trailing year it printed positive on eleven with an average of +1.08% - it remains the only long leg in my entire screened universe with positive sign against the thing that hurts everything else I own, against SPY -0.40, RSP -0.61, USMV -0.45, TLT -1.02 and GLD -1.01. It also still holds up as a crash diversifier, averaging -0.10% across SPY's ten worst trailing-year sessions with five of ten positive and a 60d beta to SPY of -0.53. I am taking the cut here rather than in COMT for three reasons: XLE realizes 23.73% at 20d against COMT's 17.85%, so it is the expensive way to buy the same signal; roughly 15% of the fund is refiners whose crack spreads compress on exactly the transit-disruption shock I am hedging; and XOM and CVX alone are 35% of it. The -22% stop is intentionally tighter in sigma terms than my core legs - about 0.9 annual sigma at this realized vol - because the driver is a geopolitical binary that can reverse on a headline, and it now caps the leg near -1.3% of NAV.

Held at 6% while XLE is cut, which makes it the larger half of the commodity hedge for the first time, and the choice is deliberate rather than incidental. COMT is direct exposure to the commodity complex through a dynamic-roll GSCI strategy, so it carries neither of the wedges that made XLE the place to take the cut: no refiner crack-spread exposure that can lose on precisely the transit-disruption shock being hedged, and no single-name concentration against two names at a third of the fund. It also lost less this week, -1.17% against XLE's -2.29%, as the Brent impulse deflated - the broader basket beyond energy did the diversifying work it was bought to do. On its own terms the numbers still stand up: beta to 10y yield changes +1.38%/10bp at 60d and +1.49 at one year, positive on nine of the twelve largest yield-up days with a +1.03% average; +0.04% average across SPY's ten worst trailing-year sessions with five of ten positive, better than XLE's -0.10%; a 60d beta to SPY of -0.21 and a correlation of -0.15; and +40.94% over the trailing year, so the protection is not bought by surrendering return. It realizes 17.85% at 20d against XLE's 23.73% - roughly the same hedge signal for three-quarters of the volatility, which is the whole reason the 6/6 split now sits where it does rather than loading the hedge into energy equity. I hold the honest caveat: if the desk is right that Warsh has moved the Fed toward hiking into 3.7% PCE, a credible tightening is medium-term bearish for the commodity complex through demand, and that is a real path in which both commodity legs and the VIXY leg can be wrong together. Twelve points total across the two is the size at which being wrong about that costs a slice rather than the book. The -20% stop caps this leg near -1.2% of NAV, and the two commodity legs together near -2.5%.

Raised from 7% to 9%, funded entirely by the XLE trim, and I want the record to show both the argument for it and the argument I lost. What I lost: last week's headline case was that VIX minus rv20 sat at 1.98 points, the 27th percentile against a 4.11 two-year mean, so implied vol was cheap. That has closed. The premium now prints 3.97 points at the 41st percentile against a 4.00 mean - exactly average, because realized vol collapsed faster than implied as VIX fell to 14.51 and SPY rv20 to 10.54. The vol LEVEL is no longer cheap and I will not pretend otherwise. What survived and strengthened: VVIX printed 82.90, the 0th percentile of my entire two-year sample and lower than the 86.27 that impressed me last week. The price of a large move in VIX has never been lower in anything I can measure. And the event that would produce one became materially more likely - the desk reports Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole moved September hike odds from 34% to 57%, so a HIKE at the 09-16 FOMC, twelve trading days inside my horizon, is now close to the modal outcome, and it is a direction none of RSP, SPY or USMV is positioned for. Three of those inputs - the dated event, the repriced probability, the floor-priced convexity - are conditional facts my backtest cannot see, which is exactly why I am overriding a test that says no: on trailing-year data every marginal point of VIXY still costs roughly a point of annual return, 13.56% to 11.05% for these two points, a real 15bp over a three-week horizon that I am choosing to pay. I am adding two points and not five because that test is right about the carry even when it is blind to the condition, and because the swap has to earn its place on the numbers, which it does: book volatility falls 5.00 to 4.75, max drawdown improves to -2.27%, the ten-worst-day average improves from -0.25% to -0.10%, and yield-up-day protection is unchanged at -0.08%. I am also adding to the leg that has lost the most since entry, -4.88%, and the justification is that it got cheaper while what it insures got more probable - the only good reason to add to a loser. Take-profit stays at +60% and I deliberately did NOT lower it despite the temptation to make it monetise an FOMC scare: I measured that VIXY captures 0.43 of a VIX percentage move on up days, so +60% implies roughly VIX 35 from a 14.51 base, whereas at VIX 18.6 the same trigger implied VIX 44. The falling VIX base already made this take-profit nine VIX points more reachable without my touching it, so tightening it further would be adjusting a parameter to feel active rather than because the design changed. No stop, for the reason that never changes: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

decisions.name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
decisions.research_notes:
PRICES/FACTS VERIFIED (2026-08-28 close). Round 2: MU $932.86 (-0.27% Fri), 6.49x fwd, tgt $1,515.11, 47 Strong Buy, 52wk $114.25-$1,255. GEV $911.93 (-4.39%), 42.58x fwd, tgt $1,236.43. ANET $195.38 (-2.84%), 42.06x fwd, tgt $241.82, Q2 rev >$3B +37.7%, FY guide $12.6B. AMAT $461.67 (-4.29%), 26.17x fwd, tgt $640.31, now 37.6% below its $739.67 high. AVGO $368.79 (-0.74%), 23.37x fwd, tgt $525.97, EARNINGS SEPT 2. VRT $257.08 (-4.53%), 32.90x fwd, tgt $338.15. CRWV $84.23 (-2.96%), -$1.93B net income, tgt $144.46. Round 3: GDX $99.65 (-3.90%), XLE $62.68 (+0.39%, 20.02x, 2.42% yld), COPX $94.42 (-2.10%), EWZ $35.55 (-0.59%, 9.68x, 3.82% yld), EWJ $95.87 (+0.03%, 19.51x, 3.72% yld), EZU $70.84 (-0.28%, 18.47x, 2.60% yld), UUP $28.18 (+0.57%). GLD $408.89 (-3.24%). TLT $82.88, near 22-yr low $81.17.

THE WEEK'S DECIDING EVENT: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech was hawkish — underlying inflation "has not meaningfully improved," the Fed will "have work to do" if above-target inflation persists. Market moved to price possible HIKES. Dollar index +0.55%, 10y to 4.722%, gold futures -3.43%, silver -4.57%, S&P -0.25% to 7,711.76, Nasdaq -0.52% to 26,402.42.

WHAT THAT DOES TO MY THINKING. Last week I traded the AI-financing-strain story. This week the market changed which variable it is pricing: NVDA reported a blowout on Aug 26 and locked in $279B of multi-year purchase commitments (+135% q/q), with memory named as the strategic bottleneck — and the entire AI-infrastructure complex still fell 3-5% on Friday. Demand was confirmed and the stocks went down anyway, which means the driver is now the discount rate. MRVL is the clean proof: 37% revenue growth, analyst targets raised, still -10.28%, because the Google custom-silicon payoff is back-half loaded and a possibly-hiking Fed will not pay forward for that. In this regime what survives is a low multiple and near-term cash earnings, not a long-duration story. My book's own tape said the same thing: MU at 6.49x fell 0.27% while GEV at 42.6x fell 4.39%, AMAT fell 4.29% and VRT fell 4.53%.

FOR ROUND 3 THE SAME SPEECH CUTS THE OTHER WAY. My mandate rests on fiscal-credibility repricing: weak dollar, gold bid, long end under pressure. The fiscal channel is intact — TLT sits at $82.88, a hair above its 22-year low of $81.17, with the 10y at 4.722%. But the monetary channel just acquired a credible defender. A chair who says inflation has not improved and that he has work to do is dollar-positive and gold-negative, and that is precisely the counterparty my UUP short was betting would not show up. I raised that leg 4 to 5 last week on five sessions of "confirmation." It was falsified by the person whose behaviour the thesis was about, so it goes, not because it lost money (it has cost me about 1%) but because the stated reason no longer exists. Meanwhile the leg the speech strengthens is energy: "inflation has not meaningfully improved" IS an energy-and-real-asset statement, and XLE was the only thing I own that rose on a day gold fell 3.4% and the Nasdaq fell. Iran commerce is down ~35% on sanctions keeping supply risk live; offsetting that, Trump announced US control of 65B+ barrels of Venezuelan oil, which is supply-bearish and is why I raise XLE to 20 rather than further. Notable that COPX fell only 2.10% against GDX's 3.90% — the industrial real-asset leg separated itself from the monetary one on exactly the day that distinction mattered, which is the evidence for keeping copper and cutting gold.

OTHER CHECKS: gold at ~$4,400-4,500 with analyst targets $5,000-5,400 on debt/de-dollarization, so miner margins stay at records and GDX stays a large core rather than an exit. Brazil's central bank is still cutting into moderating inflation, so EWZ's carry is wide even against a firmer dollar. Japan's semiconductor-led export run is intact. Eurozone August business sentiment improved. "Networking is replacing raw compute as the main constraint on AI performance" is a fresh tailwind for ANET that partly offsets its multiple. Bitcoin $77,579 (-2.30%) — no crypto exposure and I am not adding any into a tightening bias.

decisions.reason: The variable the market is pricing changed this week, and my weights were set for the old one. NVIDIA reported a blowout on Aug 26 and locked in $279B of multi-year purchase commitments, up 135% quarter over quarter, with memory named as the strategic constraint — and my entire book still fell 3-5% on Friday.
