Demand was confirmed and the stocks went down anyway, so the marginal driver is no longer AI financing strain, it is the discount rate: Warsh told Jackson Hole that underlying inflation has not meaningfully improved and that he will have work to do, and the market moved to price hikes. Marvell is the lesson in miniature — 37% revenue growth, targets raised, still down 10.28%, because its payoff is back-half loaded. So I am not cutting risk in aggregate; I am moving it along the multiple axis, out of the 42x long-duration legs and into the cheap ones whose earnings are in front of them. My own tape confirmed the sort on Friday: MU at 6.49x fell 0.27% while GEV at 42.6x fell 4.39%, AMAT 4.29%, VRT 4.53%. I am also raising the CoreWeave short, which is the only leg that benefits from both the rate regime and my structural view. I carry a -14.61% max drawdown, which is my stated budget, so I am not adding the 3x-semis kicker my mandate permits — a possibly-hiking Fed is the wrong tape to lever semiconductors into.

positions.thesis: Raised 18 to 22 and clearly the anchor, on the strongest independent confirmation the book received all week. NVIDIA's Aug 26 print disclosed $279B of multi-year purchase commitments, up 135% sequentially, and the coverage named memory specifically as having turned from a commodity into the strategic constraint of the AI race. That is exactly the argument I have been making — this is the only leg whose demand is physically rationed rather than financed, with management saying customers want roughly 50% more memory than Micron can commit. An order that cannot be filled cannot be deferred by a tighter credit market or a hawkish Fed. And it proved the point on the tape: it fell 0.27% on Friday while its 42x peers fell 4%-plus, because at 6.49x forward there is almost no multiple left to compress against a rising discount rate. $932.86 against a $1,515 consensus from 47 Strong Buy ratings is a 62% gap and by a wide margin the cheapest thing I own. Stop tightened -22 to -20: a bigger position gets a slightly shorter leash, and 20% is still a full volatility band on a memory cyclical that has run 220% this year. Earnings Sept 22, outside the window.

Raised 12 to 15 on a genuine change in the argument rather than on price. My reason for cutting this hard two weeks ago was that wafer-fab equipment is the most financing-elastic link in the chain. Nvidia's $279B of memory purchase commitments undercuts that for the part of the tool market that matters most right now: if memory is the physical bottleneck, then Micron and SK Hynix must add capacity, and they fund it from record cash flow, not from the vendor debt and SPVs that make me nervous about the neocloud end of the chain. So the tool buyer here sits on the same safe side of the financing question as MU itself. The stock fell 4.29% on Friday to $461.67 on the rate move, which now leaves it 37.6% below its $739.67 high at 26.17x forward against a $640 target from 39 Strong Buy ratings — a cheap multiple in the week the market started paying only for cheap multiples. Stop stays -18%: if the competitive threat to its share is structural rather than cyclical I still want to be taken out early rather than proved right slowly.

Trimmed 14 to 12 — a multiple decision, not a fundamental one. The record is still the cleanest in the book: revenue over $3B at +37.7% with the full-year guide at $12.6B for 40% growth, customers who are the hyperscalers paying cash, and a fresh tailwind in the week's read that networking is replacing raw compute as the binding constraint on AI performance. But it is 42.06x forward and it fell 2.84% on Friday, and in a tape where the Fed chair has just said he may have work to do on inflation, a 42x multiple is the exposure I am reducing regardless of how good the company is. The $241.82 target still leaves 24% of room, which is why it stays a core position and not a stub. Stop unchanged at -18%.

Cut 14 to 8, the largest reduction this week, because it is the intersection of the two things the regime change punishes. At 42.58x forward it is the richest multiple I own, and it is a long-duration infrastructure buildout being discounted at a 10-year that just went to 4.722% with hikes back on the table — GEV fell 4.39% to $911.93 on Friday on that combination alone. Layered on top is a company-specific fact I flagged last week and have not resolved: it missed on profit even while raising revenue guidance by $1B, so the margin record has started to deteriorate at exactly the wrong moment. The $176B backlog is real and turbines are sold to hyperscalers off their own balance sheets rather than through SPVs, and the $1,236 target still implies 36% upside, which is why I keep a genuine position rather than exiting. But it no longer earns co-largest weight against a book where MU costs 6.5x earnings. Stop stays -18%.

Held at 6 into the Sept 2 print, deliberately and with the risk sized to be survivable rather than avoided. Two things happened this week that pull in opposite directions. Marvell, the competitor whose Google deal caused me to cut this leg from 17 to 6, beat with 37% revenue growth and still fell 10.28% because the Google upside is back-half loaded across years — which says the second-source threat to Broadcom is real but slow, and that the market will not pay in advance for it. Against that, the same episode is a warning that the bar into an AI-semi print is currently high enough that a beat is not sufficient. At 23.37x forward against a $526 target from 49 Strong Buy ratings this is the second-cheapest growth multiple I own, and the Apple and Samsung work is untouched. What I will not do is add ahead of a binary event while the vendor-financing question — the reported $60B+ debt raise to finance customers' compute — is still open. At 6% a Marvell-style 10% gap costs me 0.6% of NAV. Stop stays -15%.

Trimmed 8 to 5 and now the smallest long. I have now waited three weeks for evidence that the revenue the company deferred is revenue delayed rather than lost, and it has not arrived: it missed on revenue, the CEO called the problem temporary and supply-chain related, analysts cut targets, and the stock fell another 4.53% on Friday to $257.08. A claim awaiting evidence should not carry weight while the evidence is absent, and 32.90x forward is the wrong multiple to be patient at when the discount rate is rising. I keep a position because the underlying case is the same physical-bottleneck logic that makes me own power and memory — liquid cooling and power distribution are constraints you cannot finance your way around — and $338 against $257 with 28 Strong Buy ratings is real upside if the timing story is true. Stop stays -20%: this needs room to be volatile without being a catastrophe at 5%.

Raised 6 to 9. This is the one leg that both regimes reward, and it earned the increase on two pieces of fresh news rather than on being down. First, Nvidia is reported to be shelving revenue-sharing deals with the neoclouds — the specific subsidy that made CoreWeave's economics look better than they are, withdrawn by the supplier itself, in the same week that supplier reported a blowout quarter. Second, Warsh's shift raises the cost of the money this company runs on: roughly $35B of existing debt, $35-39B of planned 2026 capex, and a $1.93B annual loss mean it is refinancing into a curve that just repriced toward hikes, with no earnings to discount. Every long in this book sells equipment into the buildout; CoreWeave is the customer buying it with borrowed money, so it is the leg that breaks first if financing strain is real and it hedges my longs if it is not. It is 9 and not larger because consensus is firmly against me — 38 analysts at a $144.46 target against $84.23 — and the stock is already 45% below its high, so squeeze risk is genuine. Stop at a 30% adverse move to survive a squeeze without it becoming an accident; take profit at 35%.

decisions.reason: One position in this book was falsified this week by the exact counterparty its thesis was about, and I am removing it. The mandate rests on fiscal-credibility repricing, and half of that is intact: TLT sits at $82.88, barely above its 22-year low of $81.17, with the 10-year at 4.722%, so the long end is still pricing fiscal risk. But the monetary half just acquired a credible defender. Warsh told Jackson Hole that underlying inflation has not meaningfully improved and that he will have work to do, the dollar index rose 0.55%, gold futures fell 3.43% and silver 4.57%. My UUP short existed on one sentence — that the dollar would break because the Fed would not defend it — and the Fed chair personally contradicted it five sessions after I raised the leg on what I called confirmation. That gets closed on the reason, not the P&L. The same speech reallocates the rest of the book: I cut the monetary real asset (gold) and raise the inflation real asset (energy), because a chair saying inflation has not improved is describing energy, and XLE was the only thing I own that rose on a day gold fell 3.4% and the Nasdaq fell. Copper stays because COPX fell only 2.10% against GDX's 3.90% — the industrial real-asset leg separated itself from the monetary one on precisely the day that distinction was tested. The proceeds go to Eurozone value and to cash at 4%, because I am not obliged to redeploy immediately into a tape where the central bank has just told me the discount rate is going up, and this book is +15% with a -3.09% max drawdown worth protecting.
decisions.novelty: This book shares no symbol and no direction with my Round 2 AI-infrastructure book — Round 2 is long US semiconductor, power and networking suppliers against a short in a debt-financed AI customer, while Round 3 is long non-US equity indices and hard-asset producers with zero AI-capex or hyperscaler-financing exposure, so same-direction gross-weight overlap is 0%; the two books are now positioned on opposite sides of the same Warsh shock, with Round 2 cutting multiple risk and Round 3 rotating from monetary to inflation real assets.

positions.thesis: Raised 18 to 20 and now the anchor, because this is the only leg the week's news made stronger. When the Fed chair says underlying inflation has not meaningfully improved, he is describing energy and real assets, and this is the hard-asset holding whose case does not require a debasing central bank — which is why XLE rose 0.39% to $62.68 on the day gold fell 3.24% and the Nasdaq fell 0.52%. That divergence is the whole argument for moving weight from one to the other. Refiner margins are at records, Iran's commerce is down roughly 35% on sanctions keeping supply risk live, and it pays 2.42% at 20.02x. I raise it only to 20 rather than further for two reasons I will not pretend away: Trump announced US control of over 65B barrels of Venezuelan oil, which is straightforwardly supply-bearish over time, and energy is the one leg in this book that is a demand cyclical as well as a hard asset at the moment the Fed is threatening to slow the economy on purpose. It pulled back from $64.70 to $62.68, so I am adding into a dip rather than into a new high, which is the discipline I said I would apply here. Stop stays -15%.

Cut 21 to 15 and I am revising a line I wrote last week. I said a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target — that is still true, and it is why I am reducing rather than exiting. But the thesis can be weakened by the arrival of monetary credibility, and that is what happened: Warsh said inflation has not improved and that he has work to do, the dollar rose, gold futures fell 3.43% and GDX fell 3.90% to $99.65. A Fed that fights inflation compresses exactly the debasement premium this position monetises, and higher real rates are the classic gold negative. What survives is the slow structural half — central bank accumulation, roughly $40T of US debt, and the long end still pinned near 22-year lows — plus the simple fact that at $4,400-4,500 an ounce producers earn record margins and analysts still carry $5,000-5,400 targets. Fifteen percent keeps this a large core position with the risk cut by nearly a third. Still no take-profit, for the reason above. Stop stays -15%, a full volatility band for a miner ETF on a position that still carries a substantial unrealised gain.

Held at 15, and the hold is the decision. On the day the dollar rose and the monetary metal broke, COPX fell only 2.10% to $94.42 against GDX's 3.90% — the industrial real-asset leg separated itself from the monetary one in exactly the test I have been arguing would eventually distinguish them. That is the distinction worth owning: copper demand from electrification and the AI buildout is realised in poured concrete and strung wire, so it is levered to physical tightness and grid capex rather than to whether the Fed defends the currency, which insulates it both from Warsh and from the equipment-financing strain taxing my Round 2 book. The honest caution is that a stronger dollar is a headwind for all dollar-priced metals and the fund has doubled over a year to within 5.6% of its $99.99 high, which is why it gets no increase despite outperforming. Stop stays -18%.

Held at 12, unchanged, and it earned that by rising to $35.55 in a week that hurt most of what it correlates with. The cheapest carry available to me at 9.68x with a 3.82% dividend yield, and Vale plus Nu Holdings give direct leverage to the commodity complex rather than to US rates. The new risk is real and I will name it: a hawkish Fed while Brazil's central bank is cutting narrows the differential and is historically an EM headwind, which is the argument against adding. The argument for not cutting is that the Selic is still enormous in absolute terms, so the carry stays wide even after both moves, and Brazil is running a domestic easing cycle ahead of the Fed's tightening bias rather than in sympathy with it — which is the diversification I actually want. The 25% US tariff and the floated sugar and ethanol penalties remain unresolved drags, so I let the 9.68x multiple do the work rather than the weight. Stop stays -18%.

Raised 10 to 12, funded directly by the closed dollar short, after three weeks of deliberately leaving it alone. The reason to add now is what it is not exposed to: the two things that broke this week were gold's monetary premium and the short-dollar trade, and this leg touches neither, while also carrying zero exposure to the hyperscaler-capex financing question costing my Round 2 book money. It is a non-US, non-AI earnings stream at 18.47x with a 2.60% yield, sitting near its 52-week high on broadening earnings, with August survey data showing Eurozone businesses more positive on prospects. In a book where I have just reduced the two most macro-reflexive legs, adding to the least reflexive one at a mid-teens multiple is the right destination for the capital rather than leaving all of it in cash. The offsetting risk is that European energy costs are elevated and the region imports the same inflation Warsh is worried about. Stop stays -18%.

Held at 10, untouched, and it behaved exactly as intended — flat at $95.87 in a week that moved everything else. The reason to own it is unchanged: Japanese exports have accelerated for five consecutive months led by semiconductor shipments, which buys me AI-cycle participation through a 19.51x index paying 3.72% rather than through the 40x US names now being derated by the rate move. The governance and buyback cycle compounds underneath that regardless of the Fed. The part of the thesis that did change is the currency leg — I bought part of this as weak-dollar expression, and a hawkish Fed against a slower BOJ widens the differential and weakens the yen, which is a drag on dollar returns here even as it helps the exporters that drive the index. Those two effects substantially offset, which is why the weight does not move in either direction. Stop stays -18%.

decisions.name: Opus Momentum
decisions.research_notes:
PRICES/MOVES CHECKED (through 2026-08-28 close, vs 2026-08-21 marks in my packet):
- SMH: 560.42 -> 546.80 (8/24) -> 555.82 -> 555.77 -> 573.00 (8/27) -> 553.11 (8/28, -3.47%). Net week -1.3% but pure whipsaw, ending on a violent break. SOXX 508.62 (-3.20%), SOXL 111.34 (-9.52%), NVDA 217.55 (-4.57%).
- MU 988.82 -> 932.86 (-5.7%); now -26% from its June peak of $1,257. AMD 476.97 -> 465.58 (-2.4%). AVGO 368.79, sitting near the low end of a 287-495 52wk range after Marvell won a Google custom-AI-chip deal.
- LMT 608.68 -> 563.85 (-7.4%). RTX 222.97 -> 211.71 (-5.1%). ITA -0.61% Friday. Both fell hard in a week SPY was roughly flat.
- SPY 769.35 (-0.23% Fri, 52wk high 779.37). QQQ 716.43 (-0.65% Fri). GOOGL 346.59 (+1.74% Fri, 17.4x PE on +20% rev / +111% NI).
- XLV 171.16, near its 52wk high of 176.60, +27% 1yr. IBB 208.95 (-2.7% Fri) but ~4% off its 52wk high, +51% 1yr. XBI 162.38, +81% 1yr, flagged as approaching its 2021 high of 174.79 after a bullish flag breakout.
- GLD 423.36 -> 408.89 (-3.4% week, -3.24% Friday alone).
- TLT 82.05 -> 82.88 (+1.0%). IEF 92.85. XLE 62.68 (+0.63% Fri), XOM 156.71 (+0.17%). USMV 101.74 (52wk high 102.21), SPLV 75.08, XLP 85.45 (+0.43%), KO 89.66 (+0.67%), T 26.01 (+2.28%), XLRE 44.48, HYG 79.74 (52wk range 78.57-81.36).
- IBIT 43.90; BTC ran from the low $60Ks to ~$80K, its best week since 2023.

WHAT I LEARNED - four catalysts inverted or newly appeared this week, and three of them sit directly under positions I own:
1. SEMIS GOT A POLICY CATALYST, NOT JUST A WOBBLE. Trump administration officials are reported to be weighing broader semiconductor tariffs extended to servers and laptops, and Bank of America told clients chip stocks face a sharp near-term decline on positioning fatigue. Morgan Stanley is pushing rotation out of chipmakers and into hyperscalers. Friday's tape confirms it: NVDA -4.6% and SMH -3.5% while QQQ was only -0.65% and SPY -0.23%. That is not a market selloff, it is a targeted de-rating of one sub-sector inside an index making new highs.
2. THE IRAN TRADE REVERSED. Iran-Oman talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a US-Venezuela deal covering 65bn barrels of reserves, and Persian Gulf exports back to two-thirds of pre-war levels have crude retreating toward $85 Brent support with the fear premium fading. Coverage is explicit that the Iran war has not helped defence stocks. My XLE and LMT/RTX legs were both bought on "Bessent details Iran sanctions Monday" - that catalyst resolved the opposite way.
3. FED CHAIR WARSH WENT HAWKISH AT JACKSON HOLE, reinforcing an inflation-fighting stance. Gold fell 3.2% on it. A credibly hawkish Fed cuts the real-rate tailwind under gold and simultaneously raises the odds that the next labour-market crack reads as a policy-induced growth scare - the branch the belly of the curve wins in.
4. THE LONG END STABILISED. Global yields fell on declining oil plus further Treasury steps on the back end; TLT +1% off its 22-year low. The term-premium shock that drove my last two rebalances is easing at the margin, mostly because oil is falling.
CROSS-CHECK: BTC's downtrend - the one my Round 2 mandate was written to short - inverted violently on the Bessent buyback and Clarity Act momentum, with a mid-September Senate deadline as the next binary.
NET READ: the money is rotating out of chips and out of geopolitics, and into hyperscalers, healthcare/biotech and low-volatility equity, while the bond shock cools. My Round 2 book was long the two things that broke and underweight the two things that are working; my Round 3 book was correctly positioned except for gold sizing and a deteriorating credit leg.

decisions.reason: Three of my four stated catalysts resolved against me, and momentum discipline is about following the tape rather than defending the reason I gave last week. The defence pair and XLE were all bought on one shared impulse - Bessent's Iran sanctions and rising crude - and that impulse inverted into Hormuz-reopening talks, a Venezuela supply deal and a fading fear premium; LMT -7.4% and RTX -5.1% in a week SPY was flat is the market telling me the catalyst is gone, so all three legs go rather than get trimmed. On semis I am cutting again but not capitulating: what changed is that the pullback acquired a policy driver (tariffs extended to servers and laptops) and a sell-side capitulation call, and Friday's split - NVDA -4.6% and SMH -3.5% against QQQ -0.65% - proves this is a targeted sub-sector de-rating, not index risk. So I keep semis as the mandate core at reduced size and move the freed capital to where the same money is going: hyperscalers (GOOGL rose 1.7% on the day NVDA fell 4.6%), healthcare and biotech (the only sector making new highs), and index-level Nasdaq leverage rather than sector-level leverage, because QQQ is 4% off its high while the chip complex is breaking. MU is halved specifically because the property that justified its 12% - being the one leg outperforming a falling sector - is gone: it fell 5.7% against SMH's 1.3% and now sits 26% below its June peak. And I am putting the crypto sleeve back on the long side, because the persistent downtrend my mandate was written to short just had its best week since 2023.

positions.thesis: Cut 13% -> 10% and kept as the mandate's core because a semis momentum book that owns zero semis is not managing a mandate, it is abandoning one. The reduction is not about the price action, which was only -1.3% on the week; it is about the arrival of a genuine policy overhang - reported administration work on semiconductor tariffs extended to servers and laptops, which lands hardest on exactly the offshore-manufactured names that dominate this index - stacked on top of a Bank of America call for a sharp near-term decline. I keep the index rather than picking winners for the same reason as always: I already paid tuition for betting on which sub-sector's pricing curve breaks. The stop tightens 9% -> 8% because the whole case for owning this is that the uptrend resumes quickly, and the intraweek path - 546.80, then 573.00, then 553.11 - is a market that has stopped trending and started thrashing, which is precisely when a wide stop stops being patience and becomes a slow bleed.

Halved 12% -> 6%, and the reason is that the specific evidence I cited to make it my largest bet has reversed. A week ago it was the one name rising while the sector fell, which is textbook leadership; this week it fell 5.7% against SMH's 1.3%, so it went from leading the sector to lagging it in a single week, and it now sits 26% below its June peak of $1,257. On any momentum measure that is a broken leader, and continuing to carry it at 12% would mean holding the position for the story rather than the trend. Not exited, because the fundamental support got stronger, not weaker: Nvidia's own results named memory supply as the binding limit on its AI growth, the stock trades at 21x with a Strong Buy consensus, and there is a dated catalyst on 30 September earnings. So this is a half-size bet on a specific event rather than a conviction hold. Stop widened from 15% to 13% in loss terms to fit the smaller size while still giving a name with this realised range room to breathe through the print; the +30% take-profit stays so a memory squeeze exits on plan.

Trimmed 9% -> 7%, a smaller cut than MU took, because it earned it on relative performance: -2.4% against MU's -5.7% in a week when the sector's own leadership changed hands. It remains the compute half of the semis expression alongside memory, which is what keeps this sleeve a claim about where AI capital is flowing rather than a single bet on DRAM pricing, and the datacenter-CPU share argument against both Intel and Nvidia is still intact. It takes a cut anyway because at 119x earnings it is the highest-multiple thing in the book and therefore the most exposed to both the tariff headline and the positioning-fatigue unwind BofA is warning about, and because Cathie Wood cutting her position is a small but real signal that the marginal holder here is a seller. Stop tightened 13% -> 12% in line with the shorter leash the semis sleeve is now on.

New position and the largest single addition, because it is the direct expression of the rotation that defined this week. Morgan Stanley is telling clients to move from chipmakers to hyperscalers, and Friday priced it: GOOGL closed +1.74% on the same session NVDA fell 4.57%, so this is a live relative-strength trade rather than a forecast. Critically it lets me stay long the AI capex cycle - which the mandate requires and which is not what broke this week - while stepping out of the leg carrying the tariff risk, since a semiconductor tariff on servers and laptops raises the buyer's input cost but does nothing to the demand for the services the buyer sells. It also happens to be the cheapest large-cap in the complex at 17.4x on +20% revenue and +111% net income growth, which means the momentum here is not being paid for with a multiple that a hawkish Warsh can compress the way he can compress a 119x name. Stop at -12%, one normal drawdown for a megacap.

New, and the deliberate answer to the question my mandate keeps asking: where does the leverage belong? I was stopped out of SOXL at -20% on 19 August and SOXL fell another 9.5% on Friday alone, so the sector is the wrong place to be levered. But the index is not the sector - QQQ closed within 4.3% of its 52-week high on a day the chip complex broke, because the hyperscalers that dominate it are the rotation's destination rather than its source. So I am putting a small amount of 3x exposure on the thing that is still trending instead of the thing that is not. Sized at 5% precisely because 3x is a size multiplier, not a conviction multiplier: 5% at 3x is 15% of effective Nasdaq beta, and the -15% stop caps the loss on this leg at 0.75% of NAV, which corresponds to roughly a 5% move in QQQ. I accept the 5bp leveraged-ETF cost and the decay drag for a position I expect to hold weeks, not quarters.

Raised 8% -> 10% and now co-largest in the book. Last week I called this a rotation destination and bought the broad, low-beta vehicle while I was cutting risk; this week the tape confirmed the call - XLV sits near its 52-week high of 176.60 and is +27% over a year while the semis complex breaks - so the position gets promoted from a hedge to a core holding. The mechanism matters as much as the price: healthcare is the sector that is absorbing the capital leaving chips, its earnings are unconnected to the AI capex debate that every other equity leg here depends on, and at a 0.56 beta it cannot be de-rated by a long-yield shock the way a 119x semi can. Stop at -10%, appropriate for something with this realised volatility, and tight enough that if the rotation reverses back into chips I am out and can redeploy.

New. Last week I explicitly chose XLV over the biotech vehicle because I was reducing book risk; that constraint was a function of the week, not of the trend, and the trend has only strengthened. IBB is +51% over a year and roughly 4% below its 52-week high, and the equal-weight XBI at +81% is being flagged as approaching its 2021 high after a bullish flag breakout - so this is the single strongest, most persistent uptrend I can find anywhere in the tape, which is what a momentum mandate is supposed to own. The driver is fundamental and self-reinforcing rather than a rate story: M&A has restarted, capital markets have reopened for the sector, and both feed on each other. Held via IBB rather than XBI because the large-cap concentration in Amgen, Vertex and Gilead gives me the trend without the single-trial binary risk that dominates equal-weight small-cap biotech. Friday's -2.7% is a pullback inside an uptrend, not a break; the -12% stop is where I stop calling it that.

The crypto sleeve comes back on, but on the opposite side. My mandate was written to short a persistent BTC/ETH/SOL downtrend; that downtrend just ended with the strongest weekly move since 2023, from the low $60Ks to roughly $80K, on Bessent's bond buyback and momentum behind the Clarity Act. A momentum manager follows the trend rather than defending the direction he wrote down, and shorting into that would be the single worst thing this mandate could do right now. Everything about the sizing reflects that I am entering late, though: 5% at only 2x, because I am buying after a 30% run and into a binary mid-September Senate deadline on the Clarity Act that can resolve either way. At 2x, liquidation needs a 47% adverse move so the only thing that can end this is my own -20% stop, which corresponds to a 10% BTC decline - roughly one bad week for this asset and the point at which the reversal thesis is simply wrong. Funding at 10% APR on the long side costs about 2bp of NAV a week here, which is immaterial relative to the move I am after.

decisions.reason: This book is doing its job - up 2.53% with a 1.13% maximum drawdown while my momentum book is down 5.33% - so the changes are calibration along the two axes that actually moved, not a reconstruction. The first is gold. I raised it to top weight last week on the fiscal-debasement argument and said the stop was there to survive post-squeeze mean reversion; the mean reversion arrived immediately, -3.4% on the week with -3.2% of it on Friday alone when Warsh used Jackson Hole to reassert an inflation-fighting stance. The fiscal fact is unchanged, but a credibly hawkish Fed removes the real-rate tailwind, and having just watched it print the largest single-day loss in the basket, inverse-vol weighting has to bind on it rather than be argued around. The second is that the long-end shock is cooling for a reason I did not have last week: oil is falling on Hormuz-reopening talks, global yields fell with it, and Treasury is acting on the back end. That does two things - it makes the belly of the curve more attractive, and it makes a hawkish Warsh raise rather than lower the odds of a policy-induced growth scare, which is the exact branch IEF wins in and the one I demoted last week for being the less likely outcome. So duration comes back at the belly, gold comes down, energy comes down because its inflation coupling is precisely what weakened, credit comes down because it has now added technical damage to thin compensation, and the low-volatility equity sleeve goes up because it is finally outperforming after a long stretch of not doing so and it is the purest form of the equity risk premium my mandate is built to harvest.
decisions.novelty: The two books now share zero symbols and zero same-direction gross weight: Round 2 owns semis, hyperscalers, leveraged Nasdaq, healthcare/biotech and a long crypto perp - all high-beta, all levered to the AI capex cycle and a trend continuing - while Round 3 owns gold, the belly of the Treasury curve, minimum-volatility and low-volatility equity, staples, REITs, energy and high yield, every one of them a carry or diversification claim that pays without needing any trend to persist, and the one name they might have shared (XLE) has been removed from Round 2 entirely rather than held in both.

positions.thesis: Raised 14% -> 17% and now the top weight in the book, which is the first time I have added to this leg rather than leaving it alone. The reason is that its relative performance finally turned: USMV closed within half a percent of its 52-week high while the S&P sits below its own and the semiconductor complex breaks, and the commentary is right that low-volatility stocks are having a moment after a long stretch of underperformance. That matters more than it sounds, because for months this sleeve was the correct structural choice that was not being paid; a factor that starts working is worth more than the same factor being merely defensible. It is also the cleanest way to keep this book's equity risk premium above 20% while gold - my other high-conviction leg - is being cut, since a min-vol equity book carries far less multiple to compress if Warsh's hawkishness does what it is meant to do to discount rates.

Raised 12% -> 16%, reversing last week's trim, because the probability weighting behind that trim has flipped. I cut this on the grounds that a growth-scare resolution was now the less likely branch and I should not hold my largest position in the scenario the market was voting against. Warsh changed that: a Fed chair who publicly recommits to fighting inflation with the labour market already cracking is a Fed chair raising the odds of a policy-induced growth scare, and the belly of the curve is the only asset in this basket that rallies outright in that outcome. Meanwhile the reason I had for avoiding duration is easing - falling oil pulled global yields down, Treasury is taking further steps at the back end, and TLT bounced off its 22-year low. My framework's distinction still holds and is why this is IEF rather than TLT: the fiscal supply problem lives at the long end, and the belly has outperformed it through every leg of this repricing. At a 4.7% ten-year I am paid genuine carry to hold the insurance.

Cut 16% -> 12%, giving back last week's promotion. I am not abandoning the argument - US debt sustainability and dollar weakness are unchanged facts, and gold remains the only asset here that is structurally paid by a fiscal shock, which is the diversification job my Treasury sleeve failed at. What changed is two things I have to respect. First, Warsh's Jackson Hole hawkishness attacks the real-rate channel that has been gold's tailwind, and the market agreed immediately with a 3.2% single-session decline. Second, and more binding for a book whose mandate is variance minimisation: gold just printed the largest one-day and one-week loss of anything I own, which means my own inverse-vol rule now says it should be a smaller position regardless of how much I like the story. Last week I wrote that adding hard after a big run is how a low-vol book imports volatility, then added hard anyway; this is me applying my own rule rather than arguing past it. Twelve percent still leaves it a top-three weight. The -12% stop stays for exactly the scenario now unfolding.

Raised 7% -> 8% alongside USMV, for the same reason - realised low volatility is being rewarded again - but kept as the smaller of the pair. The point of holding both remains that SPLV is a pure realised-volatility screen while USMV is an optimiser output subject to sector and turnover constraints, so their constituents genuinely differ and running both diversifies within the factor rather than doubling one construction. Its top holdings sit in insurance, conglomerates and regulated utilities, which is a materially different economy from USMV's healthcare and industrials tilt. The one-point add rather than three reflects that its trailing return of 4.1% shows the factor has been out of favour longer here than in USMV; I am adding to the turn, not extrapolating it.

Held at 6% and given a -10% stop it did not have before. Last week I cut this hard on the logic that a levered real-estate proxy takes a 19-year-high long yield twice, through the discount rate and through refinancing. That logic is intact but its premise softened slightly this week: yields fell globally on declining oil, TLT rose 1% off its low, and Treasury is acting on the back end. So this is the leg with the most to gain from any durable long-end relief, which is why it survives at 6% rather than getting cut again. But one week of relief off a 22-year low is not a trend, and unlike staples or gold this asset has no independent reason to work if rates go back up - so I am adding the stop I should have had while I wait for the answer, rather than raising the weight on a maybe.

Held at 6%. The distinction that earns staples their place keeps getting confirmed rather than tested: short effective duration plus pricing power that passes inflation through to revenue, which is why they are not simply a levered bet on rates falling the way REITs and the long bond are. Friday made the point cleanly - XLP closed green while the S&P, the semis complex and gold all fell - which is precisely the payoff profile a variance-minimising basket is paying for. It also remains the equity that holds up if the labour crack that Warsh appears willing to tolerate turns into a real recession print, and it does the defensive dividend job at a comparable yield to utilities without importing exposure to the AI-datacenter power buildout that this book exists to avoid.

Cut 8% -> 5%, the largest proportional reduction in the book, because the exact property I raised it for last week has weakened. I sized it up as the leg most tightly coupled to the inflation regime and the only one that does not need rates to fall - but Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz, a US-Venezuela deal covering 65bn barrels and Gulf exports back to two-thirds of pre-war levels have crude retreating toward $85 support with the fear premium draining out. When the mechanism a position is coupled to reverses, the position shrinks even though the price has not yet fallen; XLE was up 0.6% on Friday and I am cutting anyway, because sizing follows the thesis rather than the last print. Kept at 5% rather than zero because refiners are heading into a historic profit surge on supply-disruption margins, the SPR sits at its lowest since 1982, and this is still the only leg that pays if the inflation shock resumes.

Held at 5%. The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry, and unusually for a staple it is also the one with a live fundamental trend behind it - 5% volume and 6% organic revenue growth with margin expansion and double-digit EPS growth in Q2, which is why UBS and TD Cowen have both been raising targets into a tape that is de-rating almost everything else. It closed up 0.67% on Friday's red session. It shares the inflation pass-through property that is the reason I keep staples while cutting pure bond proxies, and it carries no exposure to either the AI capex debate or fiscal duration, which is the profile this basket most needs more of in weeks when the equity index and the long bond move together.

Held at 4% after last week's trim. I cut it because a structural repricing of borrowing costs hits a heavily indebted telecom through refinancing in a way it does not hit KO - that remains the reason it is not larger. But the headwind eased on both counts this week: the long end stabilised as global yields fell, and the company delivered on execution, closing its $23bn EchoStar spectrum purchase and passing 2 million 5G home internet subscribers, with the stock up 2.28% on a red Friday. At 8.6x earnings with a 4.3% dividend it is the cheapest real coupon in the basket, and regulated domestic cash flows with near-zero AI-cycle correlation is exactly the uncorrelated yield stream the mandate asks for. Holding rather than adding, because one week of long-end relief does not retire a balance-sheet argument.

Cut 6% -> 3%, continuing a direction I have now trimmed three weeks running, but this time for a different and better reason. Until now the case was purely that the compensation was thin - roughly 300bp over risk-free for a genuinely fat left tail, with cash next door at 4% carrying zero duration and zero default risk. Now there is actual damage to point at: HYG has broken below triangle support on rising volume with bearish momentum, and it sits in the bottom third of its 52-week range while the equity index is near its high, which is credit refusing to confirm equities. That divergence is the classic early tell, and it is arriving in front of a debt-funded AI complex, a contracting labour market and a Fed chair who has just said he will not rescue it. Kept at 3% rather than zero only because spread carry is explicitly in my mandate and tight spreads can stay tight for years; the -6% stop is what makes owning a fat left tail survivable at all.

decisions.name: Opus Quality Defensive
decisions.research_notes:
WEEK ENDING 2026-08-28 — what I checked and what it changed.

THE MACRO EVENT. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote (delivered 8/28) was read as deliberately hawkish: inflation is running hot, "while this summer's readings were better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," and the Fed still has "work to do." CME FedWatch September hike odds went 35.4% -> 57.5% in a day. The 2-year yield jumped ~12bp to 4.356%; the 10-year rose only ~5bp to 4.726% — versus 4.738% in my notes last week, so essentially flat w/w. That is a bear FLATTENING, the exact mirror of the bear steepening I wrote up seven days ago. DXY +0.5% Friday to 99.65 and roughly +1% on the week, reclaiming its 200-day near 99.17 and wiping out the entire prior week's dollar decline. BMO: "a deliberately hawkish speech that will put to rest any concerns about the Fed's willingness to raise rates."

WHY THAT MATTERS TO ME SPECIFICALLY. Two weeks running I built theses on a named, checkable macro configuration: dollar falling + long rates rising = debasement, buy hard assets and unhedged international. The dollar half of that has reversed hard in one week, and the front end is now pricing hikes, which lifts real rates. I am not going to defend positions whose stated driver has inverted.

INDEX/TAPE. S&P 500 +0.5% on the week to 7,711.76 (-0.25% Friday), Nasdaq +0.9% to 26,402.42, Dow +0.5%, Russell 2000 -1.5%. NVDA reported blowout results and jumped 8.7% Thursday; chips still sold off Friday. Closing my semis short two weeks ago was correct — it would have been run over by that print.

PRICES I PULLED (closes, 8/28 vs 8/21).
Round 2: XLV 171.16 vs 174.62 (-2.0%; still 3.1% off the 176.60 52w high, and 8/26 news notes healthcare had its biggest one-day gain in over a year on 8/26 (+3.5%) on rotation out of chips, with ~2/3 of healthcare names higher on the week). SCHD 34.83 vs 35.11 (-0.8%). USMV 101.74 vs 101.23 (+0.5%, NEW HIGH — the only leg in the book that rose). GLD 408.89 vs 423.36 (-3.4% w/w, -4.5% off the 428.07 high set 8/25, including -3.24% on the speech day alone). XLP 85.45 vs 85.99 (-0.6%).
Round 3: DBMF 31.41 vs 31.37 (+0.1%, near its 31.66 high, and it rose 0.61% on Friday while equities fell — the negative-beta behavior I own it for). EFA 107.72 vs 108.24 (-0.5%, 1.1% off high). JEPI 57.79 vs 57.92 (-0.2%). PDBC 18.39 vs 18.65 (-1.4%). XLF 58.10 vs 57.48 (+1.1%, printed a new closing high of 58.31 on 8/25 and rose Friday against a down tape). IWM 295.75 vs 299.96 (-1.4%, and 305.09 -> 295.75 = -3.1% over ten sessions; below where it stood a month ago). CPER 39.67 vs 39.99 (-0.8%, and 39.85 a month ago — literally flat for a month).

CRYPTO. BTC ~$79k (opened 80,262 Friday, dipped to ~79.1-79.6k intraday on the speech, ~$79k over the weekend); ETH ~$2,505. BTC +25% since 8/19, first break of $80,000 in ~3 months, its best August in nine years. Spot BTC and ETH ETFs together took in ~$2.3bn over the week, the biggest combined week since October, with nine consecutive inflow days. That streak snapped on 8/28 (-$201.9m BTC) while ETH funds extended to ten days. Important read: crypto took a hawkish Fed and a +1% dollar and gave back only ~1%. That is the strongest trend on my board and the only one that absorbed the shock.

VOLATILITY. VIX printed 14.25 on 8/14, in roughly the bottom 2.3 percentile of its trailing range vs a 12-month average of 18.1. JEPI's monthly distribution has fallen from $0.427 (Jan) to $0.367 (Aug) precisely because premium tracks implied vol. Cheap vol going into a hawkish repricing is an asymmetry.

CALENDAR AHEAD. August payrolls 9/4, CPI 9/11, FOMC decision + dot plot 9/16, PCE 9/30. Three binary macro events inside three weeks with a coin-flip hike priced. Cash earning 4% (and more if they hike) is a real position, not a failure to have an idea.

decisions.reason: One thing changed and it is the thing I named myself. Seven days ago I raised gold to 11% on an explicit, checkable configuration — 'a 1.7% monthly fall in the dollar with a fresh leg down, alongside a 19bp RISE in the 10-year. Hard assets bid while the long end sells off is a debasement signature.' Both halves have now gone the other way: the dollar rose ~1% and reclaimed its 200-day, wiping out the whole prior week's decline, while the 10-year is flat w/w and the 2-year jumped 12bp as September hike odds went 35% to 58%. Rising real rates raise the carrying cost of non-yielding bullion, and the market agreed in real time — GLD fell 3.24% on the speech day and 3.4% on the week, its only meaningful down week in two months. When the specific evidence I wrote down inverts, I give back the increase rather than argue with it, and I take it below where it stood before the raise because the case is now weaker than it was even then. That is the only conviction change. The 4 points come out 2 to min-vol and 2 to cash: USMV was the single leg in this book that made a new high this week, in a week when SPY was flat and my largest position fell 2%, which is exactly the behaviour I hold it for going into the 9/4 payrolls, 9/11 CPI, 9/16 FOMC gauntlet; and cash pays 4% risk-free that rises if the Fed does hike, which is a genuine defensive asset, not idle money. I am deliberately NOT cutting healthcare after a 2% pullback: a Fed hiking into a slowing economy makes non-cyclical earnings streams relatively more valuable, not less, and the sector news this week was a rotation INTO healthcare out of chips. I add a 12% stop to it instead, which is the honest answer to holding a third of the book in one idea.

positions.thesis: Held at full size for a fourth week, and this week strengthened the reason rather than the price. It gave back 2.0% to 171.16 after a +14% month, but the giveback followed a +3.5% session on 8/26 — its biggest one-day gain in more than a year — driven by rotation out of semiconductors, with roughly two-thirds of healthcare names higher on the week. That is consolidation of a breakout, not distribution, and it still sits only 3.1% under its 176.60 high. The macro case improved: a Fed chair openly contemplating hikes to break inflation is a Fed willing to accept economic pain, and the whole point of owning a 0.56-beta sector whose earnings depend on drug approvals and medical cost ratios rather than on the payroll count is that it does not need the cycle to cooperate. What I will not do is pretend a 34% weight is riskless because the beta is low, so I am attaching a 12% stop for the first time. That sits near 150.6 — below the 50-day and below the July base — so it fires only if the healthcare leadership trend genuinely breaks, not on the kind of 2% air pocket I just watched. Sizing to survive being wrong means naming the level at which I admit it.

Unchanged, and the rate move this week is the specific case for owning this rather than a bond-proxy defensive. SCHD screens on return on capital, free cash flow and low leverage, so what I own is near-term cash generation. When the front end reprices toward a hike and real rates rise, the defensive sleeves that suffer are the long-duration ones and the ones that hold are those whose value sits in cash flows arriving soon. It behaved accordingly: 34.83, off just 0.8% in a week that broke gold by 3.4% and small caps by 1.4%. I continue to prefer it to QUAL because QUAL's roughly 30% technology weight would import exactly the AI-capex beta this book exists to avoid, and I no longer carry a semis short to offset it. Nothing here needs fixing, so I leave it alone.

Raised two points, funded from gold, and the reason is behaviour under stress rather than a view about the future. This was the only leg in either of my books that made a new high this week: 101.74 against 101.23, up 0.5%, while SPY was flat, XLV fell 2% and GLD fell 3.4%. Min-vol earning its name on the exact day the tape got a hawkish shock is the confirmation I want before adding, and I am adding into three binary macro events in three weeks — payrolls 9/4, CPI 9/11, FOMC 9/16 — with a hike close to a coin flip. I still prefer it to SPLV: SPLV's utilities concentration is a long-duration bond proxy and the whole risk in this regime is that duration gets repriced again, whereas USMV's broader construction spares me that. No stop: a diversified low-volatility ETF is the ballast, and stopping out of ballast in a drawdown is exactly backwards.

Cut from 11% to 7% — below the 8% it was at before I raised it — because the thesis I wrote down has been falsified on its own terms. I bought the increase on a falling dollar plus rising long rates, the debasement signature. The dollar has now risen about 1% and reclaimed its 200-day, erasing the entire prior week's decline, and the hawkish repricing lifts real rates, which is the classic headwind for an asset that yields nothing. The market voted immediately: -3.24% on the speech day, -3.4% on the week, -4.5% from Tuesday's 428.07 high. I am not going to zero, and I want to be precise about why that is not stubbornness: the July-August uptrend is intact — 408.89 is still well above the 398 area of mid-August — the fund remains roughly 20% below its 509.70 high, and central-bank demand is a structural bid that one speech does not touch. But my mandate calls gold a SMALL diversifier and it should be sized as an option on the debasement regime returning, not as a bet that it is already here. The 9% stop from here sits near 372, under the entire recovery structure.

Held at the 5% marker rather than cut further, and I want to give the real reason instead of just repeating that the mandate names staples. It has again done nothing — 85.45 against 85.99, and 4.6% below the 90.14 high, the only leg here not near its own highs. But the argument I used to demote it was that staples are priced partly off long rates and long rates were rising 19bp a week; this week long rates were flat while the SHORT end moved, so that specific headwind was absent and the sector still went sideways. What has genuinely improved is the conditional case: if Warsh means it and the Fed hikes into an already-softening labour market, the scenario in which staples finally work — growth scare, not rate scare — becomes more likely, not less. Five points is cheap optionality on that, and cutting a 5% line further is transaction cost in exchange for noise. It stays a marker, not a holding I am waiting on.

decisions.reason: This is a trend-and-carry mandate, and the rule has to cut both ways: I added ETH back last week because it passed the confirmation test I set, so I am obliged to remove the legs that failed theirs. Two failed cleanly. IWM: I cut it to 6% seven days ago writing that 'this leg was powered by the market pricing aggressive cuts, and this week the front end went the other way.' The front end has now gone dramatically further the other way — 2-year +12bp, September hike odds 35% to 58% — and the price confirmed it, 305.09 to 295.75 over ten sessions, -1.5% on the week against SPY +0.5%, the only major index below where it stood a month ago. Highest rate sensitivity, highest consumer-credit sensitivity, worst possible input: that is an exit, not a token. CPER: flat at 39.67 versus 39.85 a MONTH ago, so there is no trend left, and while the backwardation carry is real, a strengthening dollar now works against it too. Carry with a dead trend and a new macro headwind is not what this mandate is for. EFA and PDBC get trimmed rather than cut because they are only half-broken: EFA's local trend is fine but I explicitly bought it as 'trend and currency carry in one instrument,' and the currency half is now a headwind with DXY back above its 200-day; PDBC is a dollar-priced commodity basket facing the same reversal. The proceeds go three places. DBMF up four points, because a regime change is precisely when a managed-futures sleeve earns its fee — it repositions across asset classes without my having to be early by hand, it is the one line that can be structurally short equities, and it rose 0.61% on Friday while the tape fell. JEPI up three, reversing last week's trim on the grounds I gave for it: I cut it because 'the tape is trending' and a covered-call sleeve is capped in a trending market. The tape stopped trending this week, and VIX near the bottom 2.3 percentile of its range going into payrolls, CPI and an FOMC with a coin-flip hike means I am buying a premium-harvesting sleeve when premium is cheap and the catalysts for it to fatten are on the calendar. XLF up two, on price rather than my old logic — I owe an honest correction there, in the leg thesis. The rest goes to cash at 4%, which in a hiking scare is a carry position that gets better if I am wrong about everything else. I am holding both crypto legs flat despite them being my strongest trend, because adding at the top of a 25% seven-session move is the same mistake I refused to make in gold miners; I let the stops carry the position instead and tighten ETH's, since a fixed dollar risk is a smaller percentage after the asset has appreciated.
decisions.novelty: Zero symbol overlap with my Round 2 book and none by construction: Round 2 is a long-only US low-beta quality core (healthcare, dividend-quality, min-vol, staples, bullion) that owns the defensiveness of cash-flow stability, while this book owns non-equity and non-US risk premia — managed futures, developed international, harvested option premium, commodity roll yield, bank NIM and crypto trend — and its two largest sources of return this week (DBMF's negative equity beta and spot crypto) have no expression whatsoever in Round 2, whose gold leg I am cutting at the same time as I hold crypto, on the deliberate view that the debasement trade is now living in coins rather than bullion.

positions.thesis: Raised from 17% to 21% and promoted to the clear anchor, because a hawkish regime break is the exact environment this instrument is built for. It closed 31.41, within 1% of its 31.66 high, and — the detail that matters — it rose 0.61% on Friday while the S&P fell 0.25% on the Warsh speech. That is the negative equity beta doing its job on the one day this quarter I most needed it. Its structural value is that it re-positions systematically across rates, FX, equities and commodities without me having to be early on each leg by hand, which is worth more now than a month ago: the dollar has just turned, the front end has just repriced, and three macro events sit inside the next three weeks. If those resolve hawkish, a managed-futures book gets short bonds and long dollars automatically while my discretionary legs are still arguing about it. No stop on this line, deliberately: it is the leg designed to make money when the others do not, and a stop would eject me from the hedge precisely in the drawdown that justifies it.

Raised from 13% to 16%, reversing last week's trim, and the reversal is on my own stated condition. I cut it saying a covered-call sleeve 'is the right trade in a choppy market and the wrong one in a trending market, and right now the tape is trending.' The tape stopped trending this week: the S&P added 0.5% but fell on the hawkish speech, the Russell lost 1.5%, and a coin-flip September hike now sits in front of payrolls on 9/4, CPI on 9/11 and the FOMC on 9/16. The second reason is that the premium is cheap to own: VIX printed 14.25 in roughly the bottom 2.3 percentile of its range against a 12-month average of 18.1, and JEPI's monthly distribution has fallen from $0.427 in January to $0.367 in August precisely because payout tracks implied volatility. Buying a vol-selling sleeve when vol is at the floor and the catalysts to lift it are on the calendar is a carry trade with the wind about to turn, and the price return badly understates the roughly 8% it earns while I wait. Keep the 10% stop and no take-profit — a capped-upside instrument has no upside target to take.

Trimmed from 17% to 13% because half of why I own it has stopped working. I wrote last week that this is 'trend and currency carry in one instrument,' with the unhedged dollar move mechanically added to local returns, and cited UUP printing a fresh low. The dollar has now reversed about 1% on the week and reclaimed its 200-day near 99.17, erasing that entire decline, so the currency leg has flipped from tailwind to headwind. The reason this is a trim rather than an exit is that the other half is intact and behaved well: 107.72 is only 1.1% off the 108.89 high and the fund lost just 0.5% in a week that cost small caps 1.4% and gold 3.4%. Developed international also never had the AI-capex air pocket the US momentum complex went through, so there is no unwind overhanging it, and if the hawkish repricing is genuinely a US-specific story then non-US equity is where I want the equity beta I still carry. I hold a smaller piece and let the dollar prove which way it is going.

Raised from 8% to 10%, and I owe a correction on the reasoning. Last week I justified this leg on bear steepening — 'the 13-week bill rose only 6bp while the 10-year rose 19bp, and a steeper curve is the textbook setup for wider net interest margin.' This week did the opposite: the 2-year jumped 12bp against roughly 5bp on the 10-year, a flattening, which weakens that argument outright. I am adding anyway, on different and better-evidenced grounds. First, price: 58.10, up 1.1% on the week, a new closing high of 58.31 on 8/25, and it rose on Friday while the index fell — the only equity leg on my board that gained on the hawkish shock. A trend mandate follows the tape, and this is the tape. Second, the substance: higher-for-longer without a recession is a good earnings environment for financials, and this fund is only 27% banks — capital markets at 26% and insurers at 25% are direct beneficiaries of elevated short rates and of the trading volume a repricing generates. I keep XLF rather than KRE for the unchanged reason that consumer credit deterioration is the live risk and money-centre balance sheets are far better collateral than regional loan books. The 12% stop stays wide because I expect volatility around the September meeting and do not want to be shaken out by it.

Held flat at 8% and I am consciously not adding, though this is the strongest trend I own. The confirmation I bought a week ago has extended: ETH is around $2,505 against the $2,427 I marked, spot ETH ETFs have now logged ten consecutive inflow days and extended their streak even on the day bitcoin funds broke theirs, and combined BTC/ETH ETF inflows of roughly $2.3bn were the biggest week since October. The genuinely important evidence is what happened Friday: a hawkish Fed chair and a 1% dollar rally took barely 1% out of it, when the same shock cost gold 3.4%. Crypto absorbing a real-rates shock while bullion did not is why I am cutting gold in my other book and keeping this. What stops me adding is that the move is seven sessions old and 25%+ from the base — adding into that is chasing the same way buying already-squeezed gold miners would have been, and my edge here was buying the base break, not the extension. I tighten the stop from 18% to 15%, near $2,130: after the asset has appreciated, the same dollar risk is a smaller percentage, and $2,130 still sits above the $1,860-1,915 four-week base, so it fires if and only if the breakout has genuinely failed. Take-profit stays 40%, near $3,500. Spot, not a perp: with liquidation at 5% of margin, leverage on something mid-move turns an ordinary shakeout into a total loss on the leg, and I want to own the trend rather than gamble on its path.

Trimmed from 10% to 8%, a small step down rather than the exit I gave copper, because this is half-impaired rather than dead. The reason I held it two weeks ago was explicit: 'the dollar fell 1.7% on the month while the 10-year rose 19bp, and a broad commodity basket is a direct beneficiary of that specific combination.' The dollar half has reversed, and commodities are dollar-priced, so the mechanical tailwind is now a mechanical headwind. Compounding it, a Fed prepared to hike into a soft labour market is demand-negative for a fund that remains majority energy. Against that, the price has not actually broken: 18.39 against 17.91 a month ago is still a positive trend, the fall was only 1.4% in a week that took 3.4% out of gold, and it rose 1.32% on 8/27 on its own energy drivers rather than on the dollar. So I reduce exposure to the part of the thesis that failed and keep a real position in the part that has not. Wide 12% stop, since a commodity basket that oscillates is normal and only a break of the July lows would tell me the trend is over.

Held at 5% — the leader of the move, and the leg that just passed a test I did not set for it. Bitcoin is around $79,000, up roughly 25% since 8/19, through $80,000 intraday on Wednesday for the first time in about three months, its best August in nine years. Then Warsh spoke, the dollar rallied 1% and rate-hike odds jumped to 58%, and it gave back about 1%. An asset that shrugs off a hawkish real-rates shock in the same session that breaks gold by 3.2% is telling me where the debasement bid has migrated, and it is the single cleanest piece of evidence I gathered this week. I am not adding for the same reason I am not adding to ETH: seven sessions and 25% into a move is the wrong place to increase size, and I already hold the higher-beta expression alongside it. One caution I am not ignoring — spot BTC ETFs snapped a nine-day inflow run with a $202m outflow on 8/28, so the flow that powered this has taken its first pause. That is what the stop is for. I keep it at 15%, near $67,200, which still sits just above the pre-breakout $62.8k-$65k base: a retrace into the base means the break failed and I want out rather than hoping. No take-profit, deliberately — capping the leader is how a trend book gives away the one position that pays for the rest. Spot rather than a perp, unchanged: 5%-of-margin liquidation turns a routine shakeout into a total loss.

decisions.name: Opus Value
decisions.research_notes:
PRICE WORK (own pulls, 2y daily, all marks 2026-08-28 close; crypto truncated to 08-28 so I am not trading on weekend prints).

THE WEEK'S TWO EVENTS.

(1) The SaaS de-rating broke. Salesforce reported 2026-08-26 after the close: FY27 Q2 revenue $11.345bn (+10.8% y/y), adjusted EPS $5.90 versus roughly $3.27 expected, net income +73.3%, cRPO +14% cc to $33.5bn, best net-new annual order value in four years, attrition near a record low, FY guidance lifted to ~$46.25bn, Agentforce ARR $1.5bn. Benioff explicitly attacked the "SaaSpocalypse" narrative. The read-across was violent and broad: IGV +7.7% on 08-27 alone (102.39 -> 110.32) and +5.9% on the week, +17.4% over four weeks, now 16.9% above its 200dma and only 7.0% below its 52-week high. CRM 205.62 -> 252.05 -> 256.00 (+22.4% w/w). NOW 125.80 -> 144.71 (+12.6% w/w, helped by its own Tech Mahindra agentic-AI expansion). OKTA +23.0% w/w, CRWD +13.8%, VEEV +11.6%, TEAM +10.8%, HUBS +8.6%, ADBE +5.9%, SAP +1.3%/+22.5% 4w, WDAY +29.5% 4w. CrowdStrike's own print (08-26) was record: revenue $1.47bn +26%, net-new ARR +51%, FY guide raised to $5.99-6.01bn. This matters to me specifically because the AI-kills-software narrative is what made my Round 2 book cheap.

(2) Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech as Chair (08-28) was hawkish: "this summer's PCE and CPI readings... do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," pledged return to 2%, signalled rates could go higher. September hike odds moved to ~57-60% from ~34%. Consequence in my book: GLD -3.2% in that single session (422.60 -> 408.89, -3.4% w/w), SLV -4.3%, GDX -3.9% on the day and -3.1% w/w, WTI -4.2% to 83.40 (26.2% below its 52-week high), UUP +1.0%, 10y 4.72%. The August debasement trade (gold's best month this century, ~+14%) took a direct policy hit.

NON-OBVIOUS TELL: TLT ROSE 1.0% on the week (82.05 -> 83.47 -> 82.88) into that hawkish shock. A credible inflation-fighter caps long-run inflation expectations, and hiking into 3.7% PCE raises the odds of the one outcome my books have no defence against. That is confirmation of the contrarian long-bond leg, not a contradiction.

POSITION-LEVEL VERIFICATION.
- ORCL 150.85 (+3.0% w/w), still 54.1% below its 52-week high. I flagged last week I could not verify the financing risk. Now I can, and it is WORSE, not better: BBB- downgrade, FY26 capex $55.7bn (from $21.2bn) funded with $43bn of debt plus $5bn equity, ~$40bn more to raise this year, and a six-month delay to the $165bn Project Jupiter pipeline reported 08-18. Offset: $75bn of prepaid/customer-supplied hardware reduces the raise. Base held (146.47 -> 150.85, higher low).
- UNH 392.95, +0.7% — the first higher weekly close in seven weeks. Group stabilised (HUM +1.8%, CI +0.5%, ELV -1.5%). Stop (~351 off the 398.76 entry) nowhere near.
- XLV 171.16 -2.0%, MRK 148.35 -2.8% — pharma cooled off the highs.
- SPMO 146.78 -1.3% against SPY +0.5%; MTUM -1.8% w/w, -5.5% 2w. The momentum factor still is not working; my stated "only if the break was noise" condition failed a second week.
- GOOGL 346.59 +0.5%, -10.9% over 13 weeks, 13.9% off its high — third straight flat week while everything I add to moves double digits.
- IBIT 43.90 +0.5%, BTC 77,830 -0.6% — orderly consolidation after the breakout, not a failure.

SCREENED AND REJECTED: SLV (43.2% below a 2026-01-28 blowoff high, but 13w -12.2% and falling into the same hawkish shock — a broken parabola, not a base). INTU (-49% off high, but FY27 guided to only 9-10% growth, below consensus, plus a securities-fraud investigation — fails the quality half of my mandate). NKE (39.60, still -14.3% over 13 weeks, 3% above its 52-week low, 23.9% below its 200dma — still making lower lows, still a pass). XBI (5-year highs and +80% 52w, but the cited driver is anticipated rate CUTS; Warsh just removed that, and it fell 2.0% this week). ADBE (re-entering above my own exit price on an unchanged thesis is churn). BABA, ALB, QCOM (all still declining).

decisions.reason: Two things happened that my own stated rules force me to act on. First, the reversion I bought arrived: CRM ran +22.4% in two sessions on a record print, and at 256.00 it sits 3.8% below its 52-week high and ABOVE the 242.29 consensus target that defined the gap I was buying. I wrote last week that a mean-reversion book that holds through the reversion is only pretending to have a rule, so CRM goes to zero, not to a stub — there is no discount left to own, and a name trading like a leader belongs in my trend book, not this one. NOW ran +12.6% and its discount narrowed from 34% to 24.7%, so it gets trimmed rather than exited, because two-thirds of the gap survives. Second, Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech reversed the specific driver I bought gold for — WTI fell 4.2%, the dollar rose, September hike odds went to ~60%, and GLD lost 3.2% in one session. I said at 423.36 that each further point of size bought a smaller contrarian edge; at 408.89 with the macro driver now hostile, an 18% weight is a momentum bet dressed as a hedge, so it comes down to 11%. The proceeds go where the evidence actually pointed: TLT rose 1.0% in the week the Fed turned hawkish, which is the market telling me a credible inflation-fighter is bullish the long bond, and it is the only asset I own that pays if a hike into 3.7% PCE produces a growth shock. I add two genuinely depressed names and hold 27% cash rather than force weight into anything I cannot defend.

positions.thesis: Held at 13% with the stop unchanged, and this is the first week the price agreed with me. 392.95 is a higher weekly close after six consecutive lower ones, and the group moved with it rather than against it — HUM +1.8%, CI +0.5% — which removes the specific evidence that made me cut from 18% last week, namely peers falling while XLV made highs. I do not restore the 18%, because one higher close is not proof the downtrend is over and 13% is the weight I said I could defend on valuation alone. That valuation is untouched: Q2 adjusted EPS beat by 30%, 18.9x forward, a just-raised dividend, and 27 analysts averaging 475.23 against a 392.95 print. The stop stays at -12% (roughly 351) because my error last week was mechanism, not price, and I want the position closed automatically if the downtrend reasserts rather than re-litigated weekly.

Raised 7 -> 13 and now my joint-largest position, on the strength of a tell most of the market read backwards. TLT rose 1.0% (82.05 to 83.47 to 82.88) during the week Warsh pledged to return inflation to 2% and pushed September hike odds to ~60%. That is not a contradiction of the long-bond case, it is the mechanism: a chair who will actually hike caps long-run inflation expectations, which is what a 20-year Treasury is priced off, and the 10-year barely moved (4.74 to 4.72) while the dollar rose 1.0%. The contrarian criteria are all still met — 10.0% below its 52-week high, 1.9% above its 52-week low, and the bearish narrative is so consensual that I quoted it as settled furniture in three consecutive writeups. Structurally this is the only leg that pays if hiking into 3.7% PCE breaks growth, which is the single outcome that takes down gold, crypto, value equity and cyclical healthcare together. I attach no stop deliberately: an asset 2% off its low with a bounded floor is the one risk shape where a stop converts a long-duration thesis into a timing bet.

Cut 18 -> 11 because the driver reversed, not because the price fell. Every element of the impulse I bought this for has now flipped: WTI went 87.06 to 83.40, TLT rose off its low, the dollar strengthened, and the debasement trade that gave gold its best month this century took a direct policy hit when Warsh raised September hike odds to ~60%. GLD lost 3.2% in that one session. I keep 11% rather than exiting because a single-session policy shock makes gold cheaper on my own framework — 17.6% below the 495.90 high set on 2026-01-29, wider than the 16.9% discount I described last week as too thin — and because a Fed determined to hike into 3.7% PCE is exactly the setup that produces the growth accident gold hedges. What I will not do is keep my largest weight in an asset whose stated rationale I just watched break. 11% is a hedge; 18% was a directional bet on a driver that no longer exists.

Held at 9% and a stop added, and the reason I am not adding despite a good week is that I finally verified the thing I said I could not check. The financing risk has not improved, it has worsened: a BBB- downgrade, FY26 capex of $55.7bn against $21.2bn the prior year funded by $43bn of debt and $5bn of equity, roughly $40bn more to raise this year, and a six-month delay to the $165bn Project Jupiter pipeline reported 08-18. The partial offset is real ($75bn of prepaid and customer-supplied hardware cuts the raise) but it does not turn a levered balance sheet into a safe one. Against that, the price did what I asked: it based at 146.47 and made a higher low at 142.45 before closing 150.85, and the narrative that crushed the whole software complex was publicly refuted this week. So the valuation case is stronger and the credit case is weaker, which nets to unchanged size — 54.1% below its 52-week high is still the most extreme large-cap dislocation available to me. The -18% stop is new and is the honest response to verified negative credit news: a BBB- issuer funding $40bn into a Fed that may hike is the one holding here that can go to zero on financing rather than on sentiment, and I want that exit automated.

New 7%, and the cleanest depressed-quality name my screen produced that is not another bet on software. At 141.07 it is 17.3% below its 171.48 high and only 4.5% above its 133.73 52-week low, down 4.5% over twelve months while SPY gained 19.6% — a 24-point relative drawdown in a franchise whose economics have not been disproven, only disappointed. The problems are known and cyclical rather than structural: soft North American demand since 2024, QFNA recalls, tariff pass-through. What makes it a position rather than a falling knife is the same test I applied to ORCL and denied to NKE: it is flat, not falling — +0.6% over four weeks and -2.2% over thirteen, basing near the low instead of setting new ones, while NKE at 39.60 is still -14.3% over thirteen weeks and 23.9% below its 200dma. It also does structural work I need more of after Jackson Hole: if the Fed hikes into 3.7% PCE, a defensive staple with pricing power and a ~4% yield is the part of the equity market least dependent on the discount rate, and my book is otherwise long duration through ORCL, NOW and HUBS. Sized at 7% as an initiation, not a core weight.

Trimmed 9 -> 6, harvesting a third of the position into a +12.6% two-session move (125.80 to 144.71) on the Salesforce read-across and its expanded Tech Mahindra agentic-AI partnership. The arithmetic is what governs: I bought a 36% discount to the 194.73 high and 24.7% of it remains, so roughly a third of the gap that justified the size was paid out in two days, and I cut roughly a third of the size. That is the same rule I applied to ETH at 9 -> 4 and to CRM at 8 -> 0, and applying it consistently is the only thing that makes it a rule. I keep 6% rather than exiting because unlike CRM this name has not closed its gap — it is still a quarter below its high with 22.2% revenue growth and $1bn+ of AI ACV — but I note the offsetting risk got worse this week, not better: at a 27x forward multiple this is my most rate-sensitive equity, and a Fed pricing a September hike moves the discount rate against it directly.

Trimmed 8 -> 5 because the job it was hired for has shrunk. I bought it as the working half of healthcare to offset managed care, and the divergence that made it valuable has closed from both ends this week: XLV fell 2.0% to 171.16 and is now 2.6% below its high rather than 1.1%, while UNH posted its first higher weekly close in seven and its peers rose with it. A hedge whose spread against the thing it hedges is compressing should be smaller. I keep 5% rather than zero because the pharma complex inside it — MRK, LLY, PFE, BMY — is still the part of healthcare with the better price record and because it remains my cheapest diagnostic: when my single names next diverge from the sector, this fund is how I will tell whether the problem is the company or the group. It stays a stub for the reason I gave when it was 8%: owning an index near its 52-week high is not what a contrarian book is for.

New 5%, and the most extreme surviving discount in the cohort whose defining narrative was publicly refuted this week. At 260.68 it is 50.2% below its 52-week high and down 44.5% over twelve months, priced as a casualty of the AI-kills-SaaS thesis that Salesforce's record quarter — best net-new order value in four years, attrition near record lows, Agentforce ARR at $1.5bn — just contradicted with numbers rather than rhetoric. The company itself is not broken: Q2 revenue $911.7m beat, EPS $3.26 versus $3.02, 17.5% revenue growth with expanding margins, FY EPS guidance raised, and a completed $743m buyback replaced by a fresh $1.0bn 24-month authorisation that puts a bid under sharp pullbacks. It is also basing rather than falling — 53% above its 52-week low, +16.3% over two weeks, reclaiming its 200dma. Sized at only 5% behind a wide -20% stop for one honest reason: this thing traded from the mid-250s to the low-190s and back inside a month, and a name with that realised volatility earns a small weight and a lot of rope, not conviction sizing.

Held at 4% with the -18% stop unchanged. Nothing material happened: 2442.54 against my 2481.83 entry is -1.6%, bitcoin consolidated at 77,830 after its breakout rather than reversing, and at 48.2% below its all-time high the discount that justifies the residual is intact. This is already the harvested remnant of a 9% position I cut after a 26.9% run, so the harvesting decision has been made and does not need remaking each week. The reason I do not add it back on a small pullback is that the macro moved against it this week specifically: a Fed pricing a ~60% chance of a September hike raises the real rate that the whole debasement complex trades off, and I have just cut gold for that exact reason — adding crypto with the same hand would be incoherent.

decisions.reason: Leadership rotated again and it was measurable in a single session. Enterprise software is now the strongest verified trend in the market: IGV rose 7.7% on 08-27 alone and 5.9% on the week, is up 17.4% over four weeks, sits 16.9% above its 200dma and only 7.0% below its 52-week high — driven by a checkable fundamental event, Salesforce's record quarter and guidance raise, plus CrowdStrike's best quarter ever with net-new ARR up 51%. Simultaneously the hard-asset sleeve I built to 37% took a direct policy hit: Warsh pushed September hike odds to roughly 60%, GDX fell 3.9% in a session, GLD 3.2%, and crude 4.2% to 26% below its 52-week high while XLE held — the driver diverging from the equity, and I said in writing I would follow the driver in both directions. So I cut hard assets from 37% to 27% and put 20% into the group that is demonstrably leading. Two exits are overdue on my own stated conditions rather than on new information. SPMO underperformed SPY again (-1.3% against +0.5%) after breaking the 151-155 consolidation I named as its hold condition, so the stub does not survive a second failed week. GOOGL was flat for a third straight week, is down 10.9% over thirteen and 13.9% below its high, and in a trend book flat is not a trend — I have now cut it twice rather than deciding, and deciding is cheaper than a fourth trim. I raise QUAL to 16% because Warsh handed me the strongest possible confirmation of the regime argument I already had: if the cost of capital is going up rather than down, high-return-on-equity businesses with little leverage are the ones that never need to visit that market.
decisions.novelty: This book shares no symbol with my Round 2 book and expresses the opposite side of the same week's evidence: Round 2 harvested CRM into strength and holds the software complex only through its most damaged names (ORCL at 54% below its high, HUBS at 50% below), while this book buys the breakout itself through IGV and CRWD at 7% and 4% below their highs, pairs it with QUAL, SCHD and JEPQ ballast rather than cash, and expresses precious metals through the miners on a stop instead of bullion.

positions.thesis: Raised 12 -> 16 and now the largest position, because Jackson Hole confirmed the regime argument I already had rather than changing it. Warsh pledging to return inflation to 2% and signalling higher rates means the cost of capital is going up, not down, and this fund holds precisely the businesses least exposed to that: high return on equity funded internally, so they never need the market that just got more expensive. The price supports it too, quietly — 223.62, up 0.2% on the week and 1.6% below its 52-week high, while the dedicated momentum factor fell 1.8% and is down 5.5% over two weeks. Holding flat while momentum breaks is relative strength by omission, and it is the second week running that this divergence has appeared, which is what turns an observation into a signal. I raise it rather than parking the money in cash because a trend book that responds to a policy shock by hoarding cash is just market-timing with extra steps. Stop stays at -10%.

New 14%, and it is the largest single change I am making because it is the clearest leadership event of the week by an enormous margin.
