IGV gained 7.7% in the 08-27 session alone (102.39 to 110.32) and 5.9% on the week, is up 17.4% over four weeks, and closed 109.50 — 16.9% above its 200dma and 7.0% below its 52-week high. What makes it a trend rather than a one-day gap is breadth and cause: the move was led by names that did not report (OKTA +23% on the week, VEEV +11.6%, TEAM +10.8%, WDAY +29.5% over four weeks, SAP +22.5%), which means a narrative re-rating of the whole group, not an earnings pop. The cause is checkable — Salesforce's record quarter with cRPO +14%, best net-new order value in four years and Agentforce ARR at $1.5bn, publicly refuting the AI-destroys-SaaS thesis that de-rated the sector all year — and it directly displaces the group that stopped leading, with SMH down 7.7% over thirteen weeks against IGV up 7.7%. I take it as an ETF rather than single names precisely because I am buying a narrative reversal across a cohort, not any one company's quarter. The stop is -10% (about 98.5), set deliberately below the 102.39 gap origin so a complete gap fill does not eject me, but a failure of the whole move does.

Trimmed 13 -> 12, a one-point reduction that is bookkeeping rather than a change of view. At 34.90 it slipped 0.6% while SPY rose 0.5%, its first week of underperformance since I reclassified it from ballast to a trend I already own, and it remains 0.9% below its high with a 27.7% twelve-month return and a 12.8% cushion over its 200dma. That is still relative strength; it is simply no longer the standout it was, so it funds a point of the software initiation. The structural job is unchanged and still needed: a 0.69 beta and a 3.04% yield against a book that still carries 27% in miners, energy and bitcoin, and its Abbott, Amgen and Merck weights keep me in the pharma complex. Stop unchanged at -10%.

Cut 16 -> 11. I raised this to 16% on a breakout and the breakout ran into a policy wall five sessions later: Warsh's hawkish speech pushed September hike odds from ~34% to ~60%, the dollar rose 1.0%, and GDX fell 3.9% in that single session to close 99.65, back inside the 88-102 range it had cleared and down 3.1% on the week. I do not exit, and the reason is that this is still one of the strongest verified trends I own — up 34.5% over four weeks, 71.0% over twelve months, 11.6% above its 200dma and 14.0% below its 117.18 high, so there is still ground to reclaim. But 16% was sized on the assumption that the debasement driver was intact, and it took a direct hit from the only person who can reprice it. Trimming five points is the difference between following a trend and refusing to notice that its cause changed. The stop stays at -13% (about 90) because it is correctly placed just under the range it is now retesting.

Cut 15 -> 10 on my own stated rule. I wrote that the commodity leads the equity and that I would follow the driver in both directions; the driver turned decisively, with WTI down 4.2% on the week to 83.40 and now 26.2% below its 52-week high, and the same rule that took this from 8% to 15% on rising crude has to take it back down on falling crude or it was never a rule. The equity has not confirmed the fall — XLE at 62.68 is off just 1.5% and still 1.7% below its high with a 46.5% twelve-month return — and that divergence is exactly the condition under which I want less, not more: when the equity holds while its input collapses, I am being paid to reduce rather than punished for it. I keep 10% because this remains the only sleeve that pays if the inflation re-acceleration Warsh just described as unimproved actually persists, which is now the Fed's own stated concern. Stop unchanged at -12%.

Held at 7% with the stop unchanged. It gave back 2.8% to 148.35 from 152.55 in a week when the whole healthcare sector cooled (XLV -2.0%), which is participation in a sector pullback rather than a break in the name: it is still 5.2% below its 52-week high, up 13.9% over four weeks, 23.4% over thirteen, 76.2% over twelve months and 26.8% above its 200dma. Nothing in those numbers says the trend ended. It also does the job I bought it for more than ever after this rebalance — with hard assets cut to 27% and software added at 20%, I need a large-cap defensive leader whose driver is drug approvals and pipeline rather than the real rate, and this is the only one on my screen making that claim on price. I do not add, because the four-week move is still something I am following rather than something I can explain, and that argues for an initiation weight with a hard stop, which is what -12% is.

New 6%, the single-name expression of the software breakout and the strongest verified relative strength in my whole screen. At 218.40 it gained 13.8% on the week, is up 106.7% over twelve months, sits 4.2% below its 52-week high and 55.5% above its 200dma. Unlike a sympathy move, this one is its own: the 08-26 print was the best quarter in the company's history — revenue $1.47bn up 26%, adjusted EPS $0.31 against $0.29, net-new ARR up 51%, and full-year guidance lifted to $5.99-6.01bn — with management attributing demand to AI-driven threats, which is the mirror image of the AI-destroys-software fear. That distinction matters for a trend book: I am buying a company whose numbers say AI expands its market, held alongside an ETF that expresses the same shift diluted. Sized at 6% rather than larger because it is a single name 55% above its own 200dma, which is where trends are real and also where they snap; the -15% stop is wider than my usual because that extension is precisely why an 8% leash would be noise.

Held at 6% with the -18% stop unchanged. At 43.90 it gained 0.5% while bitcoin eased 0.6% to 77,830 — consolidation after a 19.9% breakout week, which is what a healthy trend does, not what a failing one does. The test I set at entry still passes: 38.4% below its 71.82 52-week high, so this remains a trend resuming inside an old range rather than a vertical move into new air. I neither add nor cut. I do not add because the macro turned against the debasement channel this week and I have just cut gold miners for that exact reason, so increasing crypto with the same hand would be incoherent. I do not cut because 6% behind an 18% stop is already sized so that being wrong costs about a point of NAV, and the spot ETF rather than a perp remains deliberate: leverage that liquidates on a 5% adverse margin move turns a trend position into a timing bet.

Trimmed 8 -> 6, continuing the reduction I began last week for the same reason of consistency. Its NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft and Micron weights make it megacap and semiconductor-complex exposure with capped upside, and that complex is still the group that stopped leading — SMH down 7.7% over thirteen weeks and 17.3% below its high, MTUM down 5.5% over two weeks. Having just exited SPMO and GOOGL on that reasoning, leaving this at 8% would quietly reinstate the exposure I keep deciding against. It held up fine on the week at 60.15, up 0.5%, which is why it is a trim and not an exit: the 10.78% distribution yield is genuinely counter-cyclical income that improves as dispersion between my directional sleeves rises, and I have just raised dispersion again by swapping ten points of hard assets for twenty points of software. Stop unchanged at -10%.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet deep value
decisions.research_notes:
CHECKED THIS WEEK (prices through 2026-08-28 close):

MACRO 1 — the oil premium unwound. Brent went $94.39 -> roughly $88.50-90.07, about -5.1% on the week, after Iran and Oman agreed a Strait of Hormuz revenue-sharing framework and Hormuz flows began improving. Tehran says this is not an immediate reopening and the Trump administration says it will not return to the collapsed June terms, so the standoff is live, but the tape has taken a real bite out of the risk premium. Context on how violent this series is: Brent printed $69 on 2 July, $105 on 23 July, $94 last week, $88-90 now. Offsetting: the IEA August report now shows a Q3-26 deficit of 1.8 mb/d, more than double last month's ~0.8 mb/d, with 2026 supply falling 4.3 mb/d; EIA has Brent averaging ~$85 in Q3. So the physical balance is tighter than when I last sized CVX for $88-90 crude, even though the price is back there.

MACRO 2 — the Fed turned hawkish in a way that changes the discount rate. Warsh at Jackson Hole said the Fed still has "work to do" and that better summer PCE/CPI prints "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved"; traders moved to price a possible HIKE as soon as September. 2y +12bp to 4.356%, 10y 4.726%, 30y 5.211%. Front-end-led, so the curve flattened rather than steepened - that is not the mechanism I underwrote for C, and it is a stagflationary setup (hiking into a labour market that printed negative payrolls with 103k of downward revisions).

POSITIONS:
- CVX $201.86 (+1.05% Fri). Down only ~1.7% on the week against crude -5.1%, i.e. the equity absorbed far less than the commodity - record earnings, Permian/Hess volumes, the 20-year Microsoft power deal and beta 0.49 are carrying it.
- PFE $28.07, essentially at its 52-week high of $28.44, +15.1% in a month, +18.6% YTD. The consensus target I complained was stale has now refreshed hard: $28.61 -> $32.36, about 15% upside. FDA approved the Pfizer/BioNTech XFG-adapted COVID vaccine on 27 Aug; FY26 revenue guidance midpoint raised $500m to $61.5bn with adj. EPS $2.80-3.00 held; 28 Aug pipeline updates across obesity, oncology and autoimmune. My "consensus has not been refreshed" thesis was validated, upward.
- C $132.90, 11.38x forward, $154.50 target from 21 analysts (+16.25%), 52-week range $92.96-$147.96. August card data: delinquencies DOWN, charge-offs UP. Commentary flags elevated borrowing costs pressuring consumer credit quality.
- VZ $50.10 vs a $51.56 consensus - only 2.9% of upside left. SpaceX confirmed Starlink Mobile launching 2027 and it is now the named investor concern on the stock.
- SMH ~$553.12 (VanEck NAV) vs $560.42 last week and my $569.41 entry, about -3% on the week. The important part is HOW: NVDA beat and jumped ~7-9% on Thursday, SMH rallied 3.5% intraday, and the cohort still finished the week down, with Marvell -10% on gross-margin guidance and AMAT -5%. Rolland raised 2026 industry capex above $1trn (hyperscalers ~$815bn, +111% y/y) - so fundamentals accelerated and the cohort fell anyway. Good news failing to lift the group is the strongest confirmation my de-rating mechanism gets, and Warsh escalates it.
- VLO ~$349 (ATH $353.00 set 24 Aug), +84.7% YTD, now 11.7% ABOVE its $312.53 consensus. US refining margins peaked mid-July and have been falling since.

SCREENED FOR REPLACEMENTS, FOUND NOTHING: BMY 10.2-10.5x forward and 3.86% yield but at ~$65.3 against a $65.4-66.2 consensus - zero upside, 18 Holds. MRK $148.28 against a $148.73 target - 0.26% upside. Large-cap banks below tangible book: the sub-1x names are community/small regionals (0.4-0.7x TBV), not investable size for this book; USB is 2.30x TBV. I am not manufacturing a position to spend cash.

decisions.reason: Three pre-committed rules fired at once, and the whole value of writing rules down is that I execute them when they cut against me. (1) I raised CVX 16% -> 22% one week ago on one explicit number - Brent $94.39 - having stated in writing that 16% was the weight justified by Brent at $88-90. Brent is $88.50-90.07. If I only ever add when the driver confirms and never subtract when it reverses, the sizing arithmetic is decoration, so CVX comes down. It goes to 18% rather than back to 16% because the physical balance is genuinely tighter than when I set 16% (IEA Q3 deficit doubled to 1.8 mb/d) and because CVX fell only 1.7% against crude -5.1%, which says the equity is not a pure crude proxy. (2) VLO: my rule is that once a name trades past consensus the specific dislocation is harvested. It is now 11.7% above target at an all-time high, refining margins peaked in mid-July and are falling, and the crude leg of the crack is de-escalating. I kept 6% last week on the cheap multiple; with the driver now reversing there is nothing left to wait for, so I take the profit rather than let a mean-reverting cash flow capitalised at a peak round-trip. (3) VZ: I wrote that a deep-value book should not pay a full weight for a 4.3% gap to consensus. The gap is now 2.9%, Starlink Mobile is confirmed for 2027, and a Fed openly discussing hikes is the worst regime for a 5.7% yielder. It goes to a residual 5%. The two adds are the mirror image of the same discipline: PFE 20% -> 22% because the one thing I said was missing actually happened - consensus re-rated $28.61 -> $32.36 on the XFG approval, the raised FY26 guide and the pipeline updates, so my 'stale target' argument was proven rather than merely asserted; and SMH short 7% -> 9% because I set an explicit test last week (I refuse to add to this short unless the tape accepts the mechanism) and the tape passed it in the strongest available form - NVDA beat, capex forecasts went ABOVE $1trn, and the cohort still fell ~3% on the week - while Warsh signalling possible hikes escalates the exact discount-rate transmission I am short. The residual goes to cash, not to a new name: I screened BMY (zero upside to consensus) and MRK (0.26%) and the sub-book banks are all micro-cap, and in a deep-value mandate 'nothing is cheap enough' is a real answer. 32% cash earning 4% is also the option to re-buy CVX if Hormuz re-escalates, which this series has done twice since July.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so the cross-round overlap constraint does not bind; this is my only book.

positions.thesis: Raised 20% -> 22% and now the top weight, because the single objection I had against it was answered this week by the market rather than by me. I held it at 20% saying the $28.61 consensus visibly had not been refreshed for raised FY26 guidance, the productivity savings, or the CEO's $1m open-market purchase. It has now refreshed to $32.36 - a 13% jump in the target - after FDA approval of the XFG-adapted COVID vaccine on 27 Aug, a $500m raise to the FY26 revenue midpoint to $61.5bn with adj. EPS held at $2.80-3.00, and 28 Aug pipeline updates across obesity, oncology and autoimmune. At $28.07 that is 15.3% of upside on 10.13x forward against a roughly 19x industry, with a 6.1% yield and 28 analysts at Buy. The structural reason matters more this week than last: it is the only holding with no crude beta, no AI-capex duration and no consumer-credit cyclicality, and I have just watched both of my macro drivers reverse inside five sessions. That is precisely when the leg that answers to neither of them earns more weight, not less. The honest negative is sharper now, not softer: a 6% yield competes against a 30-year at 5.21% with a Fed chair floating hikes, so the carry argument is weak. I own it for the multiple and the pipeline, and it is trading at a 52-week high because the pipeline delivered. Stop stays wide at -18% so a multi-year re-rating is never converted into a stop-out by one session.

Cut 22% -> 18% by my own arithmetic, not by a change of mind. One week ago I raised this from 16% to 22% and stated the reason in one sentence: 16% was the weight justified by Brent at $88-90, and Brent was $94.39. Brent is now $88.50-90.07 after Iran and Oman agreed a Hormuz revenue-sharing framework and flows began improving. The condition I named is gone, so the weight I attached to it goes with it - anything else makes the sizing rule a one-way ratchet that only ever adds. I do not go all the way back to 16% for two reasons I can defend on numbers. First, the physical market is materially tighter than when 16% was set: the IEA now models a Q3-26 deficit of 1.8 mb/d, more than double last month's ~0.8 mb/d, with 2026 supply down 4.3 mb/d, so the same headline crude price sits on a much thinner cushion. Second, the equity told me something: CVX fell only about 1.7% while crude fell 5.1%, which is what beta 0.49 and a company leg of record $20.59bn quarterly net income, Permian and Hess volumes, record US refinery throughput and a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power contract look like. At $201.86 it is roughly 13x forward with a 3.5% yield and a $217.88 consensus implying about 8% upside. It stays the book's inflation hedge, which is not a small job in a week when the Fed chair said his job on inflation is not done. I keep the stop at -15% rather than loosening it back out with the smaller size, because the driver is now actively unwinding rather than confirming, and that raises the odds of the drawdown the stop exists for.

Held flat at 14% with the tension stated rather than smoothed over, because this is the one leg where the week's news genuinely cut both ways and I will not manufacture a decision to look decisive. Against me, and I have to own it: the rate mechanism I underwrote was long-end-led steepening, and what actually happened was front-end-led flattening - the 2y jumped 12bp to 4.356% on Warsh while the 30y moved 2bp to 5.211%. That is not my thesis, and a Fed hiking into a labour market with negative payrolls and 103k of downward revisions is a live credit risk for a bank whose US Personal Banking and cards book is consumer-levered. August card data was mixed in exactly that shape: charge-offs up, though delinquencies - the leading half - actually declined. For me: the discount has not closed at all. $132.90 is 11.38x forward with a $154.50 consensus from 21 analysts implying 16.3% upside, still the cheapest large-cap US bank, on 2025 revenue of $75.7bn up 6.7% with earnings up 13.6%, and the whole curve sitting at high absolute levels supports deposit spread even when its shape is wrong for me. There is a book-level reason too: I just cut oil exposure from 28% to 18% of NAV, and this leg was the internal hedge against that shock, so it is doing less hedging work and more standalone-value work now. What I will not do is add. My own correction stands - at about 1.34x tangible book there is no buyback-accretion kicker, and my mandate's 'banks below book' line is not what this is. Stop stays at -20%; I said a value thesis in a volatile rate debate needs room and I am not tightening it the first week the debate goes against me.

Raised 7% -> 9%, because the specific test I wrote down two weeks ago was passed in the strongest form it could be passed. My rule was: do not add to this short unless the tape accepts the de-rating mechanism, since adding to a losing short on a thesis the market has just refused is how a hedge becomes a bet. This week the tape did more than accept it. NVIDIA beat and jumped roughly 7-9% on Thursday, SMH rallied 3.5% intraday, industry capex forecasts were raised ABOVE $1trn for 2026 with hyperscalers at about $815bn and 111% growth - and the cohort still closed the week down about 3%, with Marvell -10% on gross-margin guidance and Applied Materials -5%. Fundamentals accelerated and the group fell anyway. Good news failing to lift a cohort is the cleanest confirmation a short gets, and it is a different and better signal than the price drop alone. The discount-rate mechanism also escalated: Warsh said the Fed still has work to do on inflation and traders moved to price a possible September hike, which is a direct multiple headwind for the longest-duration equity in the market. Valuation is unchanged and is the most stretched cohort available, which is what the mandate asks of the hedge: 44.89x, NVIDIA at 21.70% of the fund, top ten at 71.46%, beta 1.74, after a 94.6% twelve-month total return. The honest risk is that capex up 111% can squeeze this violently, which is why it is sized for survival and not for a view: 9% with a -22% stop risks about 2% of the book, and 3% borrow costs roughly 27bp a year. The +30% take-profit stays - this is insurance, and I bank it if a real de-rating arrives rather than let it round-trip.

Cut 11% -> 5%, completing the retreat I began two weeks ago, because both stated reasons to own it have now been used up rather than merely weakened. The valuation reason is finished on my own threshold: I wrote that a deep-value book should not pay a full weight for a 4.3% gap to consensus, and at $50.10 against a $51.56 target from 26 analysts the gap is 2.9%. I cannot apply that sentence to justify a trim at 4.3% and then ignore it at 2.9%. The risk reason got worse again in the way I flagged: SpaceX has confirmed Starlink Mobile launching in 2027, and it is now the named investor concern on the stock rather than a hypothetical about terminal value. And the macro turned hostile in a third, new way - a Fed chair openly discussing hikes with the 30-year at 5.211% is the worst available regime for a 5.7% yielder, and that is the argument that retired MO. What keeps a residual 5% instead of zero is that the operating leg keeps beating and the stock keeps RISING while its rate proxy sells off, which says the market is paying for the company and not the coupon: 184,000 postpaid adds, raised full-year revenue and free-cash-flow guidance, a $4.5bn buyback target, the $1bn+ Google dark-fiber deal that makes the AI buildout pay Verizon rent, and NetSense with Lockheed and NVIDIA. At 9.75x forward with beta 0.24 it is still cheap low-beta carry - it just no longer deserves a conviction weight. I tighten the stop from -15% to -12% to match that demotion: a residual position held on execution rather than on a valuation gap should not be given the room a conviction thesis gets.

decisions.research_notes:
PRICES AT 2026-08-28 CLOSE (verified individually): SCHD $34.90 (+0.20% Fri), ABBV $256.99, MDT $91.22, CVX $201.86, PEP $140.13, O $61.98, KO $89.66. My whole equity book pulled back roughly 1-3% on the week; NAV $1,050.38, +5.04% since inception, max DD -2.39%. No stop or take-profit fired.

THE WEEK'S ONE MATERIAL EVENT — THE FED. Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on 2026-08-28 was unexpectedly hawkish: he said recent inflation data gave "little comfort," that underlying trends have not improved, and that "markets are showing few signs of policy restraint." Fed funds futures now price a 57-60% chance of a 25bp HIKE at the mid-September meeting, up from ~56% pre-speech. S&P closed Friday -0.25% (7,712) on it, giving back part of a +0.49% week that had been driven by NVDA's +8.7% post-earnings move. This is a regime input for an income book, not noise: it raises my cash yield (4% APY and rising), raises the discount rate on every bond-proxy multiple I own, and specifically re-prices the duration in O and the staples.

WHY THE FED IS HAWKISH MATTERS FOR MY BOOK. The inflation Warsh is reacting to is substantially energy-led: Brent closed near $88.68 and WTI near $83 on 8/28 with the Iran war ongoing, Strait of Hormuz disruption unresolved, and Russia-Ukraine escalation now adding a second supply front. The Dallas Fed has a working paper out specifically on the 2026 Iran war's impact on US inflation. So the single sleeve a hawkish, energy-driven Fed helps rather than hurts is the one I own the least of.

UPDATED SCORECARD (yield + upside to consensus, the two axes my mandate runs on), which re-widened materially this week from last week's compressed 2.37%-6.14% upside band:
- PEP: $140.13, 4.16% yield, $155 consensus (S&P Global, 24 analysts) to $157.90 (MarketBeat) = 10.6% upside. Score 14.8.
- O: $61.98, 5.24% yield ($3.252 annualized), $67.42 consensus = 8.8% upside. Score 14.0.
- CVX: $201.86, 3.53% yield, $217.23 consensus (31 analysts), Morgan Stanley raised to $218 on 8/19 = 7.6% upside. Score 11.1.
- MDT: $91.22, 3.16% yield, $98.44 consensus = 7.9% upside. Score 11.1.
- KO: $89.66, 2.36% yield, $94.70 consensus (24 analysts) = 5.6% upside. Score 8.0.
- ABBV: $256.99, 2.69% yield ($6.92), $266.89 consensus (S&P Global, 31 analysts) = 3.85% upside. Score 6.5. Two other panels are worse: 40 analysts average $256.53 (zero upside), 29 analysts average $252.90 (negative).

THE ABBV FINDING IS THE WEEK'S REAL WORK. I expected the opposite. ABBV fell 3.0% from my $264.96 mark with no fundamental break, so the naive read was that the valuation gap I trimmed on had reopened and I should add back. It has not. The consensus came DOWN with the price — the same 31-analyst panel that read $276.59 last week now reads $266.89 — so the gap actually narrowed slightly, from 4.39% to 3.85%. Targets fell faster than the stock. The cause is unchanged and known: the Apogee Therapeutics dilution cut FY26 EPS guidance to $13.87-$14.07 from $13.91-$14.11, and the stock is -4.4% since the 7/31 Q2 print despite that print beating on revenue and earnings with Skyrizi, Rinvoq and neuroscience all strong and revenue guidance raised again. Checking this is what stopped me making the wrong trade.

CONCENTRATION I HAD NOT PRICED. I re-pulled SCHD's holdings: ABT 4.86%, MRK 4.82%, AMGN 4.75%, top ten 41.61% of the fund, $104.3B AUM, and 21.04% healthcare — the fund's single largest sector. On a 40% SCHD weight that is 8.4% of NAV in healthcare before I own a single drug stock directly. Add ABBV 10% and MDT 9% and I was carrying ~27% of NAV in healthcare on an 81% gross book. That is a sector bet I never explicitly decided to make.

MDT EARNINGS ARE TUESDAY. Q1 FY2027 reports 2026-09-01 before the open — one trading day after this reassessment. Consensus $1.38-$1.39 EPS (up ~9.5-10.3% y/y) on $8.2-9.5B revenue; FY27 guide $5.90-$6.00. Bloomberg-compiled options data implies roughly a 4% move. Watch items: Affera pulsed-field ablation ramp, Hugo robotic adoption, SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular integration, and ~$75M of Q1 tariff cost (~$250M FY, ~20bp of gross margin).

PEP CATALYST CHECKED AND PARTLY DEBUNKED. A search surfaced "Citi raises PEP target to $170 from $165," which would have been a real change to the downgrade cycle I sized around. It is stale — that raise was December 2025, and Citigroup CUT PEP from $170 to $145 on 2026-07-10. So the Hold-with-downgrades condition I sized at 5% for still holds and I am not doubling the position on a phantom upgrade. What IS real and current: PepsiCo has formalized its restructuring agreement with Elliott (~$4B stake) to cut the US product lineup by 20% with price resets on core brands, plus Frito-Lay plant closures in Orlando, Rancho Cucamonga and Liberty NY, against a 2-4% organic revenue growth guide. Real catalyst, not yet in the tape. Ex-dividend 9/4, which I collect.

INCOME CALENDAR: O goes ex-dividend Monday 8/31 ($0.271 monthly, paid 9/15) — a reason not to touch that leg this week. PEP ex-div 9/4. SCHD's latest distribution was $0.25 (8/30), forward yield 2.89%. ABBV's next ex-div is not until ~10/12-10/15, so trimming it now forfeits no income. SCHD is +27.9% YTD versus the S&P's +13.85%, which is a genuine value/dividend leadership rotation rather than a fluke, and a hiking Fed that punishes long-duration growth is more likely to extend that rotation than end it.

decisions.reason: Two things changed and they point the same way. First, ABBV failed a test I apply symmetrically: I cut KO twice on the stated rule that a name I would not initiate at its current upside cannot hold an above-initiation weight by default, and ABBV is now the lowest-scoring name I own (2.69% yield + 3.85% upside = 6.5 against a book median near 11) while carrying my largest single-name weight at 10%. I expected its gap to have reopened after a 3% price fall; instead the same 31-analyst panel cut its target from $276.59 to $266.89, so the gap narrowed. The property I paid the weight for is gone in both directions now, so the weight goes to 5% — the tier where KO, PEP and O sit, meaning worth owning and not worth overweighting. It also fixes a concentration I had not deliberately chosen: SCHD is 21.04% healthcare with ABT, MRK and AMGN as its top three, so at 40% SCHD plus ABBV 10% plus MDT 9% I was running ~27% of NAV in one sector. Second, the Fed turned. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech put a September 25bp HIKE at ~60% odds, and the inflation he is chasing is energy-led with Brent at $88.68, the Iran war unresolved and Hormuz still disrupted. That raises my cash hurdle, compresses every bond-proxy multiple I own, and helps exactly one sleeve. So 2 points of the 5 go back into CVX, my only energy line, and 3 points go to cash at a risk-free rate that is about to rise. I am deliberately NOT pushing the freed capital into PEP and O, which score highest on my scorecard at 14.8 and 14.0, because they are the two longest-duration things I own and buying duration one day after the Fed signals a hike is scorecard-following with the macro switched off. Gross falls 81% to 78%; net equity risk is barely changed, its composition is better.
decisions.novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book in this experiment, so no Round-2 overlap constraint binds; the construction remains distinct on its own terms — a 40% rules-based dividend core plus six aristocrat-tier single names, no leverage, no shorts, no crypto, and a deliberately large cash sleeve sized off the risk-free rate rather than off residual capital.

positions.thesis: Held flat at 40% for the third straight week, and this time the flat hold has an active macro reason rather than only a refusal. A Fed that is hiking because inflation will not come down is a Fed that raises the discount rate on long-duration cash flows and rewards cash flow received now — which is mechanically what the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 index screens for. That rotation is already the dominant fact of this fund's year: +27.9% YTD against the S&P's +13.85%, which is market leadership moving from mega-cap technology into value and dividend payers, not a lucky quarter. Warsh's speech makes that leadership more likely to persist, so the largest thing I own is also the thing most aligned with the regime I now expect. I still will not add to it, and the reason is the same one I gave last week and re-verified this week: its top three holdings are ABT at 4.86%, MRK at 4.82% and AMGN at 4.75%, roughly 14.4% of the fund in three names the sell-side puts at or through fair value, with 21.04% of the fund in healthcare overall. Buying more SCHD would deepen the valuation compression and the sector concentration I spent this week reducing elsewhere. What it keeps: $104.31B AUM, 0.06% fee, a 2.89% forward yield, a 0.69 beta, 101 holdings, and a mechanical quarterly rotation toward cash-flow quality that requires no opinion from me. That is a rebalancing basket, not a momentum position, so its all-time high is information rather than a signal. The 12% stop stays what it is — catastrophe protection on a 100-name vehicle, not a trading stop — and there is still no take-profit, because you do not take profits on the compounding core.

Held flat at 9% for the second week, and the reason is again the calendar, now at one day's distance: Q1 FY2027 reports Tuesday September 1 before the open. On the scorecard it improved this week — the stock fell 2.3% to $91.22 while the $98.44 consensus from 29 analysts held, so upside widened from 5.45% to 7.92% and the score rose to 11.1, tied for third-best in the book at a 3.16% yield. Last week I said it wanted more weight and the calendar was the only thing stopping me. That is still true, and options-implied pricing puts the earnings move at roughly 4%, which means adding today to capture a 2% better entry is paying a coin-flip for a rounding error. The bar Tuesday is real but not stretched: $1.38-$1.39 EPS against $1.26 a year ago, revenue up 4-6%, with the FY27 guide $5.90-$6.00 and roughly $75M of tariff cost landing in the quarter against ~$250M for the year, about 20bp of gross margin. What I need to see is the Affera pulsed-field ablation ramp and Hugo adoption converting, because the whole thesis is that 15.7x forward against 25.0x trailing means the street has modelled an earnings recovery that reported numbers have not yet shown — the margin-lag signature of a turnaround mid-flight, with revenue growing 8.43% while net income grew 2.98%. At a 0.57 beta this is the book's designated low-beta ballast, the role I moved it into when I retired JNJ. I am keeping the 10% stop rather than widening it into the print, even knowing a stop can be gapped through: at a 4% implied move the stop sits about 2.5 standard deviations out, and I said last week the tight stop was there precisely because of September 1. Loosening a stop the week it might actually be needed would be the rule that binds only when it is free. Take-profit at +10% is near $100.3, above the $98.44 consensus, where a genuine beat-and-raise lands and a drift does not.

Raised from 7% back to 9%, reversing the trim I made two weeks ago, and I want to be exact about why this is not the thing I refused to do last week. The rule I bound myself to was narrow and I will quote its logic: having flagged the Middle East geopolitical premium as this position's one-headline reversal risk, and having banked two points when that risk became an actual headline, I would not re-underwrite one week later at a HIGHER price merely because the market shrugged. That rule was about not chasing. It is not in force here on either half. The price is $201.86, which is $3.41 BELOW the $205.27 where I declined to buy last week and below where I trimmed. And the reason is genuinely new rather than the absence of bad news: Warsh's hawkish turn, the single biggest market event of the week, was driven by inflation that is substantially energy-led — Brent closed at $88.68 with WTI near $83, the Iran war unresolved, Hormuz disruption ongoing, and Russia-Ukraine escalation opening a second supply front, with the Dallas Fed publishing on exactly this channel. That makes energy the one sleeve in an income book that a hiking Fed helps rather than compresses, because the commodity causing the tightening is the same commodity that pays this company. On my own scorecard it also earns the capital independently: 3.53% yield plus 7.6% upside to a $217.23 consensus from 31 analysts, score 11.1, at 13.3x forward with a 0.49 beta, with Morgan Stanley lifting to $218 on August 19. The franchise keeps delivering — the 105-4X condensate discovery in Angola's Block 0, Equinor taking 17.4% of the offshore Namibia license. I stop at 9% and not higher because the one-headline risk cuts both ways: a ceasefire crushes the premium as fast as an escalation built it, which is exactly why the 10% stop stays. Take-profit holds at +8%, about $218, right at consensus and just through the $214.71 52-week high — reachable on a crude spike, not on drift.

Cut from 10% to 5%, the second consecutive trim, and it is the same rule that took KO from 13 to 9 to 5 applied to myself without an exemption for a name I like. I went into this week expecting to ADD. The stock fell 3.0% from my $264.96 mark to $256.99 on no fundamental break, which on last week's logic — I sized it at 13% for the widest gap in the book and cut to 10% when the gap closed to 4.39% — should have reopened the gap and earned the weight back. It did not. The consensus fell with the price: the same 31-analyst S&P Global panel that read $276.59 a week ago now reads $266.89, so upside is 3.85%, slightly WORSE than when I trimmed. Two other panels are worse still, with 40 analysts averaging $256.53 and 29 averaging $252.90, meaning the broadest coverage puts this stock at or through fair value. Targets falling faster than the price is deterioration in the sell-side's view, not a discount. On my two axes it now scores 6.5 — 2.69% yield on a $6.92 payout plus 3.85% upside — the lowest number in this book, while holding my single largest name weight. I wrote last week that paying up for a name trading 4% from consensus is precisely what I am selling elsewhere; holding 10% of one is the same error wearing a nicer suit. The business is not why I am selling and I will not pretend otherwise: Q2 beat on both lines, revenue guidance was raised again, Skyrizi, Rinvoq and neuroscience are all growing, forward PE is 17.5 with the 74.9 trailing being IPR&D accounting noise, and the 53-year raise streak is genuine aristocracy. The stock is -4.4% since the 7/31 print purely because Apogee dilution took the FY26 EPS guide to $13.87-$14.07 from $13.91-$14.11 — a known, quantified, four-cent issue the market is charging far more than four cents for. The second reason for the cut is one I only found by re-pulling holdings: SCHD is 21.04% healthcare with ABT, MRK and AMGN as its top three, so ABBV at 10% plus MDT at 9% put ~27% of NAV in one sector I never explicitly chose to bet on. This takes it to ~22%. No income is forfeited — the next ex-dividend is not until roughly October 12-15. Take-profit resets to +5%, near $270, just through the $266.89 consensus and therefore a fillable order rather than a wish; the 10% stop stands.

Held flat at 5% in its first full week, down 2.3% to $140.13, and holding flat is a decision I nearly got wrong. It is now the highest-scoring security in the book at 14.8 — a 4.16% yield plus 10.6% upside to a $155 consensus, with MarketBeat's panel at $157.90 — and a mechanical reading of my own scorecard says double it. Two things stopped me. First, I ran down a catalyst and it failed the date check: a Citi raise to $170 from $165 looked like the downgrade cycle turning, which was the exact condition I sized small for, but that raise is from December 2025 and Citigroup then CUT to $145 on July 10, 2026. The Hold-with-active-downgrades condition I underwrote is unchanged, so adding on it would have been adding on a stale headline. Second, and this is the week's discipline, PEP is a bond proxy and the Fed just signalled a September hike at ~60% odds; buying duration into that on a scorecard reading is exactly the mechanical behaviour I try to catch in myself. What is real and current is the restructuring: PepsiCo has now FORMALIZED its agreement with Elliott's ~$4B stake to cut the US product lineup by 20% with price resets on core brands, alongside Frito-Lay closures in Orlando, Rancho Cucamonga and Liberty NY, against a 2-4% organic revenue growth guide. That is a named margin catalyst not yet in the tape, and it is why 16.5x forward for a 54-year raiser sitting 18% below its $171.48 high with a freshly declared 4% increase is a thesis being priced rather than a thesis breaking — the distinction I drew when I bought this and sold P&G. Frito-Lay volume weakness and North American snacking behaviour remain the genuine bear case and I am not burying it. I collect the September 4 ex-dividend. Next earnings are October 8, well past the next reassessment, so the 12% stop stays deliberately wide: I do not want to be shaken out of a 4%-plus yield by tape noise while a restructuring works. Take-profit moves UP from +12% to +14%, near $159.7, purely to preserve the original design — because the price fell, the same dollar target now needs a larger percentage to stay above the $155-$157.90 consensus band, where a real North America inflection re-rates the multiple rather than merely closing the target gap.

Held flat at 5%, and this is the position the week's news is aimed squarely at. When I bought it seven days ago I named rate duration as its specific accepted risk and said I was taking it knowingly because the alternative use of the capital was cash at 4% while O pays 120bp more with three decades of raises attached. Warsh has now moved a September hike to roughly 60% probability, so that named risk went from ambient to likely inside one week. My own precedent with CVX says the disciplined response to a flagged risk materialising is to reduce rather than re-underwrite. I am not reducing, and the distinction is that with CVX the risk had materialised in the PRICE and I had a gain to bank; here it has materialised only in probability, the stock is down about 1% to $61.98, and one Jackson Hole speech moving futures from 56% to 60% is not the event, the September 16-17 FOMC is. Selling a 5.24% contractual yield on a four-point shift in an options-implied probability is over-trading a duration risk I explicitly chose to carry, and it would also forfeit Monday's August 31 ex-dividend of $0.271, payable September 15. On the merits nothing has broken and something improved: Q2 2026 revenue of $1.55B beat on robust investment activity, management RAISED full-year guidance to $4.44-$4.45 EPS against a $4.43 consensus, and the consensus target is $67.42 for 8.8% upside, so I am still buying into an upgrade cycle rather than a value trap. The 'funded by strong free cash flow' clause of my mandate is met more literally here than anywhere else in the book: contractual net-lease rent from 15,500-plus properties across 50 states and nine countries, tenanted toward grocery, convenience, dollar and drug stores, which is staples exposure by revenue source even though the wrapper is a REIT. Thirty consecutive annual increases and 674 consecutive monthly dividends is the longest unbroken payment record I own. The honest caveats stand: the 45.8x headline P/E is a REIT depreciation artifact with AFFO in the low-to-mid teens being the real multiple, and the consensus rating is Hold. Rate risk is now live and monitored rather than theoretical, which is precisely why this stays at 5% and does not grow despite scoring 14.0. The 10% stop is the mechanism that makes carrying the duration survivable if the long end backs up hard; take-profit at +10%, about $68.2, sits just through consensus.

Held flat at 5% after two consecutive cuts, and flat is now correct for the same reason the cuts were. I took it 13 to 9 to 5 on the stated principle that I should hold the weight I would actually initiate; at $89.66, down 1.6% on the week, it scores 8.0 — a 2.36% yield plus 5.62% upside to a $94.70 consensus from 24 analysts, with a $96 median and a $75-$104 range — which is second-worst in the book but genuinely better than the 3.95% upside that triggered the last cut, because the stock came off the $91.87 52-week high it had been pressed against. That is enough to own at 5% and not enough to own at more, so the position is exactly where my rule puts it and I am leaving it there rather than trading a name twice in three weeks for a point of scorecard. The business justifies the floor: FY26 guidance was raised on the Q2 print, 2025 earnings rose 23.29% on 1.87% revenue growth, EPS is up 18.0% to $3.33, volume and organic growth are intact, several firms pushed targets above $95 after the quarter, and the 62-year streak is the longest raise record among my direct equity lines — a Dividend King and the reason this holds a permanent seat in an aristocrat mandate. The fairlife cybersecurity incident resolved with production resumed and stays a contained subsidiary event. The pressure point is valuation into a hiking Fed: near 27x forward for a 2.36% yield, this is the most expensive bond proxy I own per unit of income, and a rising discount rate is precisely what a 27x multiple on 2% revenue growth cannot absorb. That is why the 8% stop stays the tightest in the book and why the take-profit moves only from +5% to +6%, to about $95.0 — the previous level had drifted just BELOW the $94.70 consensus as the stock fell, and a take-profit that fills before the analyst number is reached is leaving money on the table for no reason. At +6% it sits just through consensus, in the zone where the post-Q2 target raises actually landed.

decisions.research_notes:
Refreshed daily closes through 2026-08-28 for ~55 US equity ETFs and computed 1w/1m/3m/6m/12m returns, 52-week range position, date of the 52-week high, 20/50/200-day MA structure and 63-day realized vol.

Book performance: NAV $1,009.80, +0.98% since round inception, max DD -2.64%. From the 08-24 entry the marks are roughly -0.77%: XBI -1.09%, XLV -2.03%, LABU -4.08%, IWM -0.75%, XLE -0.68%, IEO -0.44%, offset by QQQ +1.43% and SMH +1.15%. The XAR stop fired on 08-24 at $265.61 and XAR has since fallen to $261.79, so that exit was correct.

THE WEEK'S ONE MATERIAL EVENT. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote on 2026-08-28 said inflation's underlying trend has not improved and the Fed may have "work to do". Fed funds futures now price a 60.4% chance of a quarter-point HIKE at the September 15-16 meeting. The tape on 08-28 was not risk-off, it was a duration repricing: 10y 4.67% -> 4.72%, UUP +0.57%, VIX FELL to 14.43, SPY only -0.23% -- while GLD -3.24%, GDX -3.90%, XBI -3.48%, LABU -10.71%, SMH -3.47%, IWM -1.35%. Energy went UP on the same day: XLE +0.63%, IEO +0.47%, XOP +0.25%. That single-session cross-section is the cleanest read I have on which of my themes carries rate duration and which does not.

BIOTECH. The trend is intact but its macro backing changed. XBI is still 91.0% of its 52-week range, above all three MAs (+1.3%/+3.8%/+21.2%), +80.7% over twelve months and only -4.23% off its 08-19 high. FBT (NYSE Arca biotech, large/profitable names) actually set a FRESH 52-week high on 2026-08-27 -- the most recent high anywhere in the biotech complex -- at 93.2% of range, +55.1% over 12m, and it fell only -2.54% on the hawkish day versus XBI's -3.48%, on 23.1% realized vol against XBI's 32.8%. IBB +51.2% and BBH +43.7% confirm the theme. So biotech is not broken; it is simply the most rate-sensitive equity theme I own going into a live hike.

SEMIS. NVDA reported and revived AI optimism on 08-27: SMH +3.10%, XLK +3.16%, IGV +7.74% (Okta +22%, Salesforce +20%, CrowdStrike +18% on agentic-AI demand). SMH gave the entire move back the next day, -3.47%. It remains -17.31% below its 2026-06-22 high, below both its 20-day (-2.8%) and 50-day (-5.1%), and -7.65% over three months. My 5% residual was explicitly an option on re-acceleration; the option got its catalyst -- the best semi news of the quarter -- and expired worthless. SOXL -62.98% off its high and XSD -25.81% confirm the damage is the basket.

ENERGY. The strongest and now the best-supported theme on the board, and I found the reason. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed since February 2026, taking out roughly 20% of global supply, with Brent near $85 and S&P 500 energy earnings projected +57% for CY26. That is a structural supply constraint, not a headline premium -- which is why energy rose on a hawkish day (a hawkish Fed implies a strong economy implies demand). XLE 95.2% of range, high 08-20; IEO 95.8%, high 08-21; XOP 94.7%; VDE 94.9%; all above every MA. ERX (2x energy) is +89.2% over twelve months at 93.0% of range with its high on 08-20 and 45.3% vol -- markedly tamer than LABU's 97.5%.

CHECKED AND REJECTED. IGV (+17.4% on the month) fails my 12-month test at +1.9%. XLF at 98.0% of range with a 08-25 high and FAS +39% over 3m both fail it too (XLF +9.7%, FAS +12.1% over 12m) -- a hiking Fed is a macro argument for banks, not a momentum signal, and my mandate is 12-month momentum. GDX +29.8% on the month but -13.98% below a February high and -3.90% on the hawkish day: a recovery, not an intact trend, and directly hostile to rising real rates. XME 3m -5.1%, OIH 3m +0.01%, URA -26% off its high: none intact.

decisions.reason: A 60% probability of a September rate hike got priced on 08-28 and the cross-section that day told me exactly which of my themes carries duration. My book was built assuming the biotech bid was a clinical/M&A story insulated from rates; on the one day that assumption was tested, XBI lost 3.48% and LABU 10.71% while energy rose and SPY barely moved. So I am not fighting the trend -- every leg I keep is still above all three moving averages -- I am moving weight down the duration curve inside the themes I own and toward the one theme that made new highs INTO the shock. Three specific changes. First, LABU goes to zero: it is 3x leverage on the most rate-sensitive equity theme there is, at 97.5% realized vol, and holding it into a live hike meeting means a 22% stop is a coin flip rather than a trend signal -- the mandate's select-leverage clause belongs on the trend that is working, so I move it to ERX at 2x on energy. Second, SMH goes to zero: I kept it for six weeks as an option on re-acceleration, NVDA's beat handed it the catalyst on 08-27, and it gave the whole move back in a session while still sitting 17% below its June high and under both its 20- and 50-day. That is the test failing, not the test being postponed, and holding it now would be paying for the +86% twelve-month number rather than for price. Third, my top position comes DOWN from 25% to 19%: I raised XBI last week on genuine acceleration and the trend has not broken, but 25% in the highest-duration theme I own into a hike meeting is asymmetric the wrong way, so I split the biotech sleeve with 9% FBT, which set a fresh 52-week high on 08-27, held up a full point better on the hawkish day, and does it at 23% vol against XBI's 33%. Same theme, less rate duration. Gross stays at 85% -- this is a rotation within the book, not a de-risking of it.
decisions.novelty: I manage no Round-2 book in this experiment, so there is no same-direction gross-weight overlap to constrain; this Round-3 book stands alone.

positions.thesis: Trimmed from 25% but still my largest position, because the trend is intact and only its macro backing got worse. XBI is +80.7% over twelve months -- the strongest 12-month trend I own now that SMH is gone -- at 91.0% of its 52-week range, above its 20-day by 1.3%, its 50-day by 3.8% and its 200-day by 21.2%, and only 4.23% below the high it set on 2026-08-19. Nothing about that is broken. What changed is that on 08-28 it fell 3.48% while SPY fell 0.23% and energy rose, which measures its rate duration precisely: XBI is an equal-weight basket stuffed with pre-revenue names whose value sits far out on the discount curve, and a Fed that may hike on September 16 is a direct de-rating input. I cut six points rather than defending a number I set a week ago, and I moved them to FBT and XLV -- the same healthcare bid held with less duration -- rather than out of the theme. The 12% stop stays wide on purpose: at 33% realized vol a tight stop on this basket exits on noise, and 12% still sits above the 200-day, so it fires on trend destruction rather than on a hawkish week.

Raised from 12% and it now shares the top of the book, on the strength of one number: it fell 0.24% on 08-28 while XBI fell 3.48%. Same healthcare theme, one-fourteenth the damage from the rate shock, because large-cap pharma earns cash now instead of in 2032. It is not ballast masquerading as momentum either -- fresh 52-week high on 2026-08-19, 89.5% of range, only 2.57% off that high, +15.0% over three months and +27.1% over twelve, above all three moving averages -- at 19.7% realized vol, the lowest in the entire book. When the thing that changed is the discount rate and not the theme, the correct response is to hold the same theme at a shorter duration, and this is the shortest-duration healthcare I can buy.

Raised from 13%. Closed at 95.2% of its 52-week range with the high set 2026-08-20, +44.9% over twelve months, above every moving average -- and, decisively, it went UP 0.63% on the day the hike odds repriced, because a hawkish Fed is a statement that the economy is strong and strong economies burn oil. I also finally have the mechanism rather than a guess: the Strait of Hormuz has been shut since February 2026, roughly 20% of global supply, Brent near $85, and sector earnings tracking +57% for the calendar year. That is a supply constraint with a physical cause, which is why it survived defense collapsing beside it. I hold the majors as the core of the theme at 22.5% vol -- five points below IEO and half of ERX -- so that if a de-escalation headline gaps the group, the largest energy leg I own is the one that gives back least.

Raised from 8% and it remains the best-ranked energy vehicle on my board: 95.8% of its 52-week range, high set 2026-08-21, +8.4% on the month, +18.7% over three months and +49.1% over twelve, sitting 3.9% above its 20-day and 10.7% above its 50-day. It beats XLE on every horizon and it beat it again through this week's shock. E&P is the right torque to a supply-driven crude move because producers capture the price directly rather than through refining spreads, and with Hormuz constraining barrels the constraint transmits to the wellhead. Stopped a point wider than XLE at 9% because 27.4% vol needs the room, and capped at 22% for the same reason.

New, and it is where six of XBI's points went. FBT set a fresh 52-week high on 2026-08-27 -- the single most recent 52-week high anywhere in the biotech complex, eight sessions later than XBI's -- closing at 93.2% of range only 2.54% below it, +19.8% over three months and +55.1% over twelve, above all three moving averages. The reason to own it alongside XBI rather than instead of it is the duration split: FBT is a modified equal-weight basket of profitable large- and mid-cap biotech, it runs 23.1% realized vol against XBI's 32.8%, and on the hawkish 08-28 session it lost 2.54% against XBI's 3.48%. That is the same theme, the same breakout, and measurably less sensitivity to the thing that actually moved this week. Holding biotech through two vehicles at two points on the duration curve is how I stay long a trend I still believe in without betting 25% of the book on the most rate-exposed slice of it.

Held flat at 7% and it is now my entire large-cap tech expression. It earns the hold and nothing more: +25.5% over twelve months, 84.6% of range, only 3.88% off its high, and it was the one leg that gained through this week's shock (+1.43% from my entry, +1.37% on the NVDA-driven 08-27 session). But its high still dates to 2026-06-02, three-month return is -2.86%, and it closed 0.2% BELOW its 20-day and a bare 0.6% above its 50-day. A theme that has produced nothing in three months and is sitting on its 50-day does not get the points I took out of SMH -- those went to trends making new highs. I keep it because mega-cap tech carries net cash and real earnings, which is the least rate-sensitive way to hold the AI complex now that the levered and semi expressions have failed, and because it has not violated a moving average.

Cut from 11% to the smallest equity leg in the book, and the stop tightened from 8% to 7%. Small-caps are the most direct casualty of what happened on 08-28: the Russell fell 1.35% on hike odds because small-caps carry floating-rate debt and near-term refinancing walls that mega-caps do not, so a hiking Fed hits their earnings mechanically rather than just their multiple. The price already agreed before the Fed spoke -- IWM peaked on 2026-08-14, now closes below both its 20-day (-1.5%) and its 50-day (-0.5%), and its three-month return is +2.07% against a +12.75% six-month figure. Its +26.7% twelve-month return is the weakest in the book. The mandate names small-caps so I keep the theme alive at a token weight, but I am sizing a theme that stopped leading, is below its moving averages, and now faces a policy path aimed at it -- and the 7% stop means the next leg down takes me out rather than bleeding me.

New, and it takes over the mandate's select-leverage clause from LABU. The comparison decides it. ERX is 2x on a theme at 93.0% of its 52-week range with its high set 2026-08-20, above all three moving averages, +89.2% over twelve months, running 45.3% realized vol -- and it rose 0.89% on the day the hike odds repriced. LABU is 3x on a theme that lost 10.71% on that same day at 97.5% vol. Leverage should sit where the trend is working and where the underlying's volatility does not eat the compounding, and energy at 22.5% underlying vol suffers far less daily-rebalancing decay than biotech at 33%. Sized at only 4% for 8% effective exposure -- half the effective leverage LABU carried -- because the underlying trend rests on a geopolitical supply constraint that could reverse on a single de-escalation headline, and 4% is what I can lose 20% of without it mattering. The 13% stop equals roughly a 6.5% move in XLE, so it fires before my XLE stop rather than after it.

decisions.name: Opus-fleet quality compounders
decisions.research_notes:
Checked, week of 2026-08-24 to 08-28 (prices through 08-28 close):

NVDA Q2 FY27 (reported 08-26, the single biggest event risk I was carrying): revenue $96.22B +105.9% YoY, EPS $2.22 (more than double), Data Center $89.0B +117% and now 92.5% of revenue, ~4% above the estimate midpoint. Q3 guide ~$108B +/-2%. First-ever full-year-forward guide: FY28 revenue growth ~70% against LSEG consensus of 44%, and management stated explicitly that the 70% is SUPPLY-constrained with underlying demand tracking nearer 100%. Non-hyperscale DC revenue +138% YoY vs hyperscale +13% — the customer base is broadening away from the five buyers the circular-financing bears point at. The one genuine negative: non-GAAP gross margin guided to ~74% in Q3 and a trough of 71-72% in Q4 on memory costs that management said exceeded expectations and are headed higher into next year. Stock +8.7% on 08-27 to close 08-28 at $217.89. Consensus target moved UP to ~$305-320 (68 analysts, avg $319.56), so upside widened to roughly +40-47% even after the move — numbers rose faster than price.

Macro, and this is the week's real change: Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote on 08-28 read hawkish — "work to do" on inflation, price stability the predominant focus. CME September rate-HIKE odds jumped from 35.4% to 57.5% intraday and ~60% by Monday; JPM Wealth Management now formally forecasts a 25bp hike. 2y +12bp to 4.356%, 10y 4.726%, 30y 5.211%. S&P -0.25% Friday to 7,711.76 but +0.5% on the week; Nasdaq -0.52% Friday, +0.9% on the week. Energy/supply shocks tied to the Iran conflict named as a driver. This is a regime question, not a data point: my whole book is 25-26x forward long-duration equity.

Position-level valuation check at 08-28 (price / consensus target / upside / discount to own 52wk high):
- NVDA $217.89 / ~$305-320 / +40-47% / ~8% below high. Widest gap in the book, and it widened this week.
- GOOGL $346.59 / $428.07 (64 analysts, Strong Buy) / +23.5% / 15.2% below its $408.61 high. Gap unchanged week-over-week — the only leg whose story price has not consumed.
- MA $592.16 / $669.46 (40 analysts) / +13.1% / 1.3% below its 08-24 all-time high of $599.86. Wolfe raised its target to $740 on 08-24.
- MSFT $513.06 / $560.27 (42 of 47 Buy) / +9.2% / 7.3% below its $553.72 high. Up 28% in a month.

That last line is the finding that drove this week's action. I raised MSFT from 23% to 25% on 08-22 on one specific argument: at $483.24 it was the cheapest of the three mega-caps on a like-for-like forward basis (24.49x vs Alphabet's 25.87x) at the deepest discount to its own high (12.7%). Five days later the price is +6.2%, the discount to its high has nearly halved to 7.3%, and — the part that matters — the consensus target went the OTHER way, from $569.56 to $560.27. Upside to consensus fell from +17.9% to +9.2%, now the thinnest in the book, thinner than Mastercard's. That is the same signature I sold Visa for last week: price outrunning the story while the target stands still. The business is fine (FY26 revenue $331.8B +18%, Azure +43% in Q4 and guided to 45% cc in Q1 FY27, Azure past $100B, commercial RPO $678B +84%, M365 Copilot seats 30M vs ~27M expected) — which is why this is a trim, not the exit Visa got.

Also checked: Alphabet's search-antitrust remedies have been read to extend to GenAI, barring exclusive distribution contracts for the Gemini app alongside Search/Chrome/Assistant, and requiring index and interaction-data syndication to rivals. Google shipped deeper Gemini-in-Chrome integration anyway. Modest negative to the "unpriced AI optionality" part of my GOOGL case; no change to the Search/YouTube moat economics or the $121.68B net cash. Mastercard: no thesis-relevant news beyond the Wolfe target raise and an EEMEA president appointment.

decisions.reason: One leg's stated reason for being oversized was paid out in five days, and the macro backdrop changed enough that I want the proceeds in cash rather than redeployed. I added to Microsoft on 08-22 for one named reason: it was the cheapest mega-cap on a like-for-like forward basis at the deepest discount to its own high. Since then it is +6.2%, its discount to its high has halved from 12.7% to 7.3%, and the consensus target has fallen from $569.56 to $560.27 — leaving +9.2% upside, now the thinnest in the book. When the price rises 6% while the target falls, the cheapness argument has been consumed, and I hold myself to the same test I applied to Visa a week ago. So Microsoft goes 25% to 20%; it stays a large position because Azure at +43% guided to +45% cc and 30M Copilot seats is not a Visa-like 2%-growth business. The five points go to cash, not to another mega-cap, because Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote moved September rate-HIKE odds from 35% to ~60% with the 30-year at 5.21%. A hiking cycle is the one scenario that hits Nvidia, Alphabet and Microsoft simultaneously, and 77% of my book sits in that correlation. I am not selling quality compounders over a two-week-out Fed meeting, but I am cutting gross from 90% to 85% and holding real dry powder that earns 4%+ — more if they actually hike — so a rate-driven drawdown in names I want to own becomes an opportunity rather than a problem. Nvidia is deliberately NOT increased despite the best print of the year: the event improved the leg's expected return, not my ability to survive being wrong in it, and 26% in a ~2x-beta name into a coin-flip Fed meeting is already the most conviction I am willing to carry. Alphabet and Mastercard are untouched at 26% and 13% — neither has had its case consumed by price. I am adding no new stops; in a broad rate shock a stop on a compounder just converts a drawdown into a realised loss, so I sized down instead. Only Nvidia keeps its wide -30% stop, because it is the one leg where a single-name AI-capex unwind, not a market move, is the tail I need to survive.
decisions.novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the distinguishing feature of this book remains that it expresses AI-infrastructure exposure through net-cash, high-ROIC incumbents financed from their own cash flow rather than through levered or single-product beneficiaries, and it now carries an explicit 15% cash buffer sized against a live Fed hiking risk rather than being fully invested by default.

positions.thesis: Held at 26%, unchanged, after the print that was the largest single risk in this book resolved decisively in favour. Q2 FY27 revenue $96.22B +105.9%, EPS $2.22, Data Center $89.0B +117% and ~4% above the estimate midpoint, Q3 guided to ~$108B. The important disclosure was the first-ever full-year-forward guide: FY28 revenue growth ~70% versus 44% consensus, and management stated that figure is supply-constrained with underlying demand nearer 100%. Non-hyperscale data-centre revenue grew 138% YoY against hyperscale's 13%, which directly answers the circular-vendor-financing objection I have been carrying — the demand is broadening beyond the handful of buyers whose capex is financed off the long end. The stock rose 8.7% but the numbers rose more, so the forward multiple compressed and the consensus target moved up to roughly $305-320, leaving +40-47% upside, still by far the widest gap in the book, at ~8% below its own 52-week high. The new negative I am underwriting honestly: gross margin is guided down from ~74% in Q3 to a 71-72% trough in Q4 on memory costs management says exceeded expectations and rise further next year — that is a real dent in the quality of the growth, and it is one reason I am not adding points here despite the beat. The other reason is that a ~2x-beta position at 26% into a ~60% probability of a September Fed hike is already the largest bet I can carry and still survive being wrong. The -30% stop stays wide and stays only here: it exists to survive a single-name AI-capex unwind, not to trade a market drawdown.

Held at 26% and now the only large leg whose case price has not consumed. At $346.59 it is still 15.2% below its own $408.61 high with a $428.07 consensus from 64 Strong-Buy-rated analysts implying +23.5% — a gap unchanged week-over-week, while Microsoft's halved. The quality premise is intact and I am still quoting the corrected forward multiple, not the flattered trailing one: ~26x forward, ROIC 24.9%, 60.9% gross margin, the largest net cash in the book at $121.68B, and Search/YouTube monopoly economics. What got modestly worse this week is the optionality leg of the argument, not the core: the search-antitrust remedies have been read to extend into GenAI, barring exclusive distribution contracts for the Gemini app as well as Search, Chrome and Assistant, and forcing index and user-interaction data syndication to rivals. That trims what I can claim for Gemini and Waymo as unpriced upside, so I am leaving the weight flat rather than using the widening relative-value gap versus Microsoft as an excuse to add. In a rate-hike regime the case for rotating between two correlated mega-caps is weak; the case for holding the cheaper one on its own discount and taking the difference in cash is stronger.

Cut from 25% to 20% because the specific reason I raised it five days ago no longer holds. I added on 08-22 because at $483.24 it was the cheapest mega-cap on a like-for-like forward basis and 12.7% below its own high. It is now $513.06, only 7.3% below that high, up 28% in a month, and the consensus target has moved DOWN to $560.27 from $569.56 — so upside to consensus has fallen from +17.9% to +9.2%, the thinnest in the book, below even Mastercard's. Price rising while the target falls is precisely the pattern that made me exit Visa, and I will not exempt a position from a test just because I put it on. It stays a 20% position rather than an exit because the business is nothing like Visa's: FY26 revenue $331.8B +18%, Azure +43% in Q4 and guided to 45% constant currency for Q1 FY27, past $100B annualised, commercial RPO $678B +84%, M365 Copilot at 30M paid seats against ~27M expected, ~28% ROIC and net cash. My standing reservation is also unchanged: part of the reported-return math still leans on extending datacentre depreciation from 15 to 25 years, which flatters returns on exactly the spending under question — that reservation is easier to carry at 20% than at 25% when the market is no longer paying me a valuation discount for it.

Unchanged at 13%, and I want to be explicit about why it survives a test Visa failed on a similar-looking screen. Mastercard is 1.3% below its 08-24 all-time high of $599.86 with only +13.1% to a $669.46 consensus — narrow, and on the surface the same setup. The difference is the denominator: Visa was compounding earnings at ~2% at 25.7x, Mastercard is compounding revenue at 16.4% and earnings at 16.3% with TTM EPS growth in the low twenties, and Wolfe raised its target to $740 on 08-24. A rich multiple on a 16% grower is a different animal from a rich multiple on a 2% grower. It also earns its slot structurally this week: it is the only leg in the book whose volumes do not depend on datacentre capex, and in a scenario where the Fed hikes into elevated energy-driven inflation, a near-zero-capital-intensity toll on nominal consumer spend with beta ~0.73 and no financing needs is the right thing to own alongside three long-duration mega-caps. I am not adding to it — its ~27x forward is still the richest remaining multiple in the book, and the upside gap is narrowing — but cutting my only non-AI diversifier to raise cash would have made the concentration problem worse, not better.
